<span class="atom-split" data-atom="193" data-title="CHAPTER XIII. (parte 23)" data-chapter="CHAPTER XIII." data-kind="atom" data-srclang="en"></span>

Edward had by his first wife, Eleanor of Castile, four sons; but Edward, his heir and successor, was the only one that survived him. She also bore him eleven daughters, most of whom died in their infancy: of the surviving, Joan was married first to the earl of Glocester, and after his death to Ralph de Monthermer: Margaret espoused John, duke of Brabant: Elizabeth espoused first John, earl of Holland, and afterwards the earl of Hereford: Mary was a nun at Ambresbury. He had by his second wife, Margaret of France, two sons and a daughter; Thomas, created earl of Norfolk and mareschal of England; and Edmund, who was created earl of Kent by his brother when king. The princess died in her infancy.

<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Da sua prima moglie, Eleanor di Castiglia, Edward ebbe quattro figli; ma solo Edward, suo erede e successore, gli sopravvisse. Eleanor gli diede anche undici figlie, la maggior parte delle quali morì in infanzia: tra quelle sopravvissute, Joan sposò prima l’ conte di Gloucester e, dopo la sua morte, Ralph de Monthermer; Margaret sposò Giovanni, duca di Brabante; Elisabetta sposò prima Giovanni, conte di Olanda, e poi l’ conte di Hereford; Maria divenne suora ad Ambresbury. Da sua seconda moglie, Margherita di Francia, ebbe due figli e una figlia: Thomas fu nominato conte di Norfolk e maresciallo d’Inghilterra; Edmund, invece, fu nominato conte di Kent dal fratello quando questi divenne re. La principessa morì in infanzia.

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="194" data-title="CHAPTER XIV. (parte 1)" data-chapter="CHAPTER XIV." data-kind="atom" data-srclang="en"></span>

EDWARD II.

1307.

The prepossessions entertained in favor of young Edward, kept the English from being fully sensible of the extreme loss which they had sustained by the death of the great monarch who filled the throne; and all men hastened with alacrity to take the oath of allegiance to his son and successor. This prince was in the twenty-third year of his age, was of an agreeable figure, of a mild and gentle disposition, and having never discovered a propensity to any dangerous vice, it was natural to prognosticate tranquillity and happiness from his government. But the first act of his reign blasted all these hopes, and showed him to be totally unqualified for that perilous situation in which every English monarch during those ages had, from the unstable form of the constitution, and the turbulent dispositions of the people derived from it, the misfortune to be placed. The indefatigable Robert Bruce, though his army had been dispersed, and he himself had been obliged to take shelter in the Western Isles, remained not long inactive; but before the death of the late king, had sallied from his retreat, had again collected his followers, had appeared in the field, and had obtained by surprise an important advantage over Aymer de Valence, who commanded the English forces. [1]

* Trivet, .

He was now become so considerable as to have afforded the king of England sufficient glory in subduing him, without incurring any danger of seeing all those mighty preparations, made by his father, fail in the enterprise. But Edward, instead of pursuing his advantages, marched but a little way into Scotland; and having an utter incapacity, and equal aversion, for all application or serious business, he immediately returned upon his footsteps, and disbanded his army. His grandees perceived, from this conduct, that the authority of the crown, fallen into such feeble hands, was no longer to be dreaded, and that every insolence might be practised by them with impunity.

The next measure taken by Edward gave them an inclination to attack those prerogatives which no longer kept them in awe. There was one Piers Gavaston, son of a Gascon knight of some distinction, who had honorably served the late king and who, in reward of his merits, had obtained an establishment for his son in the family of the prince of Wales. This young man soon insinuated himself into the affections of his master, by his agreeable behavior, and by supplying him with all those innocent though frivolous amusements which suited his capacity and his inclinations. He was endowed with the utmost elegance of shape and person, was noted for a fine mien and easy carriage, distinguished himself in all warlike and genteel exercises, and was celebrated for those quick sallies of wit in which his countrymen usually excel. By all these accomplishments, he gained so entire an ascendant over young Edward, whose heart was strongly disposed to [friendship](/concepts/friendship) and confidence, that the late king, apprehensive of the consequences, had banished him the kingdom, and had, before he died, made his son promise never to recall him. But no sooner did he find himself master, as he vainly imagined, than he sent for Gavaston; and even before his arrival at court, endowed him with the whole earldom of Cornwall, which had escheated to the crown by the death of Edmond, son of Richard, king of the Romans. [1] Not content with conferring on him those possessions, which had sufficed as an appanage for a prince of the blood, he daily loaded him with new honors and riches; married him to his own niece, sister of the earl of Glocester; and seemed to enjoy no pleasure in his royal dignity, but as it enabled him to exalt to the highest splendor this object of his fond affections.

* Rymer, vol. iii. . Heming. vol. i. . Walsing, p. 96.

The haughty barons, offended at the superiority of a minion, whose birth, though reputable, they despised as much inferior to their own, concealed not their discontent; and soon found reasons to justify their animosity in the character and conduct of the man they hated. Instead of disarming envy by the moderation and modesty of his behavior, Gavaston displayed his power and influence with the utmost ostentation; and deemed no circumstance of his good fortune so agreeable as its enabling him to eclipse and mortify all his rivals. He was vain-glorious, profuse, rapacious; fond of exterior pomp and appearance, giddy with prosperity; and as he imagined that his fortune was now as strongly rooted in the kingdom as his ascendant was uncontrolled over the weak monarch, he was negligent in engaging partisans, who might support his sudden and ill-established grandeur. At all tournaments he took delight in foiling the English nobility by his superior address: in every conversation he made them the object of his wit and raillery: every day his enemies multiplied upon him; and nought was wanting but a little time to cement their union, and render it fatal both to him and to his master. [1]

It behoved the king to take a journey to France, both in order to do homage for the duchy of Guienne, and to espouse the Princess Isabella, to whom he had long been affianced, though unexpected accidents had hitherto retarded the completion of the marriage. [2] Edward left Gavaston guardian of the realm, [3] with more ample powers than had usually been conferred; [4] and, on his return with his young queen, renewed all the proofs of that fond attachment to the favorite of which every one so loudly complained. This princess was of an imperious and intriguing spirit; and finding that her husband’s capacity required, as his temper inclined, him to be governed, she thought herself best entitled, on every account, to perform the office, and she contracted a mortal hatred against the person who had disappointed her in these expectations. She was well pleased, therefore, to see a combination of the nobility forming against Gavaston, who, sensible of her hatred, had wantonly provoked her by new insults and injuries.

* T. de la More, ; Walsing. .

* * T. de la More, . Trivet, Cont. .

* * * Rymer vol. iii. . Ypod. Neust. .

* * * * Brady’s App. No. 49.

1308.

Thomas, earl of Lancaster, cousin-german to the king, and first prince of the blood, was by far the most opulent and powerful subject in England, and possessed in his own right, and soon after in that of his wife, heiress of the family of Lincoln, no less than six earldoms, with a proportionable estate in land, attended with all the jurisdictions and power which commonly in that age were annexed to landed property. He was turbulent and factious in his disposition; mortally hated the favorite, whose influence over the king exceeded his own; and he soon became the head of that party among the barons who desired the depression of this insolent stranger. The confederated nobles bound themselves by oath to expel Gavaston: both sides began already to put themselves in a warlike posture: the licentiousness of the age broke out in robberies and other disorders, the usual prelude of civil war, and the royal authority, despised in the king’s own hands, and hated in those of Gavaston, became insufficient for the execution of the laws and the maintenance of peace in the kingdom. A parliament being summoned at Westminster, Lancaster and his party came thither with an armed retinue; and were there enabled to impose their own terms on the sovereign. They required the banishment of Gavaston, imposed an oath on him never to return, and engaged the bishops, who never failed to interpose in all civil concerns, to pronounce him excommunicated if he remained any longer in the kingdom. [1] Edward was obliged to submit; [2] but even in his compliance gave proofs of his fond attachment to his favorite. Instead of removing all umbrage by sending him to his own country, as was expected, he appointed him lord lieutenant of Ireland [3], attended him to Bristol on his journey thither, and before his departure conferred on him new lands and riches both in Gascony and England. [4] Gavaston, who did not want bravery, and possessed talents for war, [5] acted, during his government, with vigor against some Irish rebels, whom he subdued.

* Trivet, Cont. .

* * Rymer, vol. iii. .

* * * Rymer, vol. iii. . Murimuth, .

* * * * Rymer, vol. iii. .

<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

EDOARDO II.

1307.

Le prevenzioni a favore del giovane Edoardo impedirono agli inglesi di rendersi pienamente conto della grave perdita subita con la morte di quel grande monarca che aveva occupato il trono; tutti si affrettarono quindi ad giurare fedeltà a suo figlio e successore. Questo principe, all’età di ventitré anni, era di aspetto gradevole, dal carattere mite e gentile, e poiché non aveva mai mostrato alcuna propensione verso vizi pericolosi, sembrava naturale prevedere che il suo governo fosse caratterizzato da tranquillità e felicità. Tuttavia, il primo atto del suo regno distrusse tutte queste speranze, dimostrando chiaramente che egli era totalmente inadatto a quella pericolosa posizione nella quale ogni monarca inglese di quei tempi si trovava, a causa della struttura instabile della costituzione e delle turbolenti tendenze del popolo. Il tenace Robert Bruce, sebbene il suo esercito fosse stato disperso e lui stesso costretto a rifugiarsi nelle Isole Occidentali, non rimase a lungo inattivo; prima ancora della morte del re defunto, uscì dal suo nascondiglio, radunò di nuovo i suoi seguaci, tornò in campo e ottenne per sorpresa un importante vantaggio su Aymer de Valence, che comandava le forze inglesi. [1]

* Trivet.

Ora era diventato così potente da permettere al re d’Inghilterra di ottenere sufficiente gloria sottomettendolo, senza rischiare che tutte le imponenti preparazioni effettuate da suo padre fallissero nell’impresa. Ma Edoardo, invece di approfittare dei propri vantaggi, marciò soltanto per una breve distanza in Scozia; essendo del tutto incapace e profondamente avverso a qualsiasi impegno serio o attività diligente, tornò immediatamente indietro e sciolse il proprio esercito. I suoi nobili, osservando questo comportamento, compresero che l’autorità della corona, caduta in mani così deboli, non meritava più alcun rispetto, e che quindi potevano commettere qualsiasi atto di insolenza senza subire conseguenze.

La mossa successiva di Edoardo spinse quei giovani ad attaccare quelle prerogative che ormai non suscitavano più in loro alcun timore. C’era un certo Piers Gavaston, figlio di un nobile gascognone di qualche rilievo; aveva servito con onore il defunto re e, in ricompensa dei suoi meriti, gli era stata concessa l’opportunità che suo figlio entrasse a far parte della famiglia del principe di Galles. Questo giovane riuscì presto ad conquistare la simpatia del suo padrone grazie al proprio comportamento gradevole e fornendogli tutti quei divertimenti innocenti, sebbene frivoli, che si addicevano alle sue capacità e ai suoi gusti. Era dotato di una notevole eleganza fisica, si distingueva per il suo portamento dignitoso e aggraziato, eccelleva in tutte le attività militari e cortesi, e era famoso per la sua arguzia, caratteristica tipica dei suoi connazionali. Grazie a tutti questi meriti, riuscì ad avere una grande influenza su Edoardo, il cui cuore era particolarmente propenso alla fiducia e all’[amicizia](/concepts/friendship); tanto che il defunto re, temendo le conseguenze, lo aveva esiliato dal regno e, prima di morire, aveva fatto promettere a suo figlio di non richiamarlo mai. Ma non appena Edoardo si ritrovò, come credeva ingenuamente, al potere, mandò a chiamare Gavaston; ancora prima del suo arrivo alla corte, gli concesse l’intero ducato della Cornovaglia, che era passato alla corona in seguito alla morte di Edmondo, figlio di Riccardo re dei Romani. Non contento di avergli conferito tali possedimenti, che avrebbero potuto bastare come appannaggio a un principe di sangue reale, continuò ad onorarlo con nuove ricompense e ricchezze; lo sposò alla propria nipote, sorella dell’earl di Gloucester, e sembrava trarre piacere dalla sua dignità regale soltanto perché gli permetteva di elevare al massimo splendore l’oggetto dei suoi affetti più profondi.

* Rymer, vol. iii. Hemingway, vol. i. Walsing, p. 96.*

I vanitosi baroni, offesi dalla superiorità di un individuo il cui lignaggio, sebbene rispettabile, era considerato inferiore al loro, non nascondevano il proprio disappunto; e presto trovarono motivi per giustificare il proprio astio nel carattere e nel comportamento di quell’uomo che odiavano. Invece di placare la gelosia con la moderazione e la modestia del suo comportamento, Gavaston ostentava apertamente il proprio potere e influenza; non c’era nulla nella sua fortuna che gli sembrasse più gradito del fatto che gli permettesse di oscurare e umiliare tutti i suoi rivali. Era vanitoso, generoso in modo smisurato, avido; appassionato di pompa e apparizioni esteriori, esaltato dalla propria prosperità; e poiché riteneva che la sua fortuna fosse ormai saldamente radicata nel regno, così come il suo potere era incontrollabile su quel debole monarca, trascurò di farsi alleati che potessero sostenere la sua improvvisa e precaria grandezza. In ogni torneo si compiaceva di umiliare la nobiltà inglese con il proprio eloquio superiore; in ogni conversazione li prendeva di mira con battute e scherzi; giorno dopo giorno i suoi nemici aumentavano. Mancava soltanto un po’ di tempo perché si unissero tutti contro di lui, rendendo la loro alleanza fatale sia per lui che per il suo padrone. [1]

Era necessario che il re intraprendesse un viaggio in Francia, sia per rendere omaggio al ducato di Guienna sia per sposare la principessa Isabella, con cui da tempo era fidanzato, sebbene incidenti imprevisti avessero finora ritardato l’attuazione del matrimonio. [2] Edoardo lasciò Gavaston a custodia del regno, [3] conferendogli poteri più ampi del solito; [4] e al suo ritorno con la giovane regina, rinnovò tutte le dimostrazioni di quell’affetto profondo per la favorita di cui tutti si lamentavano così apertamente. Questa principessa era di carattere imperioso e intrigante; e avendo notato che le capacità di suo marito, unite al suo temperamento incline alla sottomissione, lo rendevano particolarmente suscettibile a essere guidato da lei, riteneva di avere ogni diritto di assumersi tale compito, e sviluppò un odio mortale verso chi aveva deluso le sue aspettative. Fu quindi molto soddisfatta quando vide formarsi una coalizione tra la nobiltà contro Gavaston, il quale, consapevole del suo odio, l’aveva deliberatamente provocata con nuove offese e ingiustizie.

* T. de la More,; Walsing..

* * T. de la More. Trivet, Cont..

* * * Rymer, volume III. Ypod. Neust.*

* * * * Appello di Brady n. 49.

1308.

Tommaso, conte di Lancaster, cugino del re e primo principe di sangue, era di gran lunga il suddito più potente ed influente d’Inghilterra. Possedeva personalmente, e poco dopo anche attraverso sua moglie – erede della famiglia Lincoln – non meno di sei contee, oltre a vasti possedimenti terrieri, accompagnati da tutti i diritti e le autorità che in quel periodo erano legati alla proprietà fondiaria. Di indole turbolenta e incline alle fazioni, odiava profondamente il favorito del re, il cui ascendente su di lui era superiore al proprio; ben presto divenne il capo di quella fazione tra i baroni che desideravano sopprimere quell’arrogante straniero. I nobili alleati si impegnarono con giuramento ad espellere Gavaston; entrambe le parti iniziarono a prepararsi alla guerra. La licenziosità dell’epoca sfociò in rapine e altri disordini, preludi tipici di una guerra civile. L’autorità reale, disprezzata dal re stesso e odiata da Gavaston, risultava insufficiente a far rispettare le leggi e mantenere la pace nel regno. Quando fu convocato un parlamento a Westminster, Lancaster e i suoi sostenitori vi si recarono con una scorta armata e riuscirono a imporre le loro condizioni al sovrano: chiesero l’esilio di Gavaston, gli imposero il giuramento di non tornare mai in Inghilterra e ottennero che i vescovi – sempre pronti ad intervenire nelle questioni civili – lo dichiarassero escomunicato qualora fosse rimasto nel regno. Edward fu costretto a cedere; tuttavia, anche nella sua sottomissione dimostrò un profondo attaccamento al suo favorito. Invece di allontanarlo mandandolo nella sua patria, come ci si aspettava, lo nominò luogotenente reale d’Irlanda, lo accompagnò fino a Bristol e, prima della sua partenza, gli concesse nuove terre e ricchezze sia in Guascogna che in Inghilterra. Gavaston, dotato di coraggio e abilità militari, agì con decisione durante il suo governo contro alcuni ribelli irlandesi, riuscendo a sottometterli.

* Trivet, Cont. *

* * Rymer, vol. iii..

* * * Rymer, vol. iii. Murimuth.

* * * * Rymer, vol. iii..

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="195" data-title="CHAPTER XIV. (parte 2)" data-chapter="CHAPTER XIV." data-kind="atom" data-srclang="en"></span>

Meanwhile, the king, less shocked with the illegal violence which had been imposed upon him, than unhappy in the absence of his minion, employed every expedient to soften the opposition of the barons to his return; as if success in that point were the chief object of his government. The high office of hereditary steward was conferred on Lancaster: his father-in-law, the earl of Lincoln, was bought off by other concessions: Earl Warrenne was also mollified by civilities, grants, or promises: the insolence of Gavaston, being no longer before men’s eyes, was less the object of general indignation; and Edward, deeming matters sufficiently prepared for his purpose, applied to the court of Rome, and obtained for Gavaston a dispensation from that oath which the barons had compelled him to take, that he would forever abjure the realm. [1] He went down to Chester to receive him on his first landing from Ireland; flew into his arms with transports of joy; and having obtained the formal consent of the barons in parliament to his reëstablishment, set no longer any bounds to his extravagant fondness and affection. Gavaston himself, forgetting his past misfortunes, and blind to their causes, resumed the same ostentation and insolence, and became more than ever the object of general detestation among the nobility.

The barons first discovered their animosity by absenting themselves from parliament; and finding that this expedient had not been successful, they began to think of employing sharper and more effectual remedies. Though there had scarcely been any national ground of complaint, except some dissipation of the public treasure: though all the acts of mal-administration objected to the king and his favorite, seemed of a nature more proper to excite heart-burnings in a ball or assembly, than commotions in a great kingdom: yet such was the situation of the times, that the barons were determined, and were able, to make them the reasons of a total alteration in the constitution and civil government. Having come to parliament, in defiance of the laws and the king’s prohibition, with a numerous retinue of armed followers, they found themselves entirely masters; and they presented a petition which was equivalent to a command, requiring Edward to devolve on a chosen junto the whole authority, both of the crown and of the parliament. The king was obliged to sign a commission, empowering the prelates and barons to elect twelve persons, who should, till the term of Michaelmas in the year following, have authority to enact ordinances for the government of the kingdom, and regulation of the king’s household; consenting that these ordinances should, thenceforth and forever have the force of laws; allowing the ordainers to form associations among themselves and their friends, for their strict and regular observance; and all this for the greater glory of God, the security of the church, and the honor and advantage of the king and kingdom. [2]

* Rymer, vol. iii. p., 167.

* * Brady’s App. No. 50. Heming. vol. i. ., Walsing. p. 97.,Ryley, .

The barons, in return signed a declaration, in which they acknowledged that they owed these concessions merely to the king’s free grace; promised that this commission should never be drawn into precedent; and engaged that the power of the ordainers should expire at the time appointed. [1]

1311.

The chosen junto accordingly framed their ordinances, and presented them to the king and parliament, for their confirmation in the ensuing year. Some of these ordinances were laudable, and tended to the regular execution of justice; such as those requiring sheriffs to be men of property, abolishing the practice of issuing privy seals for the suspension of justice, restraining the practice of purveyance, prohibiting the adulteration and alteration of the coin, excluding foreigners from the farms of the revenue, ordering all payments to be regularly made into the exchequer, revoking all late grants of the crown, and giving the parties damages in the case of vexatious prosecutions. But what chiefly grieved the king was the ordinance for the removal of evil counsellors, by which a great number of persons were by name excluded from every office of power and profit; and Piers Gavaston himself was forever banished the king’s dominions, under the penalty, in case of disobedience, of being declared a public enemy. Other persons, more agreeable to the barons, were substituted in all the offices. And it was ordained that, for the future, all the considerable dignities in the household, as well as by the law, revenue, and military governments, should be appointed by the baronage in parliament; and the power of making war, or assembling his military tenants, should no longer be vested solely in the king, nor be exercised without the consent of the nobility.

Edward, from the same weakness both in his temper and situation which had engaged him to grant this unlimited commission to the barons, was led to give a parliamentary sanction to their ordinances; but as a consequence of the same character, he secretly made a protest against them, and declared that, since the commission was granted only for the making of ordinances to the advantage of king and kingdom, such articles as should be found prejudicial to both, were to be held as not ratified and confirmed. [2]

* Brady’s App. No. 51.

* * Ryley’s Placit. Parl. , 541.

It is no wonder, indeed, that he retained a firm purpose to revoke ordinances which had been imposed on him by violence, which entirely annihilated the royal authority, and above all, which deprived him of the company and society of a person whom, by an unusual infatuation, he valued above all the world, and above every consideration of interest or tranquillity.

As soon, therefore, as Edward, removing to York, had freed himself from the immediate terror of the barons’ power, he invited back Gavaston from Flanders, which that favorite had made the place of his retreat; and declaring his banishment to be illegal, and contrary to the laws and customs of the kingdom, [1] openly reinstated him in his former credit and authority.

1312.

The barons, highly provoked at this disappointment, and apprehensive of danger to themselves from the declared animosity of so powerful a minion, saw that either his or their ruin was now inevitable; and they renewed with redoubled zeal their former confederacies against him. The earl of Lancaster was a dangerous head of this alliance; Guy, earl of Warwick, entered into it with a furious and precipitate passion; Humphrey Bohun, earl of Hereford, the constable, and Aymer de Valence, earl of Pembroke, brought to it a great accession of power and interest; even Earl Warrenne deserted the royal cause, which he had hitherto supported, and was induced to embrace the side of the confederates; [2] and as Robert de Winchelsey, archbishop of Canterbury, professed himself of the same party, he determined the body of the clergy, and consequently the people, to declare against the king and his minion. So predominant at that time was the power of the great nobility, that the combination of a few of them was always able to shake the throne; and such a universal concurrence became irresistible. The earl of Lancaster suddenly raised an army, and marched to York, where he found the king already removed to Newcastle: [3] he flew thither in pursuit of him, and Edward had just time to escape to Tinmouth, where he embarked, and sailed with Gavaston to Scarborough. He left his favorite in that fortress, which, had it been properly supplied with provisions, was deemed impregnable, and he marched forward to York, in hopes of raising an army which might be able to support him against his enemies.

* Brady’s App. No. 53. Walsing. .

* * Trivet, Cont. .

* * * Walsing. .

<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Nel frattempo, il re, meno scioccato dalla violenza illegale che gli era stata imposta che infastidito dall’assenza del suo fedele servitore, adottò ogni mezzo possibile per attenuare l’opposizione dei baroni al suo ritorno; come se il successo in questo ambito fosse lo scopo principale della sua politica. La nobile carica di amministratore ereditario fu conferita a Lancaster; suo suocero, l’ conte di Lincoln, venne corrotto con altre concessioni; anche l’ conte Warrenne fu placato attraverso cortesie, donazioni o promesse; l’arroganza di Gavaston, essendo ormai scomparsa dagli occhi di tutti, non suscitava più indignazione generale; e Edward, ritenendo che le cose fossero sufficientemente preparate per il suo scopo, si rivolse alla corte di Roma e ottenne per Gavaston l’esenzione da quel giuramento che i baroni lo avevano costretto a pronunciare, impegnandosi a rinunciare per sempre al regno. [1] Andò a Chester ad accoglierlo al suo primo sbarco dall’Irlanda; gli gettò le braccia al collo con gioia estrema; e, dopo aver ottenuto il consenso formale dei baroni in parlamento per il suo ristabilimento, non pose più limiti alla sua esagerata affezione per Gavaston. Anche Gavaston stesso, dimenticando i propri passati mali e ignorando le cause di essi, riprese la stessa ostentazione e arroganza, diventando ancora di più oggetto di generale disprezzo tra la nobiltà.

I baroni manifestarono per la prima volta il loro astio astenendosi dal partecipare al parlamento; e, constatando che questo mezzo non aveva avuto successo, iniziarono a pensare di ricorrere a soluzioni più drastiche ed efficaci. Sebbene quasi non esistessero motivi nazionali di lamentela, se non qualche spreco delle risorse pubbliche; sebbene tutti gli atti di cattiva amministrazione che venivano imputati al re e ai suoi favoriti sembrassero più adatti a suscitare indignazione in una riunione o in un banchetto che a scatenare rivolte in un grande regno; tuttavia, la situazione del momento era tale che i baroni riuscirono effettivamente a farne motivo di un radicale cambiamento nella costituzione e nel governo civile. Presentatisi al parlamento, in violazione delle leggi e dell’interdizione reale, accompagnati da un numeroso seguito armato, si trovarono completamente padroni della situazione; presentarono quindi una petizione che, di fatto, equivaleva a un ordine, esigendo che Edoardo cedesse l’intera autorità, sia quella della corona che quella del parlamento, a un gruppo scelto. Il re fu costretto a firmare un documento che autorizzava i vescovi e i baroni ad eleggere dodici persone le quali, per il periodo che andava fino al giorno di San Michele dell’anno successivo, avrebbero avuto il potere di emanare decreti per la governazione del regno e la gestione della casa reale; acconsentiva inoltre a che tali decreti avessero, da quel momento in poi e per sempre, lo stesso valore delle leggi ordinarie; permetteva infine ai responsabili dell’emanazione di tali decreti di formare associazioni tra loro e con i loro sostenitori al fine di garantirne il rispetto rigoroso e regolare. Tutto ciò veniva fatto, naturalmente, nel nome della maggiore gloria di Dio, della sicurezza della Chiesa, nonché dell’onore e del benessere del re e del regno. [2]

* Rymer, vol. iii, p. 167.*

* * Appello di Brady n. 50. Heming, vol. I, Walsing, p. 97; Ryley.

I baroni, in cambio, firmarono una dichiarazione nella quale riconoscevano di dovere queste concessioni esclusivamente alla grazia del re; promisero che tale provvedimento non sarebbe mai stato utilizzato come precedente; e si impegnarono a far scadere i poteri dei responsabili della sua attuazione nel termine stabilito. [1]

1311.

I membri selezionati redassero pertanto i loro decreti e li presentarono al re e al parlamento affinché venissero confermati nell’anno successivo. Alcuni di questi decreti erano lodevoli e miravano all’applicazione regolare della giustizia; ad esempio, quelli che imponevano ai sindaci di essere persone benestanti, abolivano la pratica di rilasciare sigilli reali per sospendere l’esecuzione delle sentenze, limitavano le pratiche di approvvigionamento, vietavano l’alterazione della moneta, escludevano gli stranieri dalle cariche pubbliche che generavano entrate, ordinavano che tutti i pagamenti venissero effettuati regolarmente presso la tesoreria reale, revocavano tutte le concessioni reali fatte in ritardo e prevedevano il risarcimento dei danni causati da azioni legali ingiuste. Tuttavia ciò che più addolorò il re fu il decreto relativo all’allontanamento dei consiglieri malvagi, con cui un gran numero di persone vennero escluse per nome da ogni carica pubblica e redditizia; inoltre Piers Gavaston stesso fu esiliato per sempre dai domini del re, con la minaccia, in caso di disobbedienza, di essere dichiarato nemico pubblico. Altre persone, più gradite ai baroni, furono nominate al posto loro in tutte queste cariche. Inoltre si stabilì che, d’ora in poi, tutte le importanti cariche all’interno della corte reale, nonché quelle legate alle entrate fiscali e al governo militare, dovessero essere assegnate dai baroni presenti in parlamento; inoltre il potere di dichiarare guerra o di radunare i propri soldati non sarebbe più stato esclusivamente nelle mani del re, ma avrebbe richiesto il consenso della nobiltà.

Edward, per la stessa debolezza sia nel suo carattere che nella sua situazione che lo avevano spinto a concedere ai baroni tale potere illimitato, fu indotto ad approvare ufficialmente i loro decreti; ma, sempre a causa di quella stessa debolezza, ne fece segretamente obiezione, dichiarando che, poiché il potere concesso era esclusivamente per l’emanazione di decreti a vantaggio del re e del regno, qualsiasi disposizione ritenuta dannosa per entrambi sarebbe stata considerata non ratificata e non confermata. [2]

* Appello di Brady n. 51.

* * Ryley’s Placit. Parl., 541.

Non c’è da meravigliarsi, dunque, che abbia mantenuto con fermezza la determinazione di revocare quegli ordini impostigli con la violenza, ordini che annientavano completamente l’autorità reale e, soprattutto, che lo privavano della compagnia e della presenza di una persona che, per un’insolita passione, considerava più preziosa di tutto il resto al mondo, e al di sopra di qualsiasi considerazione legata agli interessi personali o alla tranquillità.

Quindi, non appena Edward, trasferitosi a York, si fu liberato dal pericolo immediato rappresentato dal potere dei baroni, invitò Gavaston a tornare dalla Fiandra, dove quel suo favorito aveva scelto di ritirarsi; dichiarando illegale la sua esilio e contraria alle leggi e ai costumi del regno, [1] lo riabilitò apertamente nella sua precedente posizione di fiducia e autorità.

1312.

I baroni, profondamente offesi da questa delusione e temendo pericoli per se stessi a causa dell’ostilità dichiarata di un così potente alleato del re, compresero che la rovina sia sua che loro fosse ormai inevitabile; pertanto rinnovarono con ancora maggiore fervore le loro alleanze contro di lui. Il conte di Lancaster era il capo pericoloso di questa coalizione; Guy, conte di Warwick, vi aderì con passione furiosa e precipitosa; Humphrey Bohun, conte di Hereford, il connestabile reale, e Aymer de Valence, conte di Pembroke, ne aumentarono notevolmente la forza e l’influenza; persino il conte di Warrenne abbandonò la causa reale che aveva fino ad allora sostenuto, decidendo di schierarsi dalla parte degli alleati. Poiché anche Robert de Winchelsey, arcivescovo di Canterbury, si dichiarò a favore di loro, riuscirono a convincere l’intera classe clericale e, di conseguenza, il popolo intero a prendere posizione contro il re e il suo alleato. A quel tempo il potere della grande nobiltà era così dominante che la coalizione di pochi di loro era sempre in grado di minacciare il trono; un tale consenso generale risultava quindi insormontabile. Il conte di Lancaster radunò rapidamente un esercito e marciò verso York, dove scoprì che il re si era già rifugiato a Newcastle. Lo inseguì immediatamente, ma Edoardo riuscì appena in tempo a fuggire fino a Tinmouth, da dove imbarcò su una nave guidata da Gavaston e salpò verso Scarborough. Lasciò il proprio favorito in quella fortezza, che, se ben provvista di rifornimenti, era considerata imprendibile; egli stesso proseguì verso York nella speranza di poter radunare un esercito sufficiente a contrastare i suoi nemici.

* Appello di Brady n. 53. Walsing.

* * Trivet, Cont..

* * * Walsing.

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="196" data-title="CHAPTER XIV. (parte 3)" data-chapter="CHAPTER XIV." data-kind="atom" data-srclang="en"></span>

Pembroke was sent by the confederates to besiege the Castle of Scarborough, and Gavaston, sensible of the bad condition of his garrison, was obliged to capitulate, and to surrender himself prisoner. [1] He stipulated that he should remain in Pembroke’s hands for two months; that endeavors should, during that time, be mutually used for a general accommodation; that if the terms proposed by the barons were not accepted, the castle should be restored to him in the same condition as when he surrendered it; and that the earl of Pembroke and Henry Piercy should, by contract, pledge all their lands for the fulfilling of these conditions. [2] Pembroke, now master of the person of this public enemy, conducted him to the Castle of Dedington, near Banbury, where, on pretence of other business, he left him, protected by a feeble guard. [3] Warwick, probably in concert with Pembroke, attacked the castle: the garrison refused to make any resistance; Gavaston was yielded up to him, and conducted to Warwick Castle; the earls of Lancaster, Hereford, and Arundel immediately repaired thither; [4] and, without any regard either to the laws or the military capitulation, they ordered the head of the obnoxious favorite to be struck off by the hands of the executioner. [5]

The king had retired northward to Berwick, when he heard of Gavaston’s murder; and his resentment was proportioned to the affection which he had ever borne him while living. He threatened vengeance on all the nobility who had been active in that bloody scene; and he made preparations for war in all parts of England. But being less constant in his enmities than in his friendships, he soon after hearkened to terms of accommodation; granted the barons a pardon of all offences; and as they stipulated to ask him publicly pardon on their knees, [6] he was so pleased with these vain appearances of submission, that he seemed to have sincerely forgiven them all past injuries. But as they still pretended, notwithstanding their lawless conduct, a great anxiety for the maintenance of law, and required the establishment of their former ordinances, as a necessary security for that purpose, Edward told them that he was willing to grant them a free and legal confirmation of such of those ordinances as were not entirely derogatory to the prerogative of the crown. This answer was received for the present as satisfactory. The king’s person, after the death of Gavaston, was now become less obnoxious to the public; and as the ordinances insisted on appeared to be nearly the same with those which had formerly been extorted from Henry III. by Mountfort, and which had been attended with so many fatal consequences, they were, on that account, demanded with less vehemence by the nobility and people. The minds of all men seemed to be much appeased; the animosities of faction no longer prevailed; and England, now united under its head, would henceforth be able, it was hoped, to take vengeance on all its enemies, particularly on the Scots, whose [progress](/positions/progress) was the object of general resentment and indignation.

* Walsing, .

* * Rymer, vol ii. .

* * * T de la More, .

* * * * Dugd. Baron, vol. ii. .

* * * * * * Ryley, . Rymer, vol. iii. .

Immediately after Edward’s retreat from Scotland, Robert Bruce left his fastnesses, in which he intended to have sheltered his feeble army; and supplying his defect of strength by superior vigor and abilities, he made deep impression on all his enemies, foreign and domestic. He chased Lord Argyle and the chieftain of the Macdowals from their hills, and made himself entirely master of the high country; he thence invaded with success the Cummins in the low countries of the north: he took the castles of Inverness, Forfar, and Brechin; he daily gained some new accession of territory; and what was a more important acquisition, he daily reconciled the minds of the nobility to his dominion, and enlisted under his standard every bold leader, whom he enriched by the spoils of his enemies. Sir James Douglas, in whom commenced the greatness and renown of that warlike family, seconded him in all his enterprises: Edward Bruce, Robert’s own brother, distinguished himself by acts of valor; and the terror of the English power being now abated by the feeble conduct of the king, even the least sanguine of the Scots began to entertain hopes of recovering their independence; and the whole kingdom, except a few fortresses which he had not the means to attack, had acknowledged the authority of Robert.

In this situation, Edward had found it necessary to grant a truce to Scotland; and Robert successfully employed the interval in consolidating his power, and introducing order into the civil government, disjointed by a long continuance of wars and factions. The interval was very short; the truce, ill observed on both sides, was at last openly violated, and war recommenced with greater fury than ever. Robert, not content with defending himself, had made successful inroads into England, subsisted his needy followers by the plunder of that country, and taught them to despise the military genius of a people who had long been the object of their terror. Edward at last, roused from his lethargy, had marched an army into Scotland, and Robert, determined not to risk too much against an enemy so much superior, retired again into the mountains. The king advanced beyond Edinburgh; but being destitute of provisions, and being ill supported by the English nobility, who were then employed in framing their ordinances, he was soon obliged to retreat, without gaining any advantage over the enemy. But the appearing union of all the parties in England, after the death of Gavaston, seemed to restore that kingdom to its native force, opened again the prospect of reducing Scotland, and promised a happy conclusion to a war, in which both the interests and passions of the nation were so deeply engaged.

1314.

Edward assembled forces from all quarters, with a view of finishing at one blow this important enterprise. He summoned the most warlike of his vassals from Gascony; he enlisted troops from Flanders and other foreign countries; he invited over great numbers of the disorderly Irish as to a certain prey; he joined to them a body of the Welsh, who were actuated by like motives; and, assembling the whole military force of England, he marched to the frontiers with an army which, according to the Scotch writers, amounted to a hundred thousand men.

The army collected by Robert exceeded not thirty thousand combatants; but being composed of men who had distinguished themselves by many acts of valor, who were rendered desperate by their situation, and who were inured to all the varieties of fortune, they might justly, under such a leader, be deemed formidable to the most numerous and best appointed armies. The Castle of Stirling, which, with Berwick, was the only fortress in Scotland that remained in the hands of the English, had long been besieged by Edward Bruce: Philip de Mowbray, the governor, after an obstinate defence, was at last obliged to capitulate, and to promise, that if, before a certain day, which was now approaching, he were not relieved, he should open his gates to the enemy. [1]

* Rymer, vol. iii. .

Robert, therefore, sensible that here was the ground on which he must expect the English, chose the field of battle with all the skill and prudence imaginable, and made the necessary preparations for their reception. He posted himself at Bannockburn, about two miles from Stirling, where he had a hill on his right flank, and a morass on his left; and not content with having taken these precautions to prevent his being surrounded by the more numerous army of the English, he foresaw the superior strength of the enemy in cavalry, and made provision against it. Having a rivulet in front, he commanded deep pits to be dug along its banks, and sharp stakes to be planted in them; and he ordered the whole to be carefully covered over with turf. [1] The English arrived in sight on the evening, and a bloody conflict immediately ensued between two bodies of cavalry; where Robert, who was at the head of the Scots, engaged in single combat with Henry de Bohun, a gentleman of the family of Hereford; and at one stroke cleft his adversary to the chin with a battle-axe, in sight of the two armies. The English horse fled with precipitation to their main body.

<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Pembroke fu inviato dai confederati per assediare il Castello di Scarborough; Gavaston, consapevole delle cattive condizioni della sua guarnigione, fu costretto a capitolare e a consegnarsi prigioniero. [1] Stipulò che rimanesse nelle mani di Pembroke per due mesi; che durante quel periodo si facessero reciprocamente sforzi al fine di raggiungere un accordo generale; che, se le condizioni proposte dai baroni non venivano accettate, il castello gli fosse restituito nelle stesse condizioni in cui era stato consegnato; e che l’Earl di Pembroke e Henry Piercy impegnassero tutte le loro proprietà per garantire l’adempimento di tali condizioni. [2] Pembroke, ora padrone di questo nemico pubblico, lo portò al Castello di Dedington, vicino a Banbury; lì, con pretesti diversi, lo lasciò sotto la protezione di una guardia debole. [3] Warwick, probabilmente in accordo con Pembroke, attaccò il castello: la guarnigione rifiutò di resistere; Gavaston fu consegnato a lui e portato al Castello di Warwick; gli Earli di Lancaster, Hereford e Arundel si recarono immediatamente lì; [4] e, senza alcun rispetto né per le leggi né per i termini della capitolazione militare, ordinarono che la testa di quel detestato favorito venisse mozzata dalla mano dell’esecutore. [5]

Il re si era ritirato a nord, verso Berwick, quando venne a conoscenza dell’assassinio di Gavaston; la sua rabbia era proporzionata all’affetto che aveva sempre provato per lui in vita. Minacciò vendetta contro tutti i nobili coinvolti in quell’atto cruento e prese misure per prepararsi alla guerra in tutto l’Inghilterra. Tuttavia, essendo meno costante nelle sue ostilità che nelle sue amicizie, poco dopo acconsentì a negoziati di riconciliazione; concesse ai baroni il perdono per tutti i loro reati e, poiché questi chiesero pubblicamente il suo perdono in ginocchio, [6] fu così compiaciuto da queste vane apparenze di sottomissione che sembrò aver sinceramente perdonato tutte le offese ricevute in passato. Ma poiché continuavano a fingere, nonostante il loro comportamento illegale, un grande interesse per il mantenimento della legge e richiedevano l’attuazione delle loro precedenti ordinanze come garanzia necessaria per questo scopo, Edoardo rispose che era disposto ad approvare legalmente quelle ordinanze che non fossero completamente lesive dei privilegi della corona. Questa risposta fu considerata, per il momento, soddisfacente. Dopo la morte di Gavaston, la figura del re aveva perso in parte il suo carattere ostile per il popolo; inoltre, poiché le nuove ordinanze sembravano essere quasi identiche a quelle che in passato erano state imposte da Mountfort su Enrico III e che avevano avuto conseguenze così tragiche, i nobili e il popolo le chiesero con minore veemenza. L’atmosfera generale sembrava essersi calmata; le ostilità tra fazioni erano scomparse e si sperava che l’Inghilterra, ora unita sotto un unico sovrano, potesse finalmente vendicarsi di tutti i suoi nemici, in particolare degli scozzesi, il cui [progresso](/positions/progress) suscitava generale indignazione.

* Walsing.

* * Rymer, vol. II..

* * * T de la More.

* * * * Dugd. Baron, vol. ii..

* * * * * * Ryley. Rymer, vol. iii..

Immediatamente dopo la ritirata di Edoardo dalla Scozia, Roberto Bruce abbandonò le sue fortezze, nelle quali aveva intenzione di rifugiare il proprio esercito debole; compensando la mancanza di forze con un vigore e delle capacità superiori, lasciò una profonda impressione su tutti i suoi nemici, sia stranieri che nazionali. Inseguì Lord Argyle e il capo dei Macdowals dalle loro montagne, assumendo così il controllo totale della regione montuosa; successivamente invase con successo le zone pianeggianti del nord, conquistando i castelli di Inverness, Forfar e Brechin. Ogni giorno acquisiva nuovi territori; cosa ancora più importante, riusciva a far sì che la nobiltà accettasse il suo dominio e che ogni leader coraggioso si unisse alle sue forze, arricchendosi con i bottini ottenuti dai nemici. Sir James Douglas, da cui ebbe inizio la grandezza e la fama di quella nobile famiglia guerriera, lo aiutò in tutte le sue imprese; Edoardo Bruce, fratello stesso di Roberto, si distinse per i suoi atti di coraggio. Ora che la minaccia rappresentata dall’Inghilterra era diminuita a causa della debole condotta del re, anche i più scettici tra i Scozzesi iniziarono ad nutrire speranze di riconquistare la propria indipendenza; l’intero regno, ad eccezione di alcune fortezze che Robert non aveva i mezzi per attaccare, aveva riconosciuto la sua autorità.

In questa situazione, Edward ritenne necessario concedere una tregua alla Scozia; Robert, intanto, sfruttò al meglio questo periodo per rafforzare il proprio potere e ripristinare l’ordine nel governo civile, distrutto da lunghi anni di guerre e lotte interne. Tuttavia, la tregua fu scarsamente rispettata da entrambe le parti e, alla fine, venne apertamente violata; la guerra ricominciò quindi con ancora maggiore intensità di prima. Robert, non accontentandosi di difendersi, riuscì anche ad avanzare in Inghilterra, sostenendo i propri seguaci attraverso il saccheggio di quel paese e insegnando loro a disprezzare il genio militare di un popolo che da tempo era oggetto del loro terrore. Alla fine, Edward, risvegliatosi dal proprio letargo, inviò un esercito in Scozia; Robert, però, deciso a non correre troppi rischi contro un nemico così superiore, si ritirò nuovamente nelle montagne. Il re avanzò fino a Edimburgo, ma, a causa della mancanza di rifornimenti e del sostegno insufficiente da parte della nobiltà inglese impegnata in quel momento nella stesura delle proprie leggi, fu costretto a ritirarsi senza ottenere alcun vantaggio sugli avversari. Tuttavia, l’unione apparentemente totale di tutte le fazioni in Inghilterra, dopo la morte di Gavaston, sembrava restituire a quel regno la sua forza originaria; ciò riapriva nuove possibilità per sottomettere la Scozia e prometteva una conclusione felice per una guerra nella quale gli interessi e le passioni dell’intera nazione erano profondamente coinvolti.

1314.

Eduardo radunò truppe da tutte le direzioni, con l’intento di portare a termine questa importante impresa in un solo colpo. Chiamò i suoi vassalli più bellicosi dalla Guascogna; reclutò soldati dalle Fiandre e da altri paesi stranieri; invitò un gran numero di irlandesi disordinati, offrendo loro una preda comune; li unì a un gruppo di gallezi motivati dagli stessi scopi; e, radunando l’intera forza militare d’Inghilterra, marciò verso i confini con un esercito che, secondo gli scrittori scozzesi, contava centomila uomini.

L’esercito radunato da Robert non superava i trentamila combattenti; tuttavia, essendo composto da uomini che si erano distinti per numerosi atti di coraggio, che erano ridotti alla disperazione dalla loro situazione e che erano abituati a tutte le avversità della vita, sotto un tale comandante poteva essere considerato davvero temibile anche rispetto agli eserciti più numerosi e meglio organizzati. Il Castello di Stirling, insieme a Berwick, era l’unica fortezza in Scozia rimasta sotto il controllo inglese; da tempo era assediato da Edward Bruce. Il governatore, Philip de Mowbray, dopo una resistenza tenace, fu infine costretto a capitolare e promise che, se entro una data prestabilita non avesse ricevuto rinforzi, avrebbe aperto le porte al nemico. [1]

* Rymer, vol. iii.*

Robert, consapevole che proprio su questo terreno avrebbe dovuto affrontare gli inglesi, scelse il campo di battaglia con tutta la abilità e la prudenza possibili, e prese le necessarie misure per prepararsi al loro arrivo. Si posizionò a Bannockburn, a circa due miglia da Stirling: sul suo fianco destro c’era una collina, mentre a sinistra si estendeva un pantano. Non accontentandosi di queste precauzioni per evitare di essere circondato dall’esercito più numeroso degli inglesi, prevedette anche la loro superiorità in termini di cavalleria e predispose le contromisure necessarie. Davanti al suo schieramento scorreva un ruscello; ordinò quindi di scavare profonde fosse lungo le sue rive e di piantarvi stecche appuntite, facendo poi in modo che tutto venisse accuratamente coperto di erba. [1] Gli inglesi apparvero alla sera e subito scoppiò un violento scontro tra due formazioni di cavalleria; Robert, che guidava le truppe scozzesi, entrò in singolo duello con Henry de Bohun, un nobile della famiglia Hereford, e con un colpo di ascia gli tagliò la gola davanti agli occhi di entrambi gli eserciti. La cavalleria inglese fuggì precipitosamente verso il proprio corpo principale.

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="197" data-title="CHAPTER XIV. (parte 4)" data-chapter="CHAPTER XIV." data-kind="atom" data-srclang="en"></span>

The Scots, encouraged by this favorable event, and glorying in the valor of their prince, prognosticated a happy issue to the combat on the ensuing day: the English, confident in their numbers, and elated with former successes, longed for an opportunity of revenge; and the night, though extremely short in that season and in that climate, appeared tedious to the impatience of the several combatants. Early in the morning, Edward drew out his army, and advanced towards the Scots. The earl of Glocester, his nephew, who commanded the left wing of the cavalry, impelled by the ardor of youth, rushed on to the attack without precaution, and fell among the covered pits, which had been prepared by Bruce for the reception of the enemy. [2] This body of horse was disordered; Glocester himself was overthrown and slain: Sir James Douglas, who commanded the Scottish cavalry, gave the enemy no leisure to rally, but pushed them off the field with considerable loss, and pursued them in sight of their whole line of infantry. While the English army were alarmed with this unfortunate beginning of the action, which commonly proves decisive, they observed an army on the heights towards the left, which seemed to be marching leisurely in order to surround them; and they were distracted by their multiplied fears. This was a number of wagoners and sumpter boys, whom Robert had collected; and having supplied them with military standards, gave them the appearance at a distance of a formidable body.

* T. de la More, .

* * T. de la More, .

The stratagem took effect: a panic seized the English: they threw down their arms and fled: they were pursued with great slaughter for the space of ninety miles, till they reached Berwick: and the Scots, besides an inestimable booty, took many persons of quality prisoners, and above four hundred gentlemen, whom Robert treated with great humanity, [1] and whose ransom was a new accession of wealth to the victorious army. The king himself narrowly escaped by taking shelter in Dunbar, whose gates were opened to him by the earl of March; and he thence passed by sea to Berwick.

* Ypod. Neust. .

Such was the great and decisive battle of Bannockburn, which secured the independence of Scotland, fixed Bruce on the throne of that kingdom, and may be deemed the greatest overthrow that the English nation, since the conquest, has ever received. The number of slain on those occasions is always uncertain, and is commonly much magnified by the victors: but this defeat made a deep impression on the mind of the English; and it was remarked that, for some years, the superiority of numbers could encourage them to keep the field against the Scots. Robert, in order to avail himself of his present success, entered England, and ravaged all the northern counties without opposition: he besieged Carlisle; but that place was saved by the valor of Sir Andrew Harcla, the governor: he was more successful against Berwick, which he took by assault: and this prince, elated by his continued prosperity, now entertained hopes of making the most important conquests on the English.

1315.

He sent over his brother Edward, with an army of six thousand men, into Ireland; and that nobleman assumed the title of king of that island; he himself followed soon after with more numerous forces: the horrible and absurd oppressions which the Irish suffered under the English government, made them, at first, fly to the standard of the Scots, whom they regarded as their deliverers: but a grievous famine, which at that time desolated both Ireland and Britain, reduced the Scottish army to the greatest extremities; and Robert was obliged to return, with his forces much diminished, into his own country. His brother, after having experienced a variety or fortune, was defeated and slain near Dundalk by the English, commanded by Lord Bermingham: and these projects, too extensive for the force of the Scottish nation, thus vanished into smoke.

Edward, besides suffering those disasters from the invasion of the Scots and the insurrection of the Irish, was also infested with a rebellion in Wales; and above all, by the factions of his own nobility, who took advantage of the public calamities, insulted his fallen fortunes, and endeavored to establish their own independence on the ruins of the throne. Lancaster and the barons of his party, who had declined attending him on his Scottish expedition, no sooner saw him return with disgrace, than they insisted on the renewal of their ordinances, which, they still pretended, had validity; and the king’s unhappy situation obliged him to submit to their demands. The ministry was new-modelled by the direction of Lancaster: [1] that prince was placed at the head of the council: it was declared, that all the offices should be filled, from time to time, by the votes of parliament, or rather by the will of the great barons: [2] and the nation, under this new model of government, endeavored to put itself in a better posture of defence against the Scots. But the factious nobles were far from being terrified with the [progress](/positions/progress) of these public enemies: on the contrary, they founded the hopes of their own future grandeur on the weakness and distresses of the crown: Lancaster himself was suspected, with great appearance of reason, of holding a secret correspondence with the king of Scots: and though he was intrusted with the command of the English armies, he took care that every enterprise should be disappointed, and every plan of operations prove unsuccessful.

* Ryley, p, 560. Rymer, vol. iii. .

* * Brady vol. ii. , from the records, App. No. 61. Ryley .

All the European kingdoms, especially that of England, were at this time unacquainted with the office of a prime minister, so well understood at present in all regular monarchies; and the people could form no conception of a man who, though still in the rank of a subject, possessed all the power of a sovereign, eased the prince of the burden of affairs, supplied his want of experience or capacity, and maintained all the rights of the crown, without degrading the greatest nobles by their submission to his temporary authority. Edward was plainly by nature unfit to hold himself the reins of government: he had no vices, but was unhappy in a total incapacity for serious business: he was sensible of his own defects, and necessarily sought to be governed: yet every favorite whom he successively chose, was regarded as a fellow-subject exalted above his rank and station: he was the object of envy to the great nobility: his character and conduct were decried with the people: his authority over the king and kingdom was considered as a usurpation: and unless the prince had embraced the dangerous expedient of devolving his power on the earl of Lancaster, or some mighty baron, whose family interest was so extensive as to be able alone to maintain his influence, he could expect no peace or tranquillity upon the throne.

The king’s chief favorite, after the death of Gavaston, was Hugh le Despenser, or Spenser, a young man of English birth, of high rank, and of a noble family. [1] He possessed all the exterior accomplishments of person and address which were fitted to engage the weak mind of Edward; but was destitute of that moderation and prudence which might have qualified him to mitigate the envy of the great, and conduct him through all the perils of that dangerous station to which he was advanced. His father, who was of the same name, and who, by means of his son, had also attained great influence over the king, was a nobleman venerable from his years, respected through all his past life for wisdom, valor, and integrity, and well fitted by his talents and experience, could affairs have admitted of any temperament, to have supplied the defects both of the king and of his minion. [2] But no sooner was Edward’s attachment declared for young Spenser, than the turbulent Lancaster, and most of the great barons, regarded him as their rival, made him the object of their animosity, and formed violent plans for his ruin. [3] They first declared their discontent by withdrawing from parliament; and it was not long ere they found a pretence for proceeding to greater extremities against him.

1321.

The king, who set no limits to his bounty toward his minions, had married the younger Spenser to his niece one of the coheirs of the earl of Glocester, slain at Bannockburn. The favorite, by his succession to that opulent family, had inherited great possessions in the marches of Wales, [4] and being desirous of extending still farther his influence in those quarters, he is accused of having committed injustice on the barons of Audley and Ammori, who had also married two sisters of the same family.

* Dugd. Baron, vol. i. .

* * T. de la More, .

<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Gli scozzesi, incoraggiati da questo evento favorevole e orgogliosi del coraggio del loro principe, presagirono che la battaglia del giorno seguente avrebbe avuto esito positivo; gli inglesi, fiduciosi nel proprio numero e esaltati dai precedenti successi, anelavano all’opportunità di vendicarsi. La notte, sebbene estremamente breve in quella stagione e in quel clima, sembrò interminabile agli impazienti combattenti di entrambe le parti. All’alba, Edoardo schierò il proprio esercito e avanzò verso gli scozzesi. Il conte di Glocester, suo nipote e comandante dell’aquila sinistra della cavalleria, spinto dall’ardore giovanile, attaccò senza prendere alcuna precauzione e finì tra le trappole preparate da Bruce per l’invasore. Questo reparto di cavalleria si disordinò; lo stesso Glocester fu rovesciato a terra e ucciso. Sir James Douglas, comandante della cavalleria scozzese, non diede all’avversario il tempo di riorganizzarsi, spingendolo fuori dal campo con notevoli perdite e inseguendolo fino alla linea completa delle loro truppe di fanteria. Mentre l’esercito inglese era sconvolto da questo infausto inizio della battaglia, che di solito si rivela decisivo, notarono un altro esercito sulle alture a sinistra, che sembrava avanzare lentamente con l’intento di circondarli; ciò li gettò nel panico. In realtà si trattava di un gruppo di carrettieri e ragazzi addetti al trasporto delle provviste, radunati da Roberto; a questi ultimi furono forniti stendardi militari, il che dava loro, da lontano, l’aspetto di una formazione potente.

* T. de la More.

* * T. de la More.

La strategia ebbe successo: il panico si impadronì degli inglesi, che abbandonarono le armi e fuggirono. Furono inseguiti con grande violenza per una distanza di novanta miglia, fino a quando non raggiunsero Berwick. Gli scozzesi, oltre a un bottino inestimabile, catturarono molti personaggi di rilievo e oltre quattrocento gentiluomini, i quali furono trattati con grande umanità da Robert; il riscatto di questi prigionieri rappresentò un ulteriore arricchimento per l’esercito vittorioso. Il re stesso riuscì a salvarsi per un soffio rifugiandosi a Dunbar, le cui porte gli furono aperte dal conte di March; da lì proseguì via mare verso Berwick.

* Ypod. Neust..

Ecco dunque la grande e decisiva battaglia di Bannockburn, che assicurò l’indipendenza della Scozia, pose Roberto sul trono di quel regno e può essere considerata la più grave sconfitta subita dalla nazione inglese dai tempi della conquista. Il numero delle vittime in tali occasioni è sempre incerto e solitamente viene molto esagerato dai vincitori; tuttavia questa sconfitta lasciò un profondo segno nell’animo degli inglesi. Si notò che, per alcuni anni, il loro vantaggio numerico li spinse a continuare la lotta contro gli scozzesi. Roberto, volendo approfittare del proprio successo, entrò in Inghilterra e devastò tutte le contee settentrionali senza incontrare resistenza; assediò Carlisle, ma quella città fu salvata dal coraggio di Sir Andrew Harcla, il suo governatore. Riuscì anche a prendere Berwick con un attacco diretto; e questo principe, esaltato dai continui successi, iniziò ora ad alimentare speranze di ottenere le più importanti vittorie sugli inglesi.

1315.

Inviò suo fratello Edward, con un esercito di sei migliaia di uomini, in Irlanda; quel nobile assunse il titolo di re di quell’isola; poco dopo lo seguì egli stesso con forze ancora più numerose. Le orribili e assurde oppressioni subite dagli irlandesi sotto il governo inglese li spinsero, in un primo momento, a schierarsi sotto la bandiera degli scozzesi, che consideravano i loro salvatori; ma una grave carestia, che all’epoca devastò sia l’Irlanda che la Britannia, ridusse l’esercito scozzese alle più estreme difficoltà; Robert fu quindi costretto a ritornare nel proprio paese con le sue forze notevolmente indebolite. Suo fratello, dopo aver vissuto varie avventure, fu sconfitto e ucciso vicino a Dundalk dagli inglesi comandati da Lord Bermingham; così, questi progetti, troppo ambiziosi rispetto alle forze della nazione scozzese, svanirono nel nulla.

Edward, oltre ad aver subito le calamità causate dall’invasione degli scozzesi e dalla rivolta irlandese, si trovava anche di fronte a una ribellione in Galles; inoltre, le fazioni della sua stessa nobiltà approfittavano delle difficoltà pubbliche per insultare la sua sfortunata situazione e cercare di stabilire la propria indipendenza sulle rovine del trono. I membri del partito di Lancaster, che avevano rifiutato di seguirlo nell’impresa scozzese, non appena lo videro tornare in disgrazia, insistettero affinché venissero ripristinati gli ordini che, a loro dire, erano ancora validi; la sfortunata condizione del re lo costrinse ad accettare queste richieste. Il governo fu riformato su indicazioni di Lancaster: [1] quel principe fu posto a capo del consiglio; si decise che tutti gli incarichi dovessero essere assegnati, di tanto in tanto, tramite il voto del parlamento o, più precisamente, per volontà dei grandi baroni; [2] sotto questo nuovo sistema di governo, la nazione cercò di migliorare le proprie difese contro gli scozzesi. Tuttavia, i nobili divisi in fazioni non erano affatto spaventati dal “[progresso](/positions/progress)” di questi nemici pubblici: al contrario, fondavano le loro speranze per il proprio futuro su debolezze e difficoltà della corona. Lancaster stesso fu sospettato, con buone ragioni, di intrattenere una corrispondenza segreta con il re degli scozzesi; e sebbene gli fosse stato affidato il comando delle armate inglesi, si assicurò che ogni iniziativa fallisse e che ogni piano operativo risultasse inefficace.

* Ryley, p. 560. Rymer, vol. iii. *

* * Brady, vol. II, dagli atti, Appendice n. 61. Ryley. * *

In quel periodo, tutti i regni europei, in particolare quello d’Inghilterra, non conoscevano ancora la figura del primo ministro, così ben definita nelle monarchie moderne; il popolo non riusciva nemmeno a immaginare l’esistenza di una persona che, pur essendo un suddito come tutti gli altri, possedesse in realtà tutti i poteri di un sovrano: una figura in grado di alleviare il principe dal peso delle responsabilità governative, di compensarne la mancanza di esperienza o capacità, e di mantenere tutti i diritti della corona, senza per questo umiliare i nobili più influenti sottomettendoli al proprio potere temporaneo. Edward, per natura, non era adatto a ricoprire il ruolo di sovrano: non aveva vizi particolari, ma era del tutto incapace di gestire gli affari di stato in modo serio; era consapevole dei propri difetti e quindi cercava inevitabilmente qualcuno che lo guidasse. Tuttavia, ogni favorito che sceglieva veniva considerato un suddito elevato al di sopra del proprio rango sociale; suscitava invidia tra i nobili e il suo comportamento era criticato dal popolo; il suo potere sul re e sul regno veniva visto come un’usurpazione. Se non avesse adottato la rischiosa soluzione di affidare i propri poteri al conte di Lancaster o a qualche altro nobile influente, non avrebbe mai potuto godere di pace e stabilità sul trono.

Dopo la morte di Gavaston, il favorito principale del re fu Hugh le Despenser, un giovane di origine inglese, di alto rango e appartenente a una nobile famiglia. [1] Possedeva tutte quelle qualità esteriori – aspetto fisico e modo di comportarsi – che potevano attrarre l’attenzione del debole carattere di Edoardo; tuttavia, gli mancavano la moderazione e la prudenza necessarie per mitigare l’invidia dei potenti e superare i pericoli legati a quella posizione pericolosa che aveva raggiunto. Suo padre, omonimo, grazie al figlio aveva anch’egli acquisito grande influenza sul re; era un nobile rispettabile per la sua età, stimato per saggezza, coraggio e integrità nel corso della sua vita, e le sue capacità e esperienza avrebbero potuto compensare i difetti sia del re che del suo favorito. [2] Ma non appena Edoardo iniziò a mostrare un particolare affetto per il giovane Spenser, i baroni Lancaster e molti altri nobili lo considerarono un rivale e ne fecero oggetto della loro ostilità, elaborando piani violenti per la sua rovina. [3] Iniziarono manifestando il loro dissenso ritirandosi dal parlamento; poco dopo trovarono una scusa per prendere misure ancora più drastiche contro di lui.

1321.

Il re, che non impondeva limiti alla sua generosità nei confronti dei suoi sottoposti, aveva sposato la figlia minore di Spenser con sua nipote, una delle eredi del conte di Glocester ucciso a Bannockburn. Essendo diventato membro di quella ricca famiglia, il favorito del re aveva ereditato vaste possedimenti nelle marche del Galles; desideroso di estendere ulteriormente la propria influenza in quelle regioni, è accusato di aver commesso ingiustizie nei confronti dei baroni di Audley e Ammori, i quali avevano anch’essi sposato due sorelle della stessa famiglia.

* Dugd. Baron, vol. I. *

* * T. de la More.

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="198" data-title="CHAPTER XIV. (parte 5)" data-chapter="CHAPTER XIV." data-kind="atom" data-srclang="en"></span>

* * * Walsing. . T. de la More, . Murimuth, .

* * * * Trivet, Cont. .

There was likewise a baron in that neighborhood, called William de Braouse, lord of Gower, who had made a settlement of his estate on John de Mowbray, his son-in-law; and in case of failure of that nobleman and his issue, had substituted the earl of Hereford in the succession to the barony of Gower. Mowbray, on the decease of his father-in-law, entered immediately in [possession](/concepts/property) of the estate, without the formality of taking livery and seizin from the crown; but Spenser, who coveted that barony, persuaded the king to put in execution the rigor of the feudal law, to seize Gower as escheated to the crown, and to confer it upon him. [1] This transaction, which was the proper subject of a lawsuit, immediately excited a civil war in the kingdom. The earls of Lancaster and Hereford flew to arms: Audle and Ammori joined them with all their forces: the two Rogers de Mortimer and Roger de Clifford, with many others, disgusted for private reasons at the Spensers, brought a considerable accession to the party; and their army being now formidable, they sent a message to the king, requiring him immediately to dismiss or confine the younger Spenser; and menacing him, in case of refusal, with renouncing their allegiance to him, and taking revenge on that minister by their own authority. They scarcely waited for an answer; but immediately fell upon the lands of young Spenser, which they pillaged and destroyed; murdered his servants, drove off his cattle, and burned his houses. [2] They thence proceeded to commit like devastations on the estates of Spenser the father, whose character they had hitherto seemed to respect. And having drawn and signed a formal association among themselves, [3] they marched to London with all their forces, stationed themselves in the neighborhood of that city, and demanded of the king the banishment of both the Spensers.

* Monach. Malms.

* * Murimuth, .

* * * Tyrrel, vol. ii , from the register of C. C. Canterbury.

These noblemen were then absent; the father abroad, the son at sea; and both of them employed in different commissions: the king therefore replied, that his coronation oath, by which he was bound to observe the laws, restrained him from giving his assent to so illegal a demand, or condemning noblemen who were accused of no crime, nor had any opportunity afforded them of making answer. [1] Equity and reason were but a feeble opposition to men who had arms in their hands, and who, being already involved in guilt, saw no safety but in success and victory. They entered London with their troops; and giving in to the parliament, which was then sitting, a charge against the Spensers, of which they attempted not to prove one article, they procured, by menaces and violence, a sentence of attainder and perpetual exile against these ministers. [2] This sentence was voted by the lay barons alone; for the commons, though now an estate in parliament, were yet of so little consideration, that their assent was not demanded; and even the votes of the prelates were neglected amidst the present disorders. The only symptom which these turbulent barons gave of their regard to law, was their requiring from the king an indemnity for their illegal proceedings; [3] after which they disbanded their army, and separated, in security, as they imagined, to their several castles.

This act of violence, in which the king was obliged to acquiesce, rendered his person and his authority so contemptible, that every one thought himself entitled to treat him with neglect. The queen, having occasion soon after to pass by the castle of Leeds in Kent, which belonged to the lord Badlesmere, desired a night’s lodging, but was refused admittance; and some of her attendants, who presented themselves at the gate, were killed. [4] The insult upon this princess, who had always endeavored to live on good terms with the barons, and who joined them heartily in their hatred of the young Spenser, was an action which nobody pretended to justify; and the king thought that he might, without giving general umbrage, assemble an army, and take vengeance on the offender. No one came to the assistance of Badlesmere; and Edward prevailed. [5]

* Walsing. .

* * Tottle’s Collect, part ii . Walsing. .

* * * Tottle’s Collect, part ii. . Rymer, vol. iii. .

* * * * Rymer, vol. iii. . Walsing. , 115. T. de la Mare, . Murimuth, .

But having now some forces on foot, and having concerted measures with his friends throughout England, he ventured to take off the mask, to attack all his enemies, and to recall the two Spensers, whose sentence he declared illegal, unjust, contrary to the tenor of the Great Charter, passed without the assent of the prelates, and extorted by violence from him and the estate of barons. [1] Still the commons were not mentioned by either party.

1322.

The king had now got the start of the barons, an advantage which, in those times, was commonly decisive, and he hastened with his army to the marches of Wales, the chief seat of the power of his enemies, whom he found totally unprepared for resistance. Many of the barons in those parts endeavored to appease him by submission: [2] their castles were seized, and their persons committed to custody. But Lancaster, in order to prevent the total ruin of his party, summoned together his vassals and retainers; declared his alliance with Scotland, which had long been suspected; received the promise of a reënforcement from that country, under the command of Randolf, earl of Murray, and Sir James Douglas; [3] and being joined by the earl of Hereford, advanced with all his forces against the king, who had collected an army of thirty thousand men, and was superior to his enemies. Lancaster posted himself at Burton upon Trent, and endeavored to defend the passages of the river: [4] but being disappointed in that plan of operations, this prince, who had no military genius, and whose personal courage was even suspected, fled with his army to the north, in expectation of being there joined by his Scottish allies. [5] He was pursued by the king, and his army diminished daily, till he came to Boroughbridge, where he found Sir Andrew Harcla posted with some forces on the opposite side of the river, and ready to dispute the passage with him. He was repulsed in an attempt which he made to force his way: the earl of Hereford was killed; the whole army of the rebels was disconcerted: Lancaster himself was become incapable of taking any measures either for flight or defence; and he was seized without resistance by Harcla, and conducted to the king. [6]

* Rymer, vol. iii. . T. de la More, .

* * Walsing. . Murimuth, .

* * * Rymer, vol. iii. .

* * * * Walsing. .

* * * * * * T. de la More, . Walsing. .

In those violent times, the laws were so much neglected on both sides, that, even where they might, without any sensible inconvenience, have been observed, the conquerors deemed it unnecessary to pay any regard to them. Lancaster, who was guilty of open rebellion, and was taken in arms against his sovereign, instead of being tried by the laws of his country, which pronounced the sentence of death against him, was condemned by a court-martial, [1] and led to execution. Edward, however, little vindictive in his natural temper, here indulged his revenge, and employed against the prisoner the same indignities which had been exercised by his orders against Gavaston. He was clothed in a mean attire, placed on a lean jade without a bridle, a hood was put on his head, and in this posture, attended by the acclamations of the people, this prince was conducted to an eminence near Pomfret, one of his own castles, and there beheaded. [2]

* Tyrrel, vol. 11. .

* * Leland’s Coll. vol. i. .
