Anne Ascue, una giovane donna di merito e [bellezza](/concepts/beauty), che aveva stretti legami con le principali dame di corte e con la stessa regina, fu accusata di professare opinioni dogmatiche su tale delicato argomento; e Enrico, invece di mostrare indulgenza verso la debolezza del suo sesso e della sua età, ne fu ancora più offeso, che una donna osasse opporsi ai suoi convincimenti teologici.

* Burnet, vol. I, p. 344. “Antiquities of Britain” durante la vita di Cranmer.*

* * Bale. Velocità, *

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="402" data-title="CHAPTER XXXIII. (parte 8)" data-chapter="CHAPTER XXXIII." data-kind="atom" data-srclang="en"></span>

She was prevailed on by Bonner’s menaces to make a seeming recantation; but she qualified it with some reserves, which did not satisfy that zealous prelate. She was thrown into prison, and she there employed herself in composing prayers and discourses, by which she fortified her resolution to endure the utmost extremity rather than relinquish her religious principles. She even wrote to the king, and told him, that as to the Lord’s supper, she believed as much as Christ himself had said of it, and as much of his divine doctrine as the Catholic church had required: but while she could not be brought to acknowledge an assent to the king’s explications, this declaration availed her nothing, and was rather regarded as a fresh insult. The chancellor, Wriothesely, who had succeeded Audley, and who was much attached to the Catholic party, was sent to examine her with regard to her patrons at court, and the great ladies who were in correspondence with her: but she maintained a laudable fidelity to her friends, and would confess nothing. She was put to the torture in the most barbarous manner, and continued still resolute in preserving secrecy. Some authors [1] add an extraordinary circumstance; that the chancellor, who stood by, ordered the lieutenant of the Tower to stretch the rack still farther; but that officer refused compliance the chancellor menaced him, but met with a new refusal; upon which that magistrate, who was otherwise a person of merit, but intoxicated with religious zeal, put his own hand to the rack, and drew it so violently that he almost tore her body asunder. Her constancy still surpassed the barbarity of her persecutors, and they found all their efforts to be baffled. She was then condemned to be burned alive; and being so dislocated by the rack that she could not stand, she was carried to the stake in a chair. Together with her were conducted Nicholas Belenian, a priest, John Lassels, of the king’s household, and John Adams, a tailor, who had been condemned for the same crime to the same punishment. They were all tied to the stake; and in that dreadful situation the chancellor sent to inform them, that their pardon was ready drawn and signed, and should instantly be given them if they would merit it by a recantation. They only regarded this offer as a new ornament to their crown of martyrdom; and they saw with tranquillity the executioner kindle the flames which consumed them. Wriothesely did not consider, that this public and noted situation interested their honor the more to maintain a steady perseverance.

* Fox, ii. . Speed, . Baker, . But Burnet questions the truth of this circumstance; Fox, however, transcribes her own papers, where she relates it. I

must add, in justice to the king, that he disapproved of Wriothesely’s conduct, and commended the lieutenant.

Though the secrecy and fidelity of Anne Ascue saved the queen from this peril, that princess soon after fell into a new danger, from which she narrowly escaped. An ulcer had broken out in the king’s leg, which, added to his extreme corpulency and his bad [habit](/concepts/custom) of body, began both to threaten his life and to render him even more than usually peevish and passionate. The queen attended him with the most tender and dutiful care, and endeavored, by every soothing art and compliance, to allay those gusts of humor to which he was become so subject. His favorite topic of conversation was theology; and Catharine, whose good sense enabled her to discourse on any subject, was frequently engaged in the argument, and being secretly inclined to the principles of the reformers, she unwarily betrayed too much of her mind on these occasions. Henry, highly provoked that she should presume to differ from him, complained of her obstinacy to Gardiner, who gladly laid hold of the opportunity to inflame the quarrel. He praised the king’s anxious concern for preserving the orthodoxy of his subjects; and represented, that the more elevated the person was who was chastised, and the more near to his person, the greater terror would the example strike into every one, and the more glorious would the sacrifice appear to posterity. The chancellor, being consulted, was engaged by religious zeal to second these topics; and Henry, hurried on by his own impetuous temper, and encouraged by his counsellors, went so far as to order articles of impeachment to be drawn up against his consort. Wriothesely executed his commands; and soon after brought the paper to him to be signed; for, as it was high treason to throw slander upon the queen, he might otherwise have been questioned for his temerity. By some means this important paper fell into the hands of one of the queen’s friends, who immediately carried the intelligence to her. She was sensible of the extreme danger to which she was exposed; but did not despair of being able, by her prudence and address, still to elude the efforts of her enemies. She paid her usual visit to the king, and found him in a more serene disposition than she had reason to expect. He entered on the subject which was so familiar to him; and he seemed to challenge her to an argument in divinity. She gently declined the conversation, and remarked, that such profound speculations were ill suited to the natural imbecility of her sex. Women, she said, by their first creation, were made subject to men: the male was created after the image of God, the female after the image of the male: it belonged to the husband to choose principles for his wife; the wife’s duty was, in all cases, to adopt implicitly the sentiments of her husband: and as to herself, it was doubly her duty, being blest with a husband who was qualified by his judgment and learning not only to choose principles for his own family, but for the most wise and knowing of every nation. “Not so! by St. Mary,” replied the king; “you are now become a doctor, Kate, and better fitted to give than receive instruction.” She meekly replied, that she was sensible how little she was entitled to these praises; that though she usually declined not any conversation, however [sublime](/concepts/sublime), when proposed by his majesty, she well knew that her conceptions could serve to no other purpose than to give him a little momentary amusement, that she found the conversation apt to languish when not revived by some opposition, and she had ventured sometimes to feign a contrariety of sentiments, in order to give him the pleasure of refuting her; and that she also purposed, by this innocent artifice, to engage him into topics, whence she had observed, by frequent experience, that she reaped profit and instruction. “And is it so, sweetheart?” replied the king, “then are we perfect friends again.” He embraced her with great affection, and sent her away with assurances of his protection and kindness. Her enemies, who knew nothing of this sudden change, prepared next day to convey her to the Tower, pursuant to the king’s warrant. Henry and Catharine were conversing amicably in the garden, when the chancellor appeared with forty of the pursuivants. The king spoke to him at some distance from her; and seemed to expostulate with him in the severest manner: she even overheard the appellations of “knave,” “fool,” and “beast,” which he liberally bestowed upon that magistrate; and then ordered him to depart his presence. She afterwards interposed to mitigate his [anger](/concepts/anger): he said to her, “Poor soul! you know not how ill entitled this man is to your good offices.” Thenceforth the queen, having narrowly escaped so great a danger, was careful not to offend Henry’s humor by any contradiction; and Gardiner, whose malice had endeavored to widen the breach, could never afterwards regain his favor and good opinion. [1]

* Burnet, vol. i. . Herbert, . Speed . Fox’s Acts and Monuments, vol. ii. .

<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Fu convinta dalle minacce dei seguaci di Bonner ad apparentemente ritrattare le proprie convinzioni; tuttavia pose alcune condizioni che non soddisfecero quel zelante prelato. Fu gettata in prigione, dove si dedicò alla composizione di preghiere e discorsi con cui rafforzò la propria determinazione a sopportare qualsiasi sofferenza pur di non abbandonare i propri principi religiosi. Scrisse persino al re, dichiarando di credere in ciò che Cristo stesso aveva detto riguardo all’Ultima Cena e nella dottrina divina così come era insegnata dalla Chiesa cattolica; tuttavia, anche se non fu possibile convincerla ad accettare le interpretazioni del re, tale dichiarazione non ottenne alcun risultato e fu anzi considerata un nuovo insulto. Il cancelliere Wriothesely, succeduto ad Audley e molto legato al partito cattolico, fu incaricato di interrogarla riguardo ai suoi protettori alla corte e alle nobildonne che erano in corrispondenza con lei; ma ella mantenne una leale fedeltà ai propri amici e non rivelò nulla. Fu sottoposta a torture di estrema brutalità, ma rimase irremovibile nella sua decisione di mantenere il segreto. Alcuni autori aggiungono un dettaglio particolare: il cancelliere, presente durante le torture, ordinò al luogotenente della Torre di aumentare l’intensità delle sofferenze inflitte; l’ufficiale rifiutò di obbedire. Il cancelliere lo minacciò, ma ricevette un altro rifiuto; allora quel magistrato, pur essendo una persona perbene, ma accecato dal fanatismo religioso, prese personalmente in mano gli strumenti di tortura e li usò con tale violenza da quasi spezzare il corpo della prigioniera. La sua costanza superò ancora la barbarie dei suoi persecutori, e tutti i loro sforzi risultarono vani. Fu quindi condannata a essere bruciata viva; essendo così deformata dalle torture da non riuscire a stare in piedi, fu portata sul rogo su una sedia. Insieme a lei furono condotti Nicholas Belenian, un prete, John Lassels, membro della casa reale, e John Adams, un sarto anch’essi condannati allo stesso castigo per lo stesso crimine. Furono tutti legati al palo del rogo; in quella terribile situazione il cancelliere comunicò loro che la loro grazia era stata firmata e sarebbe stata concessa immediatamente se avessero ritrattato le proprie convinzioni. Ma essi considerarono questa offerta come un ulteriore ornamento al loro “corone di martiri” e, con serenità, assistettero all’incendio che li consumò. Wriothesely non si rese conto che quella situazione pubblica e notoria rendeva ancora più importante per loro mantenere una ferma determinazione nel difendere le proprie convinzioni religiose.

* Fox, II. Speed, Baker. Ma Burnet mette in dubbio la veridicità di questa circostanza; tuttavia, Fox trascrive i propri documenti, nei quali essa ne parla. I

È giusto aggiungere, a titolo di giustizia verso il re, che egli disapprovava il comportamento di Wriothesely e lodava invece il luogotenente.

Sebbene il riserbo e la fedeltà di Anne Ascue avessero salvato la regina da questo pericolo, quella principessa cadde poco dopo in un nuovo pericolo, dal quale riuscì a sfuggire per un soffio. Al re era apparso un ulcere alla gamba; questa malattia, unita alla sua estrema corpulenza e alle sue cattive [abitudini](/concepts/custom), iniziò a minacciare la sua vita e lo rese ancora più irascibile e capriccioso del solito. La regina si prendeva cura di lui con la massima tenerezza e devozione, cercando con ogni mezzo di placare i suoi umori imprevedibili. L’argomento preferito di conversazione del re era la teologia; Caterina, dotata di buon senso, spesso partecipava a queste discussioni e, essendo segretamente incline ai principi dei riformatori, a volte rivelava troppo delle sue opinioni. Enrico, offeso dal fatto che lei osasse dissentire da lui, si lamentò della sua ostinazione con Gardiner, il quale colse al volo l’occasione per alimentare la loro inimicizia. Elogiò l’attenzione del re nel preservare l’ortodossia dei suoi sudditi e sostenne che più elevata era la posizione della persona punita e più vicina a lui, maggiore sarebbe stato l’esempio di terrore che ciò avrebbe rappresentato per tutti, e più gloriosa sarebbe apparsa quella “vittima” agli occhi delle generazioni future. Il cancelliere, spinto dal fervore religioso, si unì a queste argomentazioni; Enrico, accecato dalla propria impulsività e incoraggiato dai suoi consiglieri, arrivò persino al punto di ordinare la stesura di accuse contro la sua consorte. Wriothesely eseguì i suoi ordini e poco dopo gli presentò il documento da firmare; poiché diffamare la regina costituiva alto tradimento, altrimenti Enrico avrebbe potuto essere accusato della propria temerarietà. Per qualche motivo, quel documento importante finì nelle mani di un amico della regina, che immediatamente le comunicò l’accaduto. Lei era consapevole del pericolo estremo a cui era esposta; tuttavia non disperava di riuscire, con la sua prudenza e abilità, a eludere gli sforzi dei suoi nemici. Fece come al solito visita al re e lo trovò in uno stato d’animo più sereno del previsto. Lui iniziò a parlare dell’argomento che gli era così caro e sembrava sfidarla a una discussione teologica. Lei rifiutò gentilmente di proseguire, sostenendo che tali speculazioni profonde non fossero adatte alla natura femminile. Le donne, disse, erano state create per essere soggette agli uomini: l’uomo era stato creato a immagine di Dio, la donna a immagine dell’uomo; spettava al marito scegliere i principi da seguire per la moglie; il dovere della moglie era, in ogni caso, adottare ciecamente le opinioni del marito. Per quanto riguardava lei stessa, il suo dovere era ancora più importante, poiché aveva un marito che, grazie alla sua saggezza e al suo sapere, non solo era in grado di scegliere i principi giusti per la propria famiglia, ma anche per le nazioni più sagge e istruite. “Non è affatto così, ”
“Per Santa Maria,” rispose il re; “ora sei diventata una dottoressa, Kate, e sei più adatta a dare istruzioni che a riceverle.” Lei rispose umilmente di essere consapevole di quanto poco meritasse queste lodi; che sebbene di solito non rifiutasse alcuna conversazione, per quanto [sublime](/concepts/sublime) fosse, quando proposta da Sua Maestà, sapeva bene che le sue opinioni non potevano servire ad altro scopo se non a fornirgli un breve momento di divertimento; che trovava tale conversazione destinata a languire se non veniva ravvivata da qualche opposizione, e che talvolta aveva osato fingere di essere in disaccordo con lui, solo per dargli il piacere di confutarla; e che intendeva proprio utilizzare questo innocente stratagemma per indurlo a discutere argomenti dai quali, grazie alla sua frequente esperienza, poteva trarre profitto e insegnamenti. “Davvero è così, cara?” rispose il re; “allora siamo di nuovo amici perfetti.” La abbracciò con grande affetto e la congedò assicurandola della sua protezione e gentilezza. I suoi nemici, che non sapevano nulla di questo improvviso cambiamento, prepararono il giorno seguente a portarla alla Torre, secondo l’ordine del re. Enrico e Caterina stavano conversando amichevolmente nel giardino quando il cancelliere arrivò con quaranta soldati. Il re parlò con lui a una certa distanza da lei; sembrava discutere con lui in modo molto severo: lei sentì persino come lo chiamasse “traditore”, “stupido” e “animale”; poi ordinò al cancelliere di allontanarsi. In seguito, lei cercò di placare la sua [ira](/concepts/anger); ma lui le disse: “Povera anima, non sai quanto questo uomo sia indegno del tuo aiuto.” Da quel momento in poi, la regina, essendo appena scampata a un pericolo così grave, fece attenzione a non offendere mai l’umore di Enrico con alcuna opposizione; e Gardiner, il cui malanimo aveva cercato di approfondire la loro inimicizia, non riuscì mai più a riconquistare il suo favore e la sua stima. [1]

* Burnet, vol. I. Herbert, Speed, *Fox’s Acts and Monuments*, vol. II*.

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="403" data-title="CHAPTER XXXIII. (parte 9)" data-chapter="CHAPTER XXXIII." data-kind="atom" data-srclang="en"></span>

But Henry’s tyrannical disposition, soured by ill health, burst out soon after to the destruction of a man who possessed a much superior rank to that of Gardiner. The duke of Norfolk and his father, during this whole reign, and even a part of the foregoing, had been regarded as the greatest subjects in the kingdom, and had rendered considerable service to the crown. The duke himself had in his youth acquired reputation by naval enterprises: he had much contributed to the victory gained over the Scots at Flouden: he had suppressed a dangerous rebellion in the north; and he had always done his part with honor in all the expeditions against France. Fortune seemed to conspire with his own industry in raising him to the greatest elevation. From the favors heaped on him by the crown he had acquired an immense estate: the king had successively been married to two of his nieces; and the king’s natural son, the duke of Richmond, had married his daughter; besides his descent, from the ancient family of the Moubrays, by which he was allied to the throne, he had espoused a daughter of the duke of Buckingham, who was descended by a female from Edward III.; and as he was believed still to adhere secretly to the ancient religion, he was regarded, both abroad and at home, as the head of the Catholic party. But all these circumstances, in proportion as they exalted the duke, provoked the jealousy of Henry; and he foresaw danger, during his son’s minority, both to the public tranquillity, and to the new ecclesiastical system, from the attempts of so potent a subject. But nothing tended more to expose Norfolk to the king’s displeasure, than the prejudices which Henry had entertained against the earl of Surrey, son of that nobleman.

Surrey was a young man of the most promising hopes, and had distinguished himself by every accomplishment which became a scholar, a courtier, and a soldier. He excelled in all the military exercises which were then in request: he encouraged the fine arts by his patronage and example: he had made some successful attempts in poetry; and being smitten with the romantic gallantry of the age, he celebrated the praises of his mistress by his pen and his lance, in every masque and tournament. His spirit and ambition were equal to his talents and his quality; and he did not always regulate his conduct by the caution and reserve which his situation required. He had been left governor of Boulogne when that town was taken by Henry; but though his personal bravery was unquestioned, he had been unfortunate in some rencounters [2misspelling] with the French. The king, somewhat displeased with his conduct, had sent over Hertford to command in his place; and Surrey was so imprudent as to drop some menacing expressions against the ministers, on account of this affront which was put upon him. And as he had refused to marry Hertford’s daughter, and even waived every other proposal of marriage, Henry imagined that he had entertained views of espousing the lady Mary; and he was instantly determined to repress, by the most severe expedients, so dangerous an ambition.

Actuated by all these motives, and perhaps influenced by that old disgust with which the ill conduct of Catharine Howard had inspired him against her whole family, he gave private orders to arrest Norfolk and Surrey; and they were on the same day confined in the Tower. Surrey being a commoner, his trial was the more expeditious; and as to proofs, neither parliaments nor juries seem ever to have given the least attention to them in any cause of the crown during this whole reign.

1547.

He was accused of entertaining in his family some Italians who were suspected to be spies; a servant of his had paid a visit to Cardinal Pole in Italy, whence he was suspected of holding a correspondence with that obnoxious prelate; he had quartered the arms of Edward the Confessor on his scutcheon, which made him be suspected of aspiring to the crown, though both he and his ancestors had openly, during the course of many years, maintained that practice, and the heralds had even justified it by their authority. These were the crimes for which a jury, notwithstanding his eloquent and spirited defence, condemned the earl of Surrey for high treason; and their sentence was soon after executed upon him.

The innocence of the duke of Norfolk was still, if possible, more apparent than that of his son; and his services to the crown had been greater. His duchess, with whom he lived on bad terms, had been so base as to carry intelligence to his enemies of all she knew against him: Elizabeth Holland, a mistress of his, had been equally subservient to the designs of the court; yet with all these advantages, his accusers discovered no greater crime than his once saying, that the king was sickly, and could not hold out long; and the kingdom was likely to fall into disorders, through the diversity of religious opinions. He wrote a pathetic letter to the king, pleading his past services and protesting his innocence: soon after, he embraced a more proper expedient for appeasing Henry, by making a submission and confession, such as his enemies required; but nothing could mollify the unrelenting temper of the king. He assembled a parliament, as the surest and most expeditious instrument of his tyranny; and the house of peers, without examining the prisoner, without trial or evidence, passed a bill of attainder against him, and sent it down to the commons. Cranmer, though engaged for many years in an opposite party to Norfolk, and though he had received many and great injuries from him, would have no hand in so unjust a prosecution; and he retired to his seat at Croydon. [1] The king was now approaching fast towards his end; and fearing lest Norfolk should escape him, he sent a message to the commons, by which he desired them to hasten the bill, on pretence that Norfolk enjoyed the dignity of earl marshal, and it was necessary to appoint another, who might officiate at the ensuing ceremony of installing his son prince of Wales. The obsequious commons obeyed his directions, though founded on so frivolous a pretence; and the king having affixed the royal assent to the bill by commissioners, issued orders for the execution of Norfolk on the morning of the twenty-ninth of January. But news being carried to the Tower that the king himself had expired that night, the lieutenant deferred obeying the warrant; and it was not thought advisable by the council to begin a new reign by the death of the greatest nobleman in the kingdom, who had been condemned by a sentence so unjust and tyrannical.

The king’s health had long been in a declining state; but for several days all those near him plainly saw his end approaching. He was become so froward, that no one durst inform him of his condition; and as some persons during this reign had suffered as traitors for foretelling the king’s death, [2] every one was afraid lest, in the transports of his fury, he might on this pretence punish capitally the author of such friendly intelligence. At last, Sir Anthony Denny ventured to disclose to him the fatal secret, and exhorted him to prepare for the fate which was awaiting him. He expressed his resignation, and desired that Cranmer might be sent for; but before the prelate arrived, he was speechless, though he still seemed to retain his senses. Cranmer desired him to give some sign of his dying in the faith of Christ. He squeezed the prelate’s hand, and immediately expired, after a reign of thirty-seven years and nine months; and in the fifty-sixth year of his age.

* Burnet, vol. i. . Fox.

* * Lanquet’s Epitome of Chronicles in the year 1541.

<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Ma il carattere tirannico di Enrico, aggravato da una cattiva salute, presto si manifestò, causando la rovina di un uomo che occupava una posizione molto più elevata rispetto a quella di Gardiner. Il duca di Norfolk e suo padre, durante tutto questo regno, e anche per parte del precedente, erano considerati i sudditi più importanti del regno e avevano reso notevoli servizi alla corona. Lo stesso duca, in giovane età, aveva acquisito reputazione grazie alle sue imprese navali: aveva contribuito in modo significativo alla vittoria sugli scozzesi a Flouden, aveva represso una pericolosa ribellione nel nord e aveva sempre svolto il proprio dovere con onore in tutte le spedizioni contro la Francia. La fortuna sembrava collaborare con i suoi sforzi, elevandolo al massimo rango. Grazie alle favori ricevuti dalla corona, aveva accumulato un enorme patrimonio: il re si era sposato successivamente con due delle sue nipoti; e il figlio naturale del re, il duca di Richmond, aveva sposato sua figlia. Oltre al suo lignaggio, che lo legava alla nobile famiglia dei Moubrays e quindi al trono, aveva anche sposato una figlia del duca di Buckingham, discendente per linea femminile da Edoardo III; inoltre, poiché si riteneva che continuasse segretamente ad aderire alla religione cattolica, era considerato, sia all’estero che in patria, il capo del partito cattolico. Tuttavia, tutte queste circostanze, nella misura in cui elevavano il duca di Norfolk, suscitavano l’invidia di Enrico; egli prevedeva che, durante la minore età di suo figlio, tali tentativi da parte di un suddito così potente potessero rappresentare un pericolo sia per la tranquillità pubblica che per il nuovo sistema ecclesiastico. Ma nulla contribuiva maggiormente a suscitare l’irritazione del re nei confronti di Norfolk quanto i pregiudizi che Enrico nutriva contro l’ conte di Surrey, figlio di quel nobile.

Surrey era un giovane dalle più promettenti prospettive: si era distinto in ogni ambito che fosse degno di uno studioso, di un cortigiano e di un soldato. Eccelleva in tutte le attività militari allora in voga; promuoveva le arti belle con il suo sostegno e il suo esempio; aveva anche compiuto alcuni tentativi riusciti nella poesia. Affascinato dallo spirito romantico e cavalleresco dell’epoca, celebrava le lodi della sua amante sia con la penna che con la spada, in ogni mascherata e torneo. Il suo spirito e la sua ambizione erano all’altezza dei suoi talenti; tuttavia non sempre regolava il proprio comportamento secondo la prudenza e la riservatezza richieste dalla sua posizione. Quando Boulogne fu conquistata da Enrico, gli fu affidato il governo della città; ma sebbene il suo coraggio personale fosse indiscutibile, ebbe sfortuna in alcuni scontri con i francesi. Il re, un po’ insoddisfatto del suo comportamento, inviò Hertford a sostituirlo nel comando; Surrey, però, fu così imprudente da pronunciare alcune parole minacciose nei confronti dei ministri a causa di questa offesa subita. Poiché inoltre rifiutò di sposare la figlia di Hertford e scartò ogni altra proposta matrimoniale, Enrico suppose che avesse intenzioni riguardo alla signora Mary; decise quindi immediatamente di reprimere, con i mezzi più severi, un’ambizione così pericolosa.

Spinto da tutti questi motivi, e forse influenzato da quell’antico disgusto che il cattivo comportamento di Caterina Howard aveva suscitato in lui verso tutta la sua famiglia, diede ordini segreti per arrestare Norfolk e Surrey; entrambi furono imprigionati nello stesso giorno nella Torre. Poiché Surrey era un privato cittadino, il suo processo fu più rapido; quanto alle prove, né i parlamenti né le giurie sembrarono mai prestare la minima attenzione ad esse in nessun caso riguardante la corona durante tutto questo regno.

1547.

Fu accusato di ospitare nella sua casa alcuni italiani sospettati di essere spie; un suo servitore aveva visitato il Cardinale Pole in Italia, per cui si sospettava che intrattenesse corrispondenza con quel detestabile prelato; inoltre, aveva fatto incastonare sul proprio scudo gli stemmi di Edoardo il Confessore, il che lo rese sospetto di aspirare al trono, nonostante lui e i suoi antenati avessero apertamente mantenuto tale pratica per molti anni, e gli araldici l’avessero addirittura giustificata in base alle loro competenze. Fu per questi crimini che una giuria, nonostante la sua eloquente e appassionata difesa, condannò il conte di Surrey per alto tradimento; la sentenza fu eseguita su di lui poco dopo.

L’innocenza del duca di Norfolk era, se possibile, ancora più evidente rispetto a quella di suo figlio; inoltre, i suoi servizi alla corona erano stati maggiori. Sua moglie, con cui conviveva in cattivi rapporti, era stata così meschina da rivelare ai suoi nemici tutto ciò che sapeva contro di lui; Elizabeth Holland, una delle sue amanti, aveva agito allo stesso modo per servire gli interessi della corte. Nonostante tutti questi fattori a suo favore, i suoi accusatori non trovarono prove più gravi se non il fatto che egli avesse detto in passato che il re era malato e non avrebbe vissuto a lungo, e che il regno rischiava di cadere nel disordine a causa delle diverse opinioni religiose. Scrisse una lettera commovente al re, esponendo i propri servizi passati e protestando la propria innocenza; poco dopo, adottò un approccio più diretto per placare Enrico, riconoscendo le accuse avanzate dai suoi nemici. Ma nulla poté mitigare l’irremovibile ostilità del re. Convocò quindi un parlamento, considerandolo lo strumento più sicuro e rapido per esercitare la propria tirannia; la Camera dei Lord, senza nemmeno interrogare il prigioniero, senza processi o prove, approvò una sentenza di condanna contro di lui e la inviò alla Camera dei Comuni. Cranmer, sebbene avesse militato per molti anni nel partito opposto a Norfolk e avesse subito da lui numerosi torti, rifiutò di partecipare a un processo così ingiusto; si ritirò quindi nella sua residenza di Croydon. Il re stava ormai per morire; temendo che Norfolk potesse sfuggirgli, inviò un messaggio alla Camera dei Comuni chiedendole di accelerare la procedura, adducendo come motivo il fatto che Norfolk detenesse la carica di Maresciallo del Regno e fosse necessario nominare qualcun altro per partecipare alle cerimonie legate all’insediamento di suo figlio come principe di Galles. La Camera dei Comuni, obbedendo a queste istruzioni, approvò la sentenza. Il re, dopo averla firmata ufficialmente, ordinò l’esecuzione di Norfolk la mattina del ventinovesimo gennaio. Tuttavia, quando giunse alla Torre la notizia della morte del re stesso quella stessa notte, il luogotenente decise di rinviare l’esecuzione; inoltre, il consiglio ritenne inopportuno iniziare un nuovo regno con la morte del più importante nobile del regno, condannato da una sentenza così ingiusta e tirannica.

La salute del re da tempo era in declino; ma per diversi giorni tutti coloro che gli erano vicini notarono chiaramente che la sua fine si avvicinava. Era diventato così irascibile che nessuno osava informarlo sulla sua condizione; e poiché alcune persone, durante questo regno, avevano subito conseguenze gravi per aver predetto la morte del re, [2] tutti temevano che, in preda alla furia, egli potesse punire a morte chiunque gli comunicasse una simile notizia. Alla fine, Sir Anthony Denny osò rivelargli il segreto fatale e lo esortò a prepararsi al destino che lo attendeva. Il re manifestò la propria rassegnazione e chiese che venisse chiamato Cranmer; ma prima dell’arrivo del prelato, rimase senza parole, sebbene sembrasse ancora cosciente. Cranmer gli chiese di dare qualche segno della sua fede in Cristo prima di morire. Il re strinse la mano al prelato e spirò immediatamente, dopo un regno durato trentasette anni e nove mesi; aveva cinquantasei anni.

* Burnet, vol. I. Fox.*

* * L’Epitome delle Cronache di Lanquet, pubblicato nel 1541.

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="404" data-title="CHAPTER XXXIII. (parte 10)" data-chapter="CHAPTER XXXIII." data-kind="atom" data-srclang="en"></span>

The king had made his will near a month before his demise; in which he confirmed the destination of parliament, by leaving the crown first to Prince Edward, then to the lady Mary, next to the lady Elizabeth: the two princesses he obliged, under the penalty of forfeiting their title to the crown, not to marry without consent of the council which he appointed for the government of his minor son. After his own children, he settled the succession on Frances Brandon, marchioness of Dorset, eldest daughter of his sister, the French queen; then on Eleanor, countess of Cumberland, the second daughter In passing over the posterity of the queen of Scots, his eldest sister, he made use of the power obtained from parliament, but as he subjoined that, after the failure of the French queen’s posterity, the crown should descend to the next lawful heir, it afterwards became a question, whether these words could be applied to the Scottish line. It was thought that these princes were not the next heirs after the house of Suffolk, but before that house; and that Henry, by expressing himself in this manner, meant entirely to exclude them. The late injuries which he had received from the Scots, had irritated him extremely against that nation; and he maintained to the last that character of violence and caprice by which his life had been so much distinguished. Another circumstance of his will may suggest the same reflection with regard to the strange contrarieties of his temper and conduct: he left money for masses to be said for delivering his soul from purgatory; and though he destroyed all those institutions established by his ancestors and others for the benefit of their souls, and had even left the doctrine of purgatory doubtful in all the articles of faith which he promulgated during his later years, he was yet determined, when the hour of death was approaching, to take care at least of his own future repose, and to adhere to the safer side of the question. [1]

* See his will in Fuller, Heylin, and Rymer, . There is no reasonable ground to suspect its authenticity.

It is difficult to give a just summary of this prince’s qualities: he was so different from himself in different parts of his reign, that, as is well remarked by Lord Herbert, his history is his best character and description. The absolute, uncontrolled authority which he maintained at home, and the regard which he acquired among foreign nations, are circumstances which entitle him, in some degree, to the appellation of a great prince; while his tyranny and barbarity exclude him from the character of a good one. He possessed, indeed, great vigor of mind, which qualified him for exercising dominion over men; courage, intrepidity, vigilance, inflexibility; and though these qualities lay not always under the guidance of a regular and solid judgment, they were accompanied with good parts and an extensive capacity; and every one dreaded a contest with a man who was known never to yield or to forgive, and who, in every controversy, was determined either to ruin himself or his antagonist. A catalogue of his vices would comprehend many of the worst qualities incident to [human nature](/axes/human_nature), violence, cruelty, profusion, rapacity, injustice, obstinacy, arrogance, bigotry, presumption, caprice: but neither was he subject to all these vices in the most extreme degree, nor was he, at intervals, altogether destitute of virtues: he was sincere, open, gallant, liberal, and capable at least of a temporary [friendship](/concepts/friendship) and attachment. In this respect he was unfortunate, that the incidents of his reign served to display his faults in their full light: the treatment which he met with from the court of Rome provoked him to violence; the danger of a [revolt](/positions/revolution) from his superstitious subjects seemed to require the most extreme severity. But it must at the same time be acknowledged, that his situation tended to throw an additional lustre on what was great and magnanimous in his character; the emulation between the emperor and the French king rendered his alliance, notwithstanding his impolitic conduct, of great importance in Europe; the extensive powers of his prerogative, and the submissive, not to say slavish, disposition of his parliaments, made it the more easy for him to assume and maintain that entire dominion by which his reign is so much distinguished in the English history.

It may seem a little extraordinary, that, notwithstanding his cruelty, his extortion, his violence, his arbitrary administration, this prince not only acquired the regard of his subjects, but never was the object of their hatred: he seems even, in some degree, to have possessed to the last their love and affection. [1] His exterior qualities were advantageous, and fit to captivate the multitude: his magnificence and personal bravery rendered him illustrious in vulgar eyes; and it may be said with truth, that the English in that age were so thoroughly subdued, that, like Eastern slaves, they were inclined to admire those acts of violence and tyranny which were exercised over themselves, and at their own expense.

* Strype, vol. i. .

With regard to foreign states, Henry appears long to have supported an intercourse of friendship with Francis, more sincere and disinterested than usually takes place between neighboring princes. Their common jealousy of the emperor Charles, and some resemblance in their characters, (though the comparison sets the French monarch in a very superior and advantageous light,) served as the cement of their mutual amity. Francis is said to have been affected with the king’s death, and to have expressed much regret for the loss. His own health began to decline: he foretold that he should not long survive his friend; [1] and he died in about two months after him.

There were ten parliaments summoned by Henry VIII., and twenty-three sessions held. The whole time in which these parliaments sat during this long reign, exceeded not three years and a half. It amounted not to a twelvemonth during the first twenty years. The innovations in religion obliged the king afterwards to call these assemblies more frequently; but though these were the most important transactions that ever fell under the cognizance of parliament, their devoted submission to Henry’s will, added to their earnest desire of soon returning to their country seats, produced a quick despatch of the bills, and made the sessions of short duration. All the king’s caprices were indeed blindly complied with, and no regard was paid to the safety or liberty of the subject. Besides the violent prosecution of whatever he was pleased to term heresy, the laws of treason were multiplied beyond all former precedent. Even words to the disparagement of the king, queen, or royal issue, were subjected to that penalty; and so little care was taken in framing these rigorous statutes, that they contain obvious contradictions; insomuch that, had they been strictly executed, every man, without exception, must have fallen under the penalty of treason. By one statute, [2] for instance, it was declared treason to assert the validity of the king’s marriage, either with Catharine of Arragon or Anne Boleyn; by another, [3] it was treason to say any thing to the disparagement or slander of the princesses Mary and Elizabeth; and to call them spurious would, no doubt, have been construed to their slander. Nor would even a profound silence with regard to these delicate points be able to save a person from such penalties. For by the former statute, whoever refused to answer upon oath to any point contained in that act, was subjected to the pains of treason. The king, therefore, needed only propose to any one a question with regard to the legality of either of his first marriages: if the person were silent, he was a traitor by law: if he answered either in the negative or in the affirmative, he was no less a traitor. So monstrous were the inconsistencies which arose from the furious passions of the king and the slavish submission of his parliaments. It is hard to say whether these contradictions were owing to Henry’s precipitancy, or to a formed design of tyranny.

* Le Thou.

* * 28 Henry VIII. c. 7.

* * * 34, 35 Henry VIII. c. 1.

It may not be improper to recapitulate whatever is memorable in the statutes of this reign, whether with regard to government or commerce: nothing can better show the genius of the age than such a review of the laws.

<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Il re aveva redatto il proprio testamento quasi un mese prima della sua morte; in esso confermava la disposizione del parlamento, lasciando la corona dapprima al principe Edoardo, poi alla signora Maria e successivamente alla signora Elisabetta: alle due principesse imponeva, sotto pena di perdere il diritto alla corona, di non sposarsi senza il consenso del consiglio da lui nominato per governare il figlio minorenne. Dopo i propri figli, egli assegnava la successione a Frances Brandon, marchesa di Dorset, figlia maggiore della sorella, la regina di Francia; quindi a Eleonora, contessa di Cumberland, secondogenita. Nel tralasciare la discendenza della regina di Scozia, sua sorella maggiore, egli si avvaleva del potere ottenuto dal parlamento, ma poiché aggiungeva che, dopo l'estinzione della discendenza della regina di Francia, la corona sarebbe passata al prossimo erede legittimo, sorse in seguito la questione se tali parole potessero applicarsi alla linea scozzese. Si ritenne che questi principi non fossero i prossimi eredi dopo la casa di Suffolk, bensì anteriori a quella casa; e che Enrico, esprimendosi in tal modo, intendesse escluderli del tutto. Le ingiurie subite dagli scozzesi lo avevano estremamente irritato contro quella nazione; e fino alla fine mantenne quel carattere di violenza e capriccio che aveva tanto contraddistinto la sua vita. Un'altra circostanza del suo testamento può suggerire la stessa riflessione riguardo alle strane contraddizioni del suo temperamento e della sua condotta: egli lasciò denaro perché si celebrassero messe per liberare la propria anima dal purgatorio; e benché avesse distrutto tutte le istituzioni fondate dai suoi antenati e da altri a beneficio delle loro anime, e avesse persino lasciato dubbia la dottrina del purgatorio in tutti gli articoli di fede promulgati negli ultimi anni della sua vita, fu comunque deciso, quando si avvicinava l'ora della morte, di occuparsi almeno del proprio futuro riposo e di attenersi al lato più sicuro della questione.[1]

* Vedi il suo testamento in Fuller, Heylin e Rymer. Non vi è alcun motivo ragionevole per dubitarne l'autenticità.

È difficile dare una giusta sintesi delle qualità di questo principe: egli fu così diverso da sé stesso in diverse fasi del suo regno, che, come ben osserva Lord Herbert, la sua storia costituisce la migliore descrizione e caratterizzazione di lui. L'autorità assoluta e incontrastata che mantenne in patria e il rispetto acquisito presso le nazioni straniere sono circostanze che gli conferiscono, in qualche misura, l'appellativo di grande principe; mentre la sua tirannia e barbarie lo escludono dal carattere di buono. Egli possedeva, infatti, grande vigore d'animo, che lo qualificava per esercitare dominio sugli uomini; coraggio, intrepidezza, vigilanza, inflessibilità; e sebbene queste qualità non fossero sempre guidate da un giudizio regolare e solido, erano accompagnate da buoni talenti e da una vasta capacità; e tutti temevano di confrontarsi con un uomo che era noto per non cedere né perdonare, e che, in ogni controversia, era determinato o a rovinare sé stesso o il suo avversario. Un catalogo dei suoi vizi comprenderebbe molte delle peggiori qualità connaturate alla [natura umana](/axes/human_nature): violenza, crudeltà, prodigalità, rapacità, ingiustizia, ostinazione, arroganza, bigottismo, presunzione, capriccio; tuttavia, egli non era affetto da tutti questi vizi nel grado più estremo, né era, a intervalli, completamente privo di virtù: era sincero, aperto, galante, generoso e capace almeno di una temporanea amicizia e affetto. In questo senso fu sfortunato, poiché gli eventi del suo regno servirono a mettere in piena luce le sue colpe: il trattamento ricevuto dalla corte di Roma lo spinse alla violenza; il pericolo di una [rivolta](/positions/revolution) da parte dei suoi sudditi superstiziosi sembrava richiedere la massima severità. Tuttavia bisogna riconoscere allo stesso tempo che la sua situazione contribuì a dare ulteriore lustro a ciò che di grande e magnanimo c'era nel suo carattere; l'emulazione tra l'imperatore e il re di Francia rese la sua alleanza, nonostante la sua condotta poco politica, di grande importanza in Europa; i vasti poteri della sua prerogativa e la disposizione sottomessa, per non dire servile, dei suoi parlamenti resero ancora più facile per lui assumere e mantenere quel dominio totale grazie al quale il suo regno è tanto ricordato nella storia inglese.

Può sembrare un po' straordinario che, nonostante la sua crudeltà, le sue estorsioni, la sua violenza e la sua amministrazione arbitraria, questo principe non solo conquistasse il rispetto dei suoi sudditi, ma non fu mai oggetto del loro odio: anzi, in qualche misura, pare abbia conservato fino alla fine il loro amore e affetto.[1] Le sue qualità esteriori erano vantaggiose e adatte a conquistare la moltitudine: la sua magnificenza e la sua coraggiosa bravura lo rendevano illustre agli occhi popolari; e si può dire con verità che gli inglesi di quell'epoca fossero così profondamente sottomessi che, come schiavi orientali, tendevano ad ammirare quegli atti di violenza e tirannia esercitati su di sé e a proprie spese.

* Strype, vol. i. .

Riguardo agli stati stranieri, Enrico sembra aver sostenuto a lungo un rapporto di [amicizia](/concepts/friendship) con Francesco, più sincero e disinteressato di quanto avvenga di solito tra principi vicini. La comune gelosia verso l'imperatore Carlo e qualche somiglianza nei loro caratteri (anche se il confronto presenta il monarca francese in una luce molto superiore e favorevole) servirono da collante per la reciproca amicizia. Si dice che Francesco fosse addolorato per la morte del re e avesse espresso grande rimpianto per la perdita. La sua salute cominciava a declinare: predisse che non sarebbe sopravvissuto a lungo al suo amico;[1] e morì circa due mesi dopo di lui.

Vi furono dieci parlamenti convocati da Enrico VIII e ventitré sessioni tenute. L'intero periodo in cui questi parlamenti sedettero durante il lungo regno non superò i tre anni e mezzo. Nei primi vent'anni non arrivò nemmeno a un anno. Le innovazioni nella religione obbligarono poi il re a convocare più frequentemente queste assemblee; ma sebbene fossero le più importanti deliberazioni mai sottoposte all'attenzione del parlamento, la loro devota sottomissione alla volontà di Enrico, unita al vivo desiderio di tornare presto ai propri feudi, portò a una rapida approvazione dei disegni di legge e rese le sessioni di breve durata. Tutti i capricci del re venivano infatti seguiti ciecamente, e nessuna considerazione era data alla sicurezza o alla libertà del suddito. Oltre alla violenta persecuzione di ciò che egli definiva eresia, le leggi sul tradimento furono moltiplicate oltre ogni precedente. Persino parole offensive verso il re, la regina o la discendenza reale erano soggette a tale pena; e si prestava così poca cura nella formulazione di questi rigorosi statuti che essi contengono evidenti contraddizioni; tanto che, se fossero stati applicati alla lettera, ogni uomo, senza eccezioni, sarebbe caduto sotto la pena di tradimento. Per esempio, secondo uno statuto,[2] era considerato tradimento affermare la validità del matrimonio del re, sia con Caterina d'Aragona che con Anna Bolena; secondo un altro,[3] era tradimento dire qualcosa di offensivo o calunnioso sulle principesse Maria ed Elisabetta; e definirle illegittime sarebbe stato certamente interpretato come calunnia. Nemmeno un profondo silenzio su questi delicati punti sarebbe stato sufficiente a salvare una persona da tali pene. Infatti, secondo il primo statuto, chiunque si rifiutasse di rispondere sotto giuramento a qualsiasi punto contenuto in quell'atto era soggetto alle pene del tradimento. Pertanto, bastava che il re ponesse a qualcuno una domanda sulla legalità di uno dei suoi primi matrimoni: se la persona restava in silenzio, era traditrice per legge; se rispondeva negativamente o positivamente, era ugualmente traditrice. Così mostruose erano le incongruenze derivanti dalle furiose passioni del re e dalla sottomissione servile dei suoi parlamenti. È difficile dire se queste contraddizioni fossero dovute alla precipitazione di Enrico o a un piano premeditato di tirannia.

* Le Thou.

* * 28 Enrico VIII, c. 7.

* * * 34, 35 Enrico VIII, c. 1.

Potrebbe non essere inopportuno riassumere quanto memorabile ci sia negli statuti di questo regno, sia per quanto riguarda il governo che il commercio: nulla può illustrare meglio il genio dell'epoca di una simile rassegna delle leggi.

The abolition of the ancient religion much contributed to the regular execution of justice. While the Catholic superstition subsisted, there was no possibility of punishing any crime in the clergy: the church would not permit the magistrate to try the offences of her members, and she could not herself inflict any civil penalties upon them. But Henry restrained these pernicious immunities: the privilege of clergy was abolished for the crimes of petty treason, murder, and felony, to all under the degree of a subdeacon. [1] But the former superstition not only protected crimes in the clergy; it exempted also the laity from punishment, by affording them shelter in the churches and sanctuaries. The parliament abridged these privileges. It was first declared, that no sanctuaries were allowed in cases of high treason; [2] next, in those of murder, felony, rapes, burglary, and petty treason: [3] and it limited them in other particulars. [4] The further [progress](/positions/progress) of the reformation removed all distinction between the clergy and other subjects, and also abolished entirely the privileges of sanctuaries. These consequences were implied in the neglect of the canon law.

The only expedient employed to support the military spirit during this age, was the reviving and extending of some old laws enacted for the encouragement of archery, on which the defence of the kingdom was supposed much to depend. Every man was ordered to have a bow; butts were ordered to be erected in every parish;[v*] and every bowyer was ordered, for each bow of yew which he made, to make two of elm or witch, for the service of the common people.[v* *] The use of crossbows and handguns was also prohibited.[v* * *]

What rendered the English bowmen more formidable was, that they carried halberts with them, by which they were enabled, upon occasion, to engage in close fight with the enemy. [1] Frequent musters or arrays were also made of the people, even during time of peace; and all men of substance were obliged to have a complete suit of armor or harness, as it was called. [2] The martial spirit of the English, during that age, rendered this precaution, it was thought, sufficient for the defence of the nation; and as the king had then an absolute power of commanding the service of all his subjects, he could instantly, in case of danger, appoint new officers, and levy regiments, and collect an army as numerous as he pleased. When no faction or division prevailed among the people, there was no foreign power that ever thought of invading England. The city of London alone, could muster fifteen thousand men. [3] Discipline, however, was an advantage wanting to those troops; though the garrison of Calais was a nursery of officers, and Tournay first, [4] Boulogne afterwards, served to increase the number. Every one who served abroad was allowed to alienate his lands without paying any fees. A general permission was granted to dispose of land by will.[v*] The parliament was so little jealous of its privileges, (which indeed were, at that time, scarcely worth preserving,) that there is an instance of one Strode, who, because he had introduced into the lower house some bill regarding tin, was severely treated by the stannery courts in Cornwall: heavy fines were imposed on him; and upon his refusal to pay, he was thrown into a dungeon, loaded with irons, and used in such a manner as brought his life in danger: yet all the notice which the parliament took of this enormity, even in such a paltry court, was to enact, that no man could afterwards be questioned for his conduct in parliament.[v* *] This prohibition, however, must be supposed to extend only to the inferior courts: for as to the king, and privy council, and star chamber, they were scarcely bound by any law.

There is a bill of tonnage and poundage, which shows what uncertain ideas the parliament had formed both of their own privileges and of the rights of the sovereign.[v* * *] This duty had been voted to every king since Henry IV., during the term of his own life only: yet Henry VIII. had been allowed to levy it six years, without any law; and though there had been four parliaments assembled during that time, no attention had been given either to grant it to him regularly, or restrain him from levying it. At last the parliament resolved to give him that supply; but even in this concession, they plainly show themselves at a loss to determine whether they grant it, or whether he has a right of himself to levy it. They say, that the imposition was made to endure during the natural life of the late king, and no longer: they yet blame the merchants who had not paid it to the present king: they observe, that the law for tonnage and poundage was expired; yet make no scruple to call that imposition the king’s due: they affirm, that he had sustained great and manifold losses by those who had defrauded him of it; and to provide a remedy, they vote him that supply during his lifetime, and no longer. It is remarkable that, notwithstanding this last clause, all his successors for more than a century persevered in the like irregular practice; if a practice may deserve that epithet, in which the whole nation acquiesced, and which gave no offence. But when Charles I. attempted to continue in the same course which had now received the sanction of many generations, so much were the opinions of men altered, that a furious tempest was excited by it; and historians, partial or ignorant, still represent this measure as a most violent and unprecedented enormity in that unhappy prince.

* Herbert.

The king was allowed to make laws for Wales without consent of parliament. [1] It was forgotten that, with regard both to Wales and England, the limitation was abolished by the statute which gave to the royal proclamations the force of laws.

* 34 Henry VIII.

The foreign commerce of England during this age was mostly confined to the Netherlands. The inhabitants of the Low Countries bought the English commodities, and distributed them into other parts of Europe. Hence the mutual dependence of those countries on each other; and the great loss sustained by both in case of a rupture. During all the variations of politics, the sovereigns endeavored to avoid coming to this extremity; and though the king usually bore a greater [friendship](/concepts/friendship) to Francis, the nation always leaned towards the emperor.

In 1528, hostilities commenced between England and the Low Countries; and the inconvenience was soon felt on both sides. While the Flemings were not allowed to purchase cloth in England, the English merchants could not buy it from the clothiers, and the clothiers were obliged to dismiss their workmen, who began to be tumultuous for want of bread. The cardinal, to appease them, sent for the merchants, and ordered them to buy cloth as usual: they told him that they could not dispose of it as usual; and, notwithstanding his menaces, he could get no other answer from them. [1] An agreement was at last made to continue the commerce between the states, even during war.

It was not till the end of this reign that any salads, carrots, turnips, or other edible roots were produced in England. The little of these vegetables that was used, was formerly imported from Holland and Flanders. [2] Queen Catharine, when she wanted a salad, was obliged to despatch a messenger thither on purpose. The use of hops, and the planting of them, was introduced from Flanders about the beginning of this reign, or end of the preceding.

* Hall, fol. 174.

* * Anderson, vol. i. .

L’abolizione dell’antica religione contribuì in modo significativo all’applicazione regolare della giustizia. Finché sopravvisse la superstizione cattolica, non era possibile punire alcun crimine commesso dal clero: la chiesa non permetteva al magistrato di processare i membri suoi e non poteva nemmeno infliggere loro punizioni civili. Tuttavia Enrico rese inefficaci queste immunità dannose: il privilegio del clero fu abolito per crimini come la tradizione minore, l’omicidio e altri reati gravi, per tutti i membri del clero, a partire dal grado di subdecano. [1] Ma quella superstizione non proteggeva soltanto i crimini commessi dal clero; esentava anche i laici dalla punizione, offrendo loro rifugio nelle chiese e nei santuari. Il parlamento ridusse drasticamente questi privilegi: innanzitutto fu dichiarato che non fossero ammessi alcun rifugio in casi di alto tradimento; [2] successivamente, anche in casi di omicidio, reati gravi, stupri, furto con scasso e tradizione minore; [3] inoltre tali privilegi furono limitati in altri aspetti. [4] Il [progresso](/positions/progress) ulteriore della riforma eliminò completamente ogni distinzione tra il clero e gli altri sudditi, abolendo definitivamente anche i diritti di rifugio concessi dalle chiese. Queste conseguenze derivavano già dall’ignoranza delle leggi canoniche.

L’unico mezzo adottato in quel periodo per alimentare lo spirito militare consisteva nel ripristinare e estendere alcune antiche leggi emanate al fine di promuovere la pratica del tiro con l’arco, ritenuto fondamentale per la difesa del regno. A ogni uomo veniva ordinato di possedere un arco; in ogni parrocchia venivano eretti appositi bersagli; inoltre, a ogni fabbricante di archi veniva richiesto di realizzare, per ogni arco fatto di tasso, altri due fatti di olmo o frassino, da destinare al uso del popolo comune. L’uso delle balestre e delle pistole veniva anch’esso proibito.

* 23 Enrico VIII, cap. 1.

Ciò che rendeva i balestrieri inglesi ancora più temibili era il fatto che portassero con sé gli alabardi, grazie ai quali potevano, in caso di necessità, impegnarsi in combattimenti corpo a corpo contro il nemico.[1] Anche in tempo di pace si tenevano spesso adunate e raduni popolari; tutti gli uomini di condizione dovevano possedere un completo equipaggiamento da battaglia.[2] Lo spirito marziale degli inglesi, in quel periodo, rendeva questa precauzione sufficiente per la difesa della nazione; inoltre, poiché il re aveva il potere assoluto di chiamare alle armi tutti i suoi sudditi, poteva immediatamente, in caso di pericolo, nominare nuovi ufficiali, reclutare reggimenti e formare un esercito tanto numeroso quanto desiderasse. Quando non esistevano fazioni o divisioni interne nel popolo, nessuna potenza straniera osava invadere l’Inghilterra; solo la città di Londra era in grado di mobilitare quindicimila uomini.[3] Tuttavia, la disciplina rappresentava un punto debole di quelle truppe; sebbene la guarnigione di Calais fungesse da scuola per gli ufficiali, e successivamente anche Tournay e Boulogne contribuissero ad aumentarne il numero, chi prestava servizio all’estero poteva disporre delle proprie terre senza pagare alcuna tassa. Era inoltre consentito disporre dei propri beni per testamento.[v*] Il parlamento, del resto, non era affatto geloso dei propri privilegi (che, a quel tempo, in realtà non valevano molto la pena di essere difesi); esiste un caso in cui un certo Strode, avendo presentato alla camera bassa una proposta riguardante il piombo, fu severamente punito dalle autorità della Cornovaglia: gli furono imposte pesanti multe e, rifiutandosi di pagarle, fu gettato in prigione, incatenato e sottoposto a trattamenti crudeli che minacciarono la sua vita. Tuttavia, l’unica reazione del parlamento di fronte a tale atto ingiusto fu quella di emanare una legge che vietava a chiunque di essere accusato per il proprio comportamento in parlamento in futuro.[v* *] Questo divieto, tuttavia, doveva riguardare soltanto i tribunali inferiori; poiché re, consiglio privato e camera stellata erano praticamente al di sopra di qualsiasi legge.

Esiste un registro relativo alle tasse sulla tonnellata e al peso, che rivela quali idee incerte il parlamento avesse riguardo sia ai propri privilegi che ai diritti del sovrano.[v* * *] Questa tassa era stata approvata per ogni re a partire da Enrico IV, ma soltanto durante il corso della sua vita; tuttavia a Enrico VIII fu permesso di riscuoterla per sei anni, senza alcuna legge ufficiale; e nonostante in quel periodo si fossero tenuti quattro parlamenti, nessuno si preoccupò né di approvarla regolarmente né di impedirgli di riscuoterla. Alla fine il parlamento decise di concedergliela; ma anche in questa concessione, era evidente che non erano sicuri se fossero loro a doverla concedere o se il re avesse diritto di riscuoterla autonomamente. Affermavano che tale imposta fosse stata istituita soltanto per tutta la durata della vita del defunto re e non oltre; tuttavia rimproveravano i commercianti che non l’avevano pagata al re attuale; osservavano che la legge relativa alle tasse sulla tonnellata e al peso era scaduta; eppure non esitavano a definire tale imposta un diritto legittimo del re. Sostenevano inoltre che il re avesse subito gravi perdite a causa di coloro che lo avevano truffato riguardo a essa; e per rimediare a ciò, gli concedevano quella somma soltanto per tutta la durata della sua vita. È degno di nota che, nonostante questa ultima disposizione, tutti i suoi successori abbiano continuato nella stessa pratica irregolare per oltre un secolo; se si può definire “pratica irregolare” quella che l’intera nazione accettava senza alcuna obiezione. Tuttavia quando Carlo I tentò di proseguire sulla stessa strada, ormai approvata da molte generazioni, le opinioni delle persone cambiarono radicalmente, scatenando un grande tumulto; e gli storici, sia prevenuti che ignoranti, continuano a considerare questa misura come un atto estremamente violento e senza precedenti da parte di quel sfortunato principe.

* Herbert.

Al re era concesso di emanare leggi per il Galles senza il consenso del parlamento. [1] Si dimenticava che, sia per il Galles che per l’Inghilterra, tale limitazione venne abolita dallo statuto che conferì alle proclamazioni reali la forza di legge.

* 34 Enrico VIII.

Il commercio estero dell’Inghilterra in questo periodo era per lo più limitato ai Paesi Bassi. Gli abitanti dei Paesi Bassi acquistavano i prodotti inglesi e li distribuivano nelle altre parti d’Europa. Da ciò derivava la reciproca dipendenza tra questi paesi; inoltre, entrambi ne subivano gravi perdite in caso di rottura delle relazioni diplomatiche. Durante tutte le variazioni politiche, i sovrani si sforzavano di evitare questa situazione estrema; e sebbene il re nutrisse solitamente una maggiore [affinità](/concepts/friendship) verso Francesco, la nazione tendeva sempre a favore dell’imperatore.

Nel 1528 iniziarono le ostilità tra l’Inghilterra e i Paesi Bassi; entrambe le parti subirono presto delle difficoltà. Mentre ai fiamminghi non era permesso acquistare stoffe in Inghilterra, i mercanti inglesi non riuscivano a comprarle dai tessitori locali, i quali furono costretti a licenziare i propri operai, i quali iniziarono ad agitarsi a causa della mancanza di cibo. Il cardinale, nel tentativo di placarli, convocò i mercanti e ordinò loro di continuare le loro transazioni come al solito; essi risposero che non erano in grado di vendere la merce come prima. Nonostante le sue minacce, non ottenne alcuna altra risposta da loro.[1] Alla fine fu raggiunto un accordo per proseguire il commercio tra i due paesi anche durante la guerra.

Fu solo verso la fine di questo regno che in Inghilterra iniziarono ad essere coltivate insalate, carote, rape e altre radici commestibili. La scarsa quantità di queste verdure utilizzata in passato veniva importata dall’Olanda e dalle Fiandre. [2] Quando la regina Caterina desiderava mangiare un’insalata, era costretta a inviare appositamente un messaggero per ordinarla. L’uso dell’orzo luppolino e la sua coltivazione furono introdotti dalle Fiandre all’inizio di questo regno, o alla fine di quello precedente.

* Hall, foglio 174.

* * Anderson, volume I..

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="406" data-title="CHAPTER XXXIII. (parte 12)" data-chapter="CHAPTER XXXIII." data-kind="atom" data-srclang="en"></span>

Foreign artificers, in general, much surpassed the English in dexterity, industry, and frugality: hence the violent animosity which the latter on many occasions expressed against any of the former who were settled in England. They had the assurance to complain, that all their customers went to foreign tradesmen; and in the year 1517, being moved by the seditious sermons of one Dr. Bele, and the intrigues of Lincoln, a broker, they raised an insurrection. The apprentices, and others of the poorer sort, in London, began by breaking open the prisons, where some persons were confined for insulting foreigners. They next proceeded to the house of Meutas, a Frenchman, much hated by them; where they committed great disorders; killed some of his servants; and plundered his goods. The mayor could not appease them; nor Sir Thomas More, late under sheriff, though much respected in the city. They also threatened Cardinal Wolsey with some insult; and he thought it necessary to fortify his house, and put himself on his guard. Tired at last with these disorders, they dispersed themselves; and the earls of Shrewsbury and Surrey seized some of them. A proclamation was issued, that women should not meet together to babble and talk, and that all men should keep their wives in their houses. Next day the duke of Norfolk came into the city, at the head of thirteen hundred armed men, and made inquiry into the tumult. Bele and Lincoln, and several others, were sent to the Tower, and condemned for treason. Lincoln and thirteen more were executed. The other criminals, to the number of four hundred, were brought before the king with ropes about their necks, fell upon their knees, and cried for mercy. Henry knew at that time how to pardon; he dismissed them without further punishment. [1]

So great was the number of foreign artisans in the city, that at least fifteen thousand Flemings alone were at one time obliged to leave it, by an order of council, when Henry became jealous of their favor for Queen Catharine. [2] Henry himself confesses, in an edict of the star chamber, printed among the statutes, that the foreigners starved the natives, and obliged them from idleness to have recourse to theft, murder, and other enormities. [3] He also asserts, that the vast multitude of foreigners raised the price of grain and bread. [4] And to prevent an increase of the evil, all foreign artificers were prohibited from having above two foreigners in their house, either journeymen or apprentices. A like jealousy arose against the foreign merchants; and to appease it, a law was enacted obliging all denizens to pay the duties imposed upon aliens. The parliament had done better to have encouraged foreign merchants and artisans to come over in greater numbers to England; which might have excited the emulation of the natives, and have improved their skill. The prisoners in the kingdom for debts and crimes are asserted, in an act of parliament, to be sixty thousand persons and above; which is scarcely credible. Harrison asserts, that seventy-two thousand criminals were executed during this reign for theft and robbery, which would amount nearly to two thousand a year. He adds, that, in the latter end of Elizabeth’s reign, there were not punished capitally four hundred in a year; it appears that, in all England, there are not at present fifty executed for those crimes. If these facts be just, there has been a great improvement in morals since the reign of Henry VIII. And this improvement has been chiefly owing to the increase of industry and of the arts, which have given maintenance, and what is almost of equal importance, occupation to the lower classes.

* Stowe, . Holingshed, .

* * Le Grand, vol. iii. .

* * * 21 Henry VIII.

* * * * 21 Henry VIII., 22 Henry VIII. C 8., 3 Henry VIII. c.

There is a remarkable clause in a statute passed near the beginning of this reign, [1] by which we might be induced to believe that England was extremely decayed from the flourishing condition which it had attained in preceding times. It had been enacted in the reign of Edward II., that no magistrate in town or borough, who by his office ought to keep assize, should, during the continuance of his magistracy, sell, either in wholesale or retail, any wine or victuals. This law seemed equitable, in order to prevent fraud or private views in fixing the assize: yet the law is repealed in this reign. The reason assigned is, that “since the making of that statute and ordinance, many and the most part of all the cities, boroughs, and towns corporate, within the realm of England, are fallen in ruin and decay, and are not inhabited by merchants, and men of such substance as at the time of making that statute: for at this day the dwellers and inhabitants of the same cities and boroughs are commonly bakers, vintners, fishmongers, and other victuallers, and there remain few others to bear the offices.” Men have such a propensity to exalt past times above the present, that it seems dangerous to credit this reasoning of the parliament without further evidence to support it. So different are the views in which the same object appears, that some may be inclined to draw an opposite inference from this fact. A more regular police was established in the reign of Henry VIII. than in any former period, and a stricter administration of justice; an advantage which induced the men of landed property to leave the provincial towns, and to retire into the country. Cardinal Wolsey, in a speech to parliament, represented it as a proof of the increase of riches, that the customs had increased beyond what they were formerly. [2]

But if there were really a decay of commerce, and industry, and populousness in England, the statutes of this reign, except by abolishing monasteries and retrenching holydays — circumstances of considerable moment — were not in other respects well calculated to remedy the evil. The fixing of the wages of artificers was attempted: [3] luxury in apparel was prohibited by repeated statutes; [4] and probably without effect.

* Henry VIII. c. 8.

* * Hall, fol. 110.

* * * 6 Henry VIII. c. 3.

* * * * 1 Henry VIII. c. 14. 6 Henry VIII. c. I 7 Henry VIII. c. 7

The chancellor and other ministers were empowered to fix the price of poultry, cheese, and butter. [1] A statute was even passed to fix the price of beef, pork, mutton, and veal. [2] Beef and pork were ordered to be sold at a halfpenny a pound; mutton and veal at a halfpenny half a farthing, money of that age. The preamble of the statute says, that these four species of butcher’s meat were the food of the poorer sort. This ace was afterwards repealed. [3]

The practice of depopulating the country by abandoning tillage, and throwing the lands into pasturage, still continued; [4] as appears by the new laws which were from time to time enacted against that practice. The king was entitled to half the rents of the land, where any farm houses were allowed to fall to decay. The unskilful husbandry was probably the cause why the proprietors found no profit in tillage. The number of sheep allowed to be kept in one flock, was restrained to two thousand.[v*] Sometimes, says the statute, one proprietor or farmer would keep a flock of twenty-four thousand. It is remarkable, that the parliament ascribes the increasing price of mutton to this increase of sheep: because, say they, the [commodity](/concepts/commodity) being gotten into few hands, the price of it is raised at pleasure.[v* *] It is more probable, that the effect proceeded from the daily increase of money; for it seems almost impossible that such a commodity could be engrossed.

In the year 1544, it appears that an acre of good land in Cambridgeshire was let at a shilling, or about fifteen pence of our present money.[v* * *] This is ten times cheaper than the usual rent at present. But commodities were not above four times cheaper; a presumption of the bad husbandry in that age.

Some laws were made with regard to beggars and vagrants;[v* * * *] one of the circumstances in government, which humanity would most powerfully recommend to a benevolent legislator; which seems, at first sight, the most easily adjusted; and which is yet the most difficult to settle in such a manner as to attain the end without destroying industry. The convents formerly were a support to the poor; but at the same time tended to encourage idleness and beggary.
