L’obiezione principale che egli sollevò riguardava il segno della croce durante il battesimo. Un altro membro aggiunse l’atto di inginocchiarsi durante il [sacramento](/concepts/sacrament); e osservò che, se in quell’atto di devozione fosse richiesto un atteggiamento di umiliazione, sarebbe meglio che i partecipanti si prostrassero a terra, al fine di mantenere la massima distanza possibile dalle antiche superstizioni. [1]

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="488" data-title="CHAPTER XL (parte 7)" data-chapter="CHAPTER XL" data-kind="atom" data-srclang="en"></span>

Religion was a point of which Elizabeth was, if possible, still more jealous than of matters of state. She pretended, that in quality of supreme head or governor of the church, she was fully empowered, by her prerogative alone, to decide all questions which might arise with regard to doctrine, discipline, or [worship](/concepts/religion); and she never would allow her parliaments so much as to take these points into consideration. [2] The courtiers did not forget to insist on this topic: the treasurer of the household, though he allowed that any heresy might be repressed by parliament, (a concession which seems to have been rash and unguarded, since the act investing the crown with the supremacy, or rather recognizing that prerogative, gave the sovereign full power to reform all heresies,) yet he affirmed, that it belonged to the queen alone, as head of the church, to regulate every question of ceremony in worship. [3] The comptroller seconded this argument; insisted on the extent of the queen’s prerogative; and said that the house might, from former examples, have taken warning not to meddle with such matters. One Pistor opposed these remonstrances of the courtiers. He was scandalized, he said, that affairs of such infinite consequence (namely, kneeling, and making the sign of the cross) should be passed over so lightly. These questions, he added, concern the salvation of souls, and interest every one more deeply than the monarchy of the whole world. This cause he showed to be the cause of God; the rest were all but terrene, yea, trifles in comparison, call them ever so great: subsidies, crowns, kingdoms, he knew not what weight they had, when laid in the balance with subjects of such unspeakable importance. [4] Though the zeal of this member seems to have been approved of, the house, overawed by the prerogative, voted upon the question, that a petition should be presented to her majesty for her license to proceed further in this bill; and in the mean time that they should stop all debate or reasoning concerning it.

* D’Ewes, .

* * D’Ewes, .

* * * D’Ewes, .

* * * * D’Ewes, .

v D’Ewes, .

Matters would probably have rested here, had not the queen been so highly offended with Stricland’s presumption in moving the bill for reformation of the liturgy, that she summoned him before the council, and prohibited him thenceforth from appearing in the house of commons. [1] This act of power was too violent even for the submissive parliament to endure. Carleton took notice of the matter; complained that the liberties of the house were invaded; observed that Stricland was not a private man, but represented a multitude: and moved that he might be sent for, and if he were guilty of any offence, might answer for it at the bar of the house, which he insinuated to be the only competent tribunal. [2] Yelverton enforced the principles of liberty with still greater boldness. He said, that the precedent was dangerous; and though, in this happy time of lenity, among so many good and honorable personages as were at present invested with authority, nothing of extremity or injury was to be apprehended, yet the times might alter; what now is permitted, might hereafter be construed as duty, and might be enforced even on the ground of the present permission. He added, that all matters not treasonable, or which implied not “too much” derogation of the imperial crown, might, without offence, be introduced into parliament; where every question that concerned the community must be considered, and where even the right of the crown itself must finally be determined. He remarked, that men sat not in that house in their private capacities, but as elected by their country; and though it was proper that the prince should retain his prerogative, yet was that prerogative limited by law: as the sovereign could not of himself make laws, neither could he break them merely from his own authority. [3]

* D’Ewes, .

* * D’Ewes, .

* * * D’Ewes, , 176.

These principles were popular, and noble, and generous; but the open assertion of them was, at this time, somewhat new in England; and the courtiers were more warranted by present practice, when they advanced a contrary doctrine. The treasurer warned the house to be cautious in their proceedings; neither to venture further than their assured warrant might extend, nor hazard their good opinion with her majesty in any doubtful cause. The member, he said, whose attendance they required, was not restrained on account of any liberty of speech, but for his exhibiting a bill in the house against the prerogative of the queen; a temerity which was not to be tolerated. And he concluded with observing, that even speeches made in that house had been questioned and examined by the sovereign. [1] Cleere, another member, remarked, that the sovereign’s prerogative is not so much as disputable, and that the safety of the queen is the safety of the subject. He added, that in questions of divinity, every man was for his instruction to repair to his ordinary; and he seems to insinuate, that the bishops themselves, for their instruction, must repair to the queen. [2] Fleetwood observed, that in his memory, he knew a man who, in the fifth of the present queen, had been called to account for a speech in the house. But lest this example should be deemed too recent, he would inform them, from the parliament rolls, that, in the reign of Henry V., a bishop was committed to prison by the king’s command, on account of his freedom of speech; and the parliament presumed not to go further than to be humble suitors for him: in the subsequent reign, the speaker himself was committed, with another member; and the house found no other remedy than a like submissive application. He advised the house to have recourse to the same expedient, and not to presume either to send for their member, or demand him as of right. [3] During this speech, those members of the privy council who sat in the house whispered together; upon which the speaker moved that the house should make stay of all further proceedings: a motion which was immediately complied with. The queen, finding that the experiment which she had made was likely to excite a great ferment, saved her honor by this silence of the house; and lest the question might be resumed, she sent next day to Stricland her permission to give his attendance in parliament. [4]

* D’Ewes, .

* * D’Ewes, .

* * * D’Ewes, .

* * * * D’Ewes, .

Notwithstanding this rebuke from the throne, the zeal of the commons still engaged them to continue the discussion of those other bills which regarded religion; but they were interrupted by a still more arbitrary proceeding of the queen, in which the lords condescended to be her instruments. This house sent a message to the commons, desiring that a committee might attend them. Some members were appointed for that purpose; and the upper house informed them, that the queen’s majesty, being informed of the articles of reformation which they had canvassed, approved of them, intended to publish them, and to make the bishops execute them by virtue of her royal authority, as supreme head of the church of England; but that she would not permit them to be treated of in parliament. [1] The house, though they did not entirely stop proceedings on account of this injunction, seem to have been nowise offended at such haughty treatment; and in the issue, all the bills came to nothing.

<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

La religione era un argomento su cui Elisabetta era, se possibile, ancora più gelosa che riguardo alle questioni di stato. Fingeva che, in qualità di sovrana suprema e governatrice della Chiesa, le fosse concesso il pieno potere, esclusivamente grazie alla sua prerogativa, di decidere su ogni questione relativa alla dottrina, alla disciplina o al [culto](/concepts/religion); inoltre, non permetteva mai ai suoi parlamenti nemmeno di prendere in considerazione tali argomenti. [2] I cortigiani non dimenticavano mai di insistere su questo punto: il tesoriere della casa reale, sebbene ammettesse che qualsiasi eresia potesse essere repressa dal parlamento (una concessione che sembrava imprudente e incauta, poiché l’atto che conferiva alla corona la supremazia religiosa le dava il pieno potere di combattere ogni forma di eresia), affermava comunque che fosse esclusivamente compito della regina, in qualità di capo della Chiesa, regolamentare tutte le questioni relative alle cerimonie e ai riti religiosi. [3] Anche il contabile approvava questo punto di vista; sottolineava l’entità delle prerogative della regina e sosteneva che i parlamenti avrebbero dovuto trarre insegnamento dagli esempi precedenti per non intromettersi in tali questioni. Un certo Pistor si oppose a queste argomentazioni dei cortigiani: trovava scandaloso che questioni di tale importanza (come il fatto di inginocchiarsi o di fare il segno della croce) venissero trattate con così poca serietà. Questi argomenti, aggiungeva, riguardavano la salvezza delle anime e interessavano tutti molto più della sovranità su tutto il mondo; considerava quindi tale causa come una questione di natura divina, mentre le altre erano quasi insignificanti, per quanto importanti potessero sembrare: sussidi, corone, regni, non avevano alcun valore rispetto a questioni di tale portata. [4] Sebbene lo zelo di questo membro del parlamento fosse stato apprezzato, la maggioranza dei presenti, intimidita dalle prerogative reali, decise di presentare una petizione alla regina per chiederle il permesso di proseguire con l’esame di questa proposta; nel frattempo, si stabilì che non dovesse più esserci alcuna discussione o dibattito al riguardo.

* D’Ewes.

* * D’Ewes.

* * * D’Ewes.

* * * * D’Ewes.

v D’Ewes.

Le cose probabilmente si sarebbero fermate qui, se la regina non fosse stata così profondamente offesa dall’arroganza di Stricland nel proporre il disegno di legge per la riforma della liturgia; per questo lo convocò davanti al consiglio e gli vietò per sempre di comparire nella Camera dei Comuni. [1] Un simile atto di autorità era troppo violento anche per un parlamento sottomesso a tali decisioni. Carleton si occupò della questione, lamentandosi che le libertà del parlamento venissero violate; osservò inoltre che Stricland non era una persona privata, ma rappresentava un intero gruppo di persone, e propose quindi che venisse convocato nuovamente e, qualora fosse stato ritenuto colpevole di qualche reato, potesse rispondere delle sue azioni davanti al parlamento, considerandolo l’unico tribunale competente in materia. [2] Yelverton difese con ancora maggiore audacia i principi della libertà: sostenne che tale precedente fosse pericoloso e che, sebbene in quel periodo di tolleranza, tra tante persone buone e onorate incaricate di poteri, non ci fosse nulla di estremo o offensivo da temere, le circostanze potevano cambiare; ciò che oggi era permesso poteva in futuro essere interpretato come un dovere obbligatorio e quindi imposto anche sulla base delle autorizzazioni attuali. Aggiunse inoltre che qualsiasi argomento non fosse considerato tradimento, né implicasse una “troppa” umiliazione della corona imperiale, poteva essere presentato senza problemi al parlamento; lì, infatti, ogni questione riguardante la comunità doveva essere esaminata e anche i diritti della stessa corona dovevano essere definiti. Sottolineò inoltre che le persone presenti in quel parlamento non vi si recavano in qualità privata, ma come rappresentanti del loro popolo; e sebbene fosse giusto che il principe mantenesse i suoi privilegi, tali privilegi erano comunque limitati dalla legge: il sovrano, infatti, non poteva emanare leggi da solo, né poteva violarle semplicemente per proprio volere. [3]

* D’Ewes.

* * D’Ewes.

* * * D’Ewes,, 176.

Questi principi erano nobili e generosi; tuttavia, la loro aperta enunciazione era, a quel tempo, piuttosto nuova in Inghilterra. I cortigiani, d’altra parte, si basavano su pratiche consolidate per sostenere dottrine contrarie. Il tesoriere avvertì il parlamento di procedere con cautela: non dovevano spingersi oltre i limiti delle autorizzazioni concesse, né rischiare di compromettere la propria stima presso la sovrana su questioni dubbi. Aggiunse che il membro richiesto per partecipare alle discussioni non era stato trattenuto a causa della sua libertà di espressione, ma perché aveva presentato una proposta nel parlamento contro i privilegi della regina: un atto di temerarietà inaccettabile. Concluse sottolineando che persino i discorsi tenuti in quel luogo venivano esaminati e valutati dalla sovrana stessa. [1] Un altro membro, Cleere, osservò che i privilegi della regina non erano nemmeno suscettibili di discussione, e che la sicurezza della regina rappresentava in realtà la sicurezza di tutti i sudditi. Aggiunse che, in questioni di religione, ognuno doveva rivolgersi ai propri autorità competenti per ricevere istruzioni; sembrava insinuare che anche i vescovi stessi dovessero chiedere indicazioni direttamente alla regina. [2] Fleetwood ricordò di aver conosciuto una persona che, durante il regno della quinta regina attuale, era stata chiamata a rispondere delle proprie dichiarazioni in parlamento. Tuttavia, per evitare che questo esempio fosse considerato troppo recente, fornì ulteriori informazioni: secondo i registri del parlamento, durante il regno di Enrico V un vescovo era stato imprigionato su ordine del re proprio a causa della sua libertà di parola; il parlamento stesso non aveva osato fare di più che chiedere umilmente la sua liberazione. In un periodo successivo, lo stesso oratore, insieme ad altri membri del parlamento, era stato imprigionato, e l’assemblea non aveva trovato altra soluzione se non ricorrere a una richiesta altrettanto sottomessa. Consigliò quindi al parlamento di seguire lo stesso approccio, senza osare chiamare indietro i propri membri o rivendicarne il diritto di partecipazione. [3] Durante questo discorso, alcuni membri del consiglio privato presenti in aula si scambiarono sussurri; di conseguenza, l’oratore propose che le discussioni venissero temporaneamente sospese, e la proposta fu immediatamente accettata. La regina, rendendosi conto che l’esperimento da lei tentato avrebbe potuto scatenare grandi controversie, salvò la propria reputazione grazie al silenzio dell’assemblea; per evitare che la questione venisse ripresa, il giorno seguente inviò a Stricland il permesso di partecipare alle riunioni del parlamento. [4]

* D’Ewes.

* * D’Ewes.

* * * D’Ewes.

* * * * D’Ewes.

Nonostante questa rimprovera da parte del trono, lo zelo dei comuni li spinse comunque a proseguire la discussione di quei progetti di legge riguardanti la religione; tuttavia furono interrotti da un comportamento ancora più arbitrario da parte della regina, nel quale i lord si degnarono di essere i suoi strumenti. Questa camera inviò un messaggio ai comuni, chiedendo che venisse nominata una commissione per partecipare alle discussioni. Furono designati alcuni membri a tale scopo; la camera alta comunicò loro che Sua Maestà, essendo stata informata sugli articoli di riforma discussi, li approvava, intendeva pubblicarli e farli attuare dai vescovi in virtù della sua autorità regale, in qualità di capo supremo della Chiesa d’Inghilterra; ma non avrebbe permesso che tali questioni venissero trattate in parlamento. [1] Sebbene la camera non abbia interrotto del tutto le proprie deliberazioni a causa di questo divieto, sembra comunque che non si sia affatto offesa per tale comportamento arrogante; alla fine, tutti i progetti di legge risultarono vani.

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="489" data-title="CHAPTER XL (parte 8)" data-chapter="CHAPTER XL" data-kind="atom" data-srclang="en"></span>

A motion made by Robert Bell, a Puritan, against an exclusive patent granted to a company of merchants in Bristol, [2] gave also occasion to several remarkable incidents. The queen, some days after the motion was made, sent orders, by the mouth of the speaker, commanding the house to spend little time in motions, and to avoid long speeches. All the members understood that she had been offended, because a matter had been moved which seemed to touch her prerogative. [3] Fleetwood accordingly spoke of this delicate subject. He observed, that the queen had a prerogative of granting patents; that to question the validity of any patent was to invade the royal prerogative; that all foreign trade was entirely subjected to the pleasure of the sovereign; that even the statute which gave liberty of commerce, admitted of all prohibitions from the crown; and that the prince, when he granted an exclusive patent, only employed the power vested in him, and prohibited all others from dealing in any particular branch of commerce. He quoted the clerk of the parliament’s book to prove, that no man might speak in parliament of the statute of wills, unless the king first gave license; because the royal prerogative in the wards was thereby touched. He showed, likewise, the statutes of Edward I., Edward III., and Henry IV., with a saving of the prerogative. And in Edward VI.’s time, the protector was applied to for his allowance to mention matters of prerogative. [4]

* D’Ewes, , 185.

* * D’Ewes, .

* * * D’Ewes, .

* * * * D’Ewes, .

Sir Humphrey Gilbert, the gallant and renowned sea adventurer, carried these topics still further. He endeavored to prove the motion made by Bell to be a vain device, and perilous to be treated of; since it tended to the derogation of the prerogative imperial, which whoever should attempt so much as in fancy, could not, he said, be otherwise accounted than an open enemy. For what difference is there between saying, that the queen is not to use the privilege of the crown and saying, that she is not queen? And though experience has shown so much clemency in her majesty, as might, perhaps, make subjects forget their [duty](/positions/duty_imperative), it is not good to sport or venture too much with princes. He reminded them of the fable of the hare, who, upon the proclamation that all horned beasts should depart the court, immediately fled, lest his ears should be construed to be horns; and by this apologue he seems to insinuate, that even those who heard or permitted such dangerous speeches, would not themselves be entirely free from danger. He desired them to beware, lest if they meddled further with these matters, the queen might look to her own power; and finding herself able to suppress their challenged liberty, and to exert an arbitrary authority, might imitate the example of Lewis XI. of France, who, as he termed it, delivered the crown from wardship. [1]

Though this speech gave some disgust, nobody, at the time, replied any thing, but that Sir Humphrey mistook the meaning of the house, and of the member who made the motion: they never had any other purpose, than to represent their grievances, in due and seemly form, unto her majesty. But in a subsequent debate, Peter Wentworth, a man of a superior free spirit, called that speech an insult on the house; noted Sir Humphrey’s disposition to flatter and fawn on the prince; compared him to the chameleon, which can change itself into all colors, except white; and recommended to the house a due care of liberty of speech, and of the privileges of parliament. [2]

* D’Ewes, .

* * D’Ewes, .

It appears, on the whole, that the motion against the exclusive patent had no effect. Bell, the member who first introduced it, was sent for by the council, and was severely reprimanded for his temerity. He returned to the house with such an amazed countenance, that all the members, well informed of the reason, were struck with terror; and during some time no one durst rise to speak of any matter of importance, for fear of giving offence to the queen and council. Even after the fears of the commons were somewhat abated, the members spoke with extreme precaution; and by employing most of their discourse in preambles and apologies, they showed their conscious terror of the rod which hung over them. Wherever any delicate point was touched, though ever so gently; nay, seemed to be approached, though at ever so great a distance; the whisper ran about the house, “The queen will be offended; the council will be extremely displeased:” and by these surmises men were warned of the danger to which they exposed themselves. It is remarkable that the patent, which the queen defended with such imperious violence, was contrived for the profit of four courtiers, and was attended with the utter ruin of seven or eight thousand of her industrious subjects. [1]

Thus every thing which passed the two houses was extremely respectful and submissive; yet did the queen think it incumbent on her, at the conclusion of the session, to check and that with great severity, those feeble efforts of liberty which had appeared in the motions and speeches of some members. The lord keeper told the commons, in her majesty’s name, that though the majority of the lower house had shown themselves in their proceedings discreet and dutiful, yet a few of them had discovered a contrary character, and had justly merited the reproach of audacious, arrogant, and presumptuous: contrary to their duty, both as subjects and parliament men; nay, contrary to the express injunctions given them from the throne at the beginning of the session; injunctions which it might well become them to have better attended to; they had presumed to call in question her majesty’s grants and prerogatives. But her majesty warns them, that since they thus wilfully forget themselves, they are otherwise to be admonished: some other species of correction must be found for them; since neither the commands of her majesty, nor the example of their wiser brethren, can reclaim their audacious, arrogant, and presumptuous folly, by which they are thus led to meddle with what nowise belongs to them, and what lies beyond the compass of their understanding. [2]

* D’Ewes, .

* * D’Ewes,

In all these transactions appears clearly the opinion which Elizabeth had entertained of the duty and authority of parliaments. They were not to canvass any matters of state; still less were they to meddle with the church. Questions of either kind were far above their reach, and were appropriated to the prince alone, or to those councils and ministers with whom he was pleased to intrust them. What then was the office of parliaments? They might give directions for the due tanning of leather, or milling of cloth; for the preservation of pheasants and partridges; for the reparation of bridges and highways; for the punishment of vagabonds or common beggars. Regulations concerning the police of the country came properly under their inspection; and the laws of this kind which they prescribed, had, if not a greater, yet a more durable authority, than those which were derived solely from the proclamations of the sovereign. Precedents or reports could fix a rule for decisions in private property, or the punishment of crimes; but no alteration or innovation in the municipal law could proceed from any other source than the parliament; nor would the courts of justice be induced to change their established practice by an order of council. But the most acceptable part of parliamentary proceedings was the granting of subsidies; the attainting and punishing of the obnoxious nobility, or any minister of state after his fall; the countenancing of such great efforts of power, as might be deemed somewhat exceptionable, when they proceeded entirely from the sovereign. The redress of grievances were sometimes promised to the people; but seldom could have place, while it was an established rule, that the prerogatives of the crown must not be abridged, or so much as questioned and examined in parliament. Even though monopolies and exclusive companies had already reached an enormous height, and were every day increasing to the destruction of all liberty, and extinction of all industry, it was criminal in a member to propose, in the most dutiful and regular manner, a parliamentary application against any of them.

<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Una proposta presentata da Robert Bell, un puritano, contro un brevetto esclusivo concesso a una compagnia di mercanti di Bristol diede origine anche a diversi episodi significativi. Qualche giorno dopo la presentazione della proposta, la regina ordinò, tramite il portavoce del parlamento, che si dedicasse poco tempo alle discussioni e si evitassero discorsi lunghi. Tutti i membri del parlamento compresero che lei si era offesa, poiché l’argomento trattato sembrava riguardare le sue prerogative reali. Di conseguenza, Fleetwood affrontò questo delicato tema: osservò che la regina aveva il potere di concedere brevetti; che mettere in discussione la validità di un brevetto equivaleva a violare tale prerogativa; che tutto il commercio estero era interamente soggetto al volere del sovrano; che persino lo statuto che garantiva la libertà di commercio prevedeva l’eventualità di divieti da parte della corona; e che, quando il principe concedeva un brevetto esclusivo, si limitava semplicemente ad esercitare il potere conferitogli, vietando agli altri di operare in quel settore commerciale. Citò inoltre i registri del parlamento per dimostrare che nessuno poteva discutere nello stesso degli statuti relativi alle volontà testamentarie senza l’autorizzazione preventiva del re, poiché ciò avrebbe violato le sue prerogative reali. Mostrò inoltre gli statuti di Edoardo I, Edoardo III e Enrico IV, sottolineando sempre il rispetto delle prerogative regali. Durante il regno di Edoardo VI, si chiese addirittura al protettore del regno il permesso di affrontare argomenti legati alle prerogative reali.

* D’Ewes,, 185.

* * D’Ewes.

* * * D’Ewes.

* * * * D’Ewes.

Sir Humphrey Gilbert, il nobile e rinomato avventuriero marittimo, portò questi argomenti ancora più in là. Si sforzò di dimostrare che le proposte avanzate da Bell fossero soltanto inutili e pericolose; tali proposte, infatti, tendevano a denigrare i privilegi imperiali, e chiunque osasse anche solo concepirle o proporle non poteva essere considerato altro che un nemico dichiarato del sovrano. Qual è infatti la differenza tra affermare che la regina non debba esercitare i privilegi della corona e affermare che lei non sia regina? E sebbene l’esperienza abbia dimostrato quanto la maestà sua possa essere clemente, al punto di far dimenticare ai sudditi i loro doveri, non è certo saggio scherzare o correre troppi rischi con i principi. Ricordò loro la favola del coniglio che, alla notizia che tutti gli animali a corna dovevano lasciare la corte, fuggì immediatamente per paura che le sue orecchie venissero scambiate per corna; con questo esempio sembrava voler sottolineare che anche coloro che ascoltavano o permettevano simili discorsi pericolosi non erano del tutto al sicuro. Li esortò quindi a stare attenti, temendo che, se avessero continuato a immischiarsi in queste questioni, la regina potesse ricorrere alle proprie facoltà e, trovandosi in grado di sopprimere la loro libertà contestata, esercitare un potere arbitrario, imitando così l’esempio di Luigi XI di Francia, che, secondo lui, aveva “liberato” la corona dal controllo dei tutori. [1]

Sebbene quel discorso suscitasse disgusto in alcuni, nessuno, all’epoca, replicò nulla, se non che Sir Humphrey aveva frainteso il significato della proposta e di colui che l’aveva presentata: il loro unico scopo era sempre stato quello di esprimere le proprie lamentele in modo appropriato e decoroso davanti alla maestà regale. Tuttavia, in un dibattito successivo, Peter Wentworth, uomo dallo spirito libero e indipendente, definì quel discorso un insulto nei confronti dell’assemblea parlamentare; sottolineò la tendenza di Sir Humphrey a lusingare e adularre il principe; lo paragonò al camaleonte, in grado di cambiare colore tranne che in bianco; e esortò l’assemblea a prestare attenzione alla libertà di espressione e ai privilegi del parlamento. [2]

* D’Ewes.

* * D’Ewes.

In generale, sembra che la mozione contro il brevetto esclusivo non abbia avuto alcun effetto. Bell, il membro che ne fu il primo promotore, fu convocato dal consiglio e rimproverato severamente per la sua temerarietà. Tornò in aula con un’espressione così sorpresa che tutti i membri, ben informati sul motivo della convocazione, ne furono terrorizzati; per un certo periodo nessuno osò sollevare argomenti di rilievo, per paura di offendere la regina e il consiglio. Anche dopo che le paure dei membri del parlamento si erano in parte placate, essi continuarono a parlare con estrema cautela; utilizzando gran parte delle loro dichiarazioni come preamboli o scuse, dimostravano chiaramente il terrore che provavano di fronte alle conseguenze negative delle loro azioni. Ogni volta che veniva affrontato un argomento delicato, anche se in modo molto delicato; anzi, ogni volta che sembrava essere solo accennato, anche a grande distanza, si diffondeva immediatamente la voce: “La regina si offenderà; il consiglio sarà estremamente scontento, ”. Grazie a queste voci, le persone venivano avvertite del pericolo che correvano. È degno di nota che quel brevetto, difeso con tanta violenza dalla regina, fosse in realtà concepito al solo scopo di arricchire quattro cortigiani, causando nel contempo la rovina totale di sette o otto migliaia dei suoi sudditi laboriosi. [1]

Pertanto, tutto ciò che veniva discusso nelle due camere era estremamente rispettoso e sottomesso; tuttavia, la regina riteneva fosse suo dovere, al termine delle sessioni, reprimere con grande severità quegli deboli tentativi di libertà che emergevano dalle proposte e dai discorsi di alcuni membri. Il lord custode comunicò ai comuni, in nome della sua maestà, che sebbene la maggioranza dei membri della camera bassa si fosse comportata con discrezione e devozione durante le deliberazioni, alcuni di loro avevano dimostrato un atteggiamento opposto, meritando giustamente rimproveri per la loro audacia, arroganza e presunzione: un comportamento contrario sia al loro [dovere](/positions/duty_imperative) di sudditi che a quello di membri del parlamento; anzi, contrario anche alle esplicite istruzioni ricevute dal trono all’inizio delle sessioni. Queste istruzioni avrebbero dovuto essere rispettate con maggiore attenzione; invece, alcuni avevano osato mettere in discussione i doni e le prerogative della regina. Ma la regina li avvertiva che, poiché si comportavano così volontariamente in modo irrispettoso, sarebbe stato necessario trovare altri mezzi per correggerli; poiché né gli ordini della regina né l’esempio dei loro colleghi più saggi riuscivano a farli rinsavire da quella follia audace e presuntuosa che li spingeva a immischiarsi in questioni che non appartenevano affatto a loro e che andavano ben oltre la loro comprensione. [2]

* D’Ewes.

* * D’Ewes,

In tutte queste operazioni emergeva chiaramente l’opinione che Elisabetta aveva riguardo al dovere e all’autorità dei parlamenti. Essi non dovevano affrontare questioni di stato, né tantomeno immischiarsi nelle faccende della chiesa. Questioni di entrambi questi tipi erano ben al di là delle loro competenze e venivano riservate esclusivamente al principe, o a quei consigli e ministri a cui egli decideva di affidarle. Quale allora era il ruolo dei parlamenti? Potevano emettere disposizioni riguardanti la corretta conciatura della pelle o la lavorazione del tessuto; la conservazione delle fagiane e delle pernici; la riparazione di ponti e strade; la punizione dei vagabondi o dei mendicanti. Le normative relative alla polizia del paese rientravano effettivamente nella loro giurisdizione; e le leggi di questo tipo che essi stabilivano avevano, se non una maggiore, almeno una più duratura autorità rispetto a quelle derivanti esclusivamente dalle proclamazioni del sovrano. I precedenti o i rapporti giudiziari potevano fornire indicazioni per la risoluzione di controversie relative alla proprietà privata o alla punizione dei reati; ma nessuna modifica o innovazione nella legge municipale poteva provenire da altre fonti se non dal parlamento; né i tribunali avrebbero cambiato le loro pratiche consolidate su ordine di un consiglio. Tuttavia, la parte più apprezzata delle attività parlamentari consisteva nell’erogazione di sovvenzioni; nella condanna e punizione dei nobili o dei ministri considerati pericolosi dopo la loro caduta; nel sostegno a iniziative di potere che, pur potendo essere ritenute discutibili, provenivano interamente dal sovrano. A volte al popolo veniva promesso il rimedio delle ingiustizie; ma ciò accadeva raramente, poiché era una regola ferma che le prerogative della corona non potessero essere ridotte, né tantomeno messe in discussione o esaminate in parlamento. Anche se i monopoli e le compagnie esclusive avevano ormai raggiunto un livello estremamente elevato, minacciando la distruzione di ogni libertà e l’estinzione di ogni forma di attività economica, era considerato crimine da parte di un membro del parlamento proporre, in modo assolutamente rispettoso delle regole, una richiesta per contrastarli.

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="490" data-title="CHAPTER XL (parte 9)" data-chapter="CHAPTER XL" data-kind="atom" data-srclang="en"></span>

These maxims of government were not kept secret by Elizabeth, nor smoothed over by any fair appearances or plausible pretences. They were openly avowed in her speeches and messages to parliament; and were accompanied with all the haughtiness, nay, sometimes bitterness of expression, which the meanest servant could look for from his offended master. Yet, notwithstanding this conduct, Elizabeth continued to be the most popular sovereign that ever swayed the sceptre of England; because the maxims of her reign were conformable to the principles of the times, and to the opinion generally entertained with regard to the constitution. The continued encroachments of popular assemblies on Elizabeth’s successors have so changed our ideas in these matters, that the passages above mentioned appear to us extremely curious, and even, at first, surprising; but they were so little remarked, during the time, that neither Camden, though a contemporary writer, nor any other historian, has taken any notice of them. So absolute, indeed, was the authority of the crown, that the precious spark of liberty had been kindled, and was preserved, by the Puritans alone; and it was to this sect, whose principles appear so frivolous, and habits so ridiculous, that the English owe the whole freedom of their constitution. Actuated by that zeal which belongs to innovators, and by the courage which enthusiasm inspires, they hazarded the utmost indignation of their sovereign, and employing all their industry to be elected into parliament, — a matter not difficult while a seat was rather regarded as a burden than an advantage — they first acquired a majority in that assembly, and then obtained an ascendent over the church and monarchy.

The following were the principal laws enacted this session. It was declared treason, during the lifetime of the queen, to affirm that she was not the lawful sovereign, or that any other possessed a preferable title, or that she was a heretic, schismatic, or infidel, or that the laws and statutes cannot limit and determine the right of the crown and the successor thereof: to maintain, in writing or printing, that any person, except the “natural issue” of her body, is, or ought to be, the queen’s heir or successor, subjected the person and all his abettors, for the first offence, to imprisonment during a year, and to the forfeiture of half their goods: the second offence subjected them to the penalty of a præmunire. [1] This law was plainly levelled against the queen of Scots and her partisans; and implied an avowal, that Elizabeth never intended to declare her successor. It may be noted, that the usual phrase of “lawful issue,” which the parliament thought indecent towards the queen, as if she could be supposed to have any other, was changed into that of “natural issue.” But this alteration was the source of pleasantry during the time; and some suspected a deeper design, as if Leicester intended, in case of the queen’s demise, to produce some bastard of his own, and affirm that he was her offspring. [2]

* 13 Eliz. c. I.

* * Camden, .

It appeared this session, that a bribe of four pounds had been given to a mayor for a seat in parliament. D’Ewes, p.

181. It is probable that the member had no other view than the privilege of being free from arrests.

It was also enacted, that whosoever by bulls should publish absolutions or other rescripts of the pope, or should, by means of them, reconcile any man to the church of Rome, such offenders, as well as those who were so reconciled, should be guilty of treason. The penalty of a præmunire was imposed on every one who imported any Agnus Dei, crucifix, or such other implement of superstition, consecrated by the pope. [1] The former laws against usury were enforced by a new statute. [2] A supply of one subsidy and two fifteenths was granted by parliament. The queen, as she was determined to yield to them none of her power, was very cautious in asking them for any supply. She endeavored, either by a rigid frugality to make her ordinary revenues suffice for the necessities of the crown, or she employed her prerogative, and procured money by the granting of patents, monopolies, or by some such ruinous expedient.

* 13 Eliz. c. 2.

* * 13 Eliz. c. 8.

Though Elizabeth possessed such uncontrolled authority over her parliaments, and such extensive influence over her people; though, during a course of thirteen years, she had maintained the public tranquillity, which was only interrupted by the hasty and ill-concerted insurrection in the north; she was still kept in great anxiety, and felt her throne perpetually totter under her. The violent commotions excited in France and the Low Countries, as well as in Scotland, seemed in one view to secure her against any disturbance; but they served, on more reflection, to instruct her in the danger of her situation, when she remarked that England, no less than these neighboring countries, contained the seeds of intestine discord; the differences of religious opinion, and the furious intolerance and animosity of the opposite sectaries.

The league, formed at Bayonne in 1566, for the extermination of the Protestants, had not been concluded so secretly but intelligence of it had reached Condé, Coligny, and the other leaders of the Hugonots; and finding that the measures of the court agreed with their suspicions, they determined to prevent the cruel perfidy of their enemies, and to strike a blow before the Catholics were aware of the danger. The Hugonots, though dispersed over the whole kingdom, formed a kind of separate empire; and being closely united, as well by their religious zeal as by the dangers to which they were perpetually exposed, they obeyed with entire submission the orders of their leaders, and were ready on every signal to fly to arms. The king and queen mother were living in great security at Monceaux, in Brie, when they found themselves surrounded by Protestant troops, which had secretly marched thither from all quarters; and had not a body of Swiss come speedily to their relief, and conducted them with great intrepidity to Paris, they must have fallen, without resistance, into the hands of the malecontents. A battle was afterwards fought in the plains of St. Denis; where, though the old constable, Montmorency, the general of the Catholics, was killed combating bravely at the head of his troops, the Hugonots were finally defeated. Condé, collecting his broken forces and receiving a strong reënforcement from the German Protestants, appeared again in the field; and laying siege to Chartres, a place of great importance, obliged the court to agree to a new accommodation.

So great was the mutual animosity of those religionists, that even had the leaders on both sides been ever so sincere in their intentions for peace, and reposed ever so much confidence in each other, it would have been difficult to retain the people in tranquillity; much more where such extreme jealousy prevailed, and where the court employed every pacification as a snare for their enemies. A plan was laid for seizing the person of the prince and admiral; who narrowly escaped to Rochelle, and summoned their partisans to their assistance. [1]

* [Davila](/schools/reactionary_traditionalism), lib. iv.

The civil wars were renewed with greater fury than ever, and the parties became still more exasperated against each other. The young duke of Anjou, brother to the king, commanded the forces of the Catholics; and fought in 1569, a great battle at Jarnac with the Hugonots, where the prince of Condé was killed, and his army defeated. This discomfiture, with the loss of so great a leader, reduced not the Hugonots to despair. The admiral still supported the cause; and having placed at the head of the Protestants the prince of Navarre, then sixteen years of age, and the young prince of Condé, he encouraged the party rather to perish bravely in the field, than ignominiously by the hands of the executioner. He collected such numbers, so determined to endure every extremity, that he was enabled to make head against the duke of Anjou; and being strengthened by a new reënforcement of Germans, he obliged that prince to retreat and to divide his forces.

Questi principi di governo non furono tenuti segreti da Elisabetta, né mascherati da alcuna apparenza plausibile o pretesto credibile. Furono apertamente enunciati nei suoi discorsi e nelle sue comunicazioni al parlamento; e venivano espressi con tutta la presunzione, anzi a volte con l’asprezza tipica di un padrone offeso nei confronti del proprio servitore. Eppure, nonostante questo comportamento, Elisabetta rimase la sovrana più popolare che abbia mai regnato sull’Inghilterra; perché i principi del suo governo erano in linea con i valori dell’epoca e con l’opinione comune riguardo alla costituzione. Tuttavia, le continue intrusioni delle assemblee popolari nei poteri dei successori di Elisabetta hanno modificato profondamente le nostre concezioni su questi argomenti; perciò i passaggi menzionati sopra ci sembrano estremamente curiosi, persino sorprendenti. Ma all’epoca non furono quasi notati: né Camden, che era uno scrittore contemporaneo, né alcun altro storico vi prestò attenzione. L’autorità della corona era davvero assoluta; fu soltanto grazie ai Puritani che la preziosa “scintilla di libertà” poté essere accesa e preservata. Fu proprio a questa setta, i cui principi sembrano così frivoli e le cui abitudini così ridicole, che gli inglesi devono tutta la loro libertà costituzionale. Spinti dallo zelo tipico degli innovatori e dal coraggio ispirato dall’entusiasmo, osarono sfidare l’estrema indignazione della sovrana; impegnandosi al massimo per essere eletti al parlamento – un compito che all’epoca non rappresentava certo un vantaggio, ma piuttosto un onere – riuscirono prima ad ottenere la maggioranza in quell’assemblea, e poi a prendere il sopravvento sulla chiesa e sulla monarchia.

I seguenti furono i principali leggi approvati in questa sessione del parlamento. Fu dichiarato tradimento, durante la vita della regina, affermare che lei non fosse la sovrana legittima, o che qualcun altro possedesse un titolo più appropriato, oppure che lei fosse eretica, scismatica o infedele; inoltre, si stabilì che le leggi e i decreti non potessero limitare o definire i diritti della corona e del suo successore. Chiunque, per iscritto o con la stampa, sostenesse che una persona diversa dall’“erede naturale” della regina fosse il suo erede legittimo, veniva punito, nella prima infrazione, con un anno di prigione e la confisca della metà dei suoi beni; nella seconda infrazione, veniva applicata la pena del præmunire. [1] Questa legge era chiaramente diretta contro la regina di Scozia e i suoi sostenitori, e implicava l’ammissione che Elisabetta non avesse mai intenzione di designare un successore. È degno di nota che l’espressione “erede legittimo”, ritenuta dal parlamento indecente nei confronti della regina – come se potesse esistere un altro erede possibile – fu sostituita con “erede naturale”. Tuttavia, questo cambiamento divenne oggetto di scherzi e commenti ironici; alcuni sospettarono che nascondesse intenti più profondi, come se Leicester volesse, in caso di morte della regina, presentare un figlio illegittimo come suo erede. [2]

* 13 Elizabetta, capitolo I.

* * Camden.

Durante questa sessione emerse che era stata offerta una tangente di quattro sterline a un sindaco in cambio di un seggio in parlamento. D’Ewes, p.

È probabile che quel membro non avesse altro obiettivo se non quello di godere del privilegio di essere esentato dagli arresti.

Fu inoltre stabilito che chiunque, attraverso bolle papali, pubblicasse assoluzioni o altri decreti del papa, o utilizzasse tali documenti per riconciliare qualcuno con la Chiesa di Roma, sia tale individuo che coloro che venivano riconciliati, fossero considerati colpevoli di tradimento. A chiunque importasse oggetti come l’Agnus Dei, i crocifissi o altri strumenti legati alla superstizione, consacrati dal papa, veniva inflitta la pena del præmunire. Le precedenti leggi contro l’usura furono rese più efficaci da un nuovo statuto. Il parlamento concesse una somma di denaro sotto forma di sussidio e di due quindicesimi delle entrate fiscali. La regina, essendo determinata a non cedere loro alcun potere, era molto cauta nell’chiedere aiuti finanziari. Si sforzava, da un lato, di far bastare i propri introiti ordinari alle esigenze della corona attraverso una rigida frugalità; dall’altro, faceva ricorso alle proprie prerogative per ottenere denaro concedendo licenze commerciali o monopoli, anche se ciò comportava spese considerevoli.

* 13 Elizabetta, cap. 2.

* * 13 Eliz. c. 8.

Sebbene Elisabetta possedesse un’autorità incontrollata sui suoi parlamenti e una vasta influenza sul suo popolo; sebbene, nel corso di tredici anni, avesse mantenuto la tranquillità pubblica, interrotta soltanto da insurrezioni affrettate e mal organizzate nel nord; ella continuava a provare grande ansia, sentendo il proprio trono vacillare costantemente sotto i suoi piedi. Le violente agitazioni scatenatesi in Francia, nei Paesi Bassi e in Scozia sembravano, a prima vista, proteggerla da qualsiasi disturbo; ma, riflettendoci meglio, queste situazioni le fecero comprendere la gravità della sua posizione. Notò infatti che anche l’Inghilterra, come questi paesi vicini, conteneva i semi del dissenso interno: le differenze di opinione religiosa, nonché l’intolleranza e l’animosità furiose delle fazioni opposte.

La lega, fondata a Bayonne nel 1566 con lo scopo di estermine i protestanti, non era stata creata in modo così segreto da impedire che le sue intenzioni venissero a conoscenza di Condé, Coligny e degli altri leader degli ugonotti. Riconoscendo che le misure adottate dalla corte corrispondevano alle loro supposizioni, decisero di impedire la crudelissima perfidia dei loro nemici e di colpire prima che i cattolici si rendessero conto del pericolo. Gli ugonotti, sebbene dispersi in tutto il regno, formavano una sorta di “impero separato”; uniti sia dal loro zelo religioso che dai pericoli a cui erano costantemente esposti, obbedivano ciecamente agli ordini dei loro leader ed erano pronti a prendere le armi al minimo segnale. Il re e la regina madre vivevano in grande sicurezza a Monceaux, nella regione della Brie, quando si trovarono circondati dalle truppe protestanti, che avevano marciato segretamente da tutte le direzioni. Se non fosse stato per l’arrivo tempestivo di un corpo di svizzeri che li salvò e li condusse con grande coraggio a Parigi, sarebbero sicuramente caduti senza resistenza nelle mani dei ribelli. In seguito si combatté una battaglia nei campi di Saint-Denis; sebbene il vecchio maresciallo Montmorency, comandante delle truppe cattoliche, fosse morto combattendo valorosamente in prima linea, gli ugonotti furono infine sconfitti. Condé, radunando le sue forze disperse e ricevendo un forte rinforzo dai protestanti tedeschi, riapparve sul campo di battaglia; assediando Chartres, una città di grande importanza, costrinse la corte ad accettare nuove condizioni di pace.

L’animosità reciproca di quei religiosi era tale che, anche se i leader di entrambe le parti avessero avuto intenzioni sinceramente pacifiche e si fossero fidati a vicenda, sarebbe stato difficile mantenere la calma tra le persone; tanto più in presenza di un’invidia così estrema e quando la corte utilizzava ogni tentativo di pacificazione come trappola contro i propri nemici. Fu quindi elaborato un piano per catturare il principe e l’ammiraglio, i quali riuscirono a fuggire per un soffio verso Rochelle e chiamarono i loro sostenitori in loro aiuto. [1]

* [Davila](/schools/reactionary_traditionalism), libro IV.

I guerre civili ripresero con ancora maggiore violenza di prima, e le parti in conflitto divennero sempre più ostili l’una verso l’altra. Il giovane duca d’Angiò, fratello del re, comandava le forze cattoliche; nel 1569 si svolse una grande battaglia a Jarnac contro gli Ugonotti, nella quale il principe di Condé fu ucciso e il suo esercito sconfitto. Questa sconfitta, unita alla perdita di un leader così importante, non portò tuttavia gli Ugonotti al dispero. L’ammiraglio continuò a sostenerne la causa; nominando a capo dei protestanti il principe di Navarra, allora sedicenne, e il giovane principe di Condé, incoraggiò il loro partito a preferire morire coraggiosamente in battaglia piuttosto che essere umiliati dalle mani dell’esecutore. Riuscì a radunare un esercito così determinato a sopportare qualsiasi sacrificio, da poter fronteggiare il duca d’Angiò; con l’arrivo di nuove truppe tedesche, costrinse quel principe a ritirarsi e a dividere le sue forze.

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="491" data-title="CHAPTER XL (parte 10)" data-chapter="CHAPTER XL" data-kind="atom" data-srclang="en" data-tags="positions/liberty_of_conscience,positions/toleration"></span>

Coligny then laid siege to Poietiers; and as the eyes of all France were fixed on this enterprise, the duke of Guise, emulous of the renown which his father had acquired by the defence of Metz, threw himself into the place, and so animated the garrison by his valor and conduct, that the admiral was obliged to raise the siege. Such was the commencement of that unrivalled fame and grandeur afterwards attained by this duke of Guise. The attachment which all the Catholics had borne to his father, was immediately transferred to the son; and men pleased themselves in comparing all the great and shining qualities which seemed, in a manner, hereditary in that family. Equal in affability, in munificence, in address, in eloquence, and in every quality which engages the affections of men; equal also in valor, in conduct, in enterprise, in capacity; there seemed only this difference between them, that the son, educated in more turbulent times, and finding a greater dissolution of all law and order, exceeded the father in ambition and temerity, and was engaged in enterprises still more destructive to the authority of his sovereign, and to the repose of his native country.

Elizabeth, who kept her attention fixed on the civil commotions of France, was nowise pleased with this new rise of her enemies, the Guises; and being anxious for the fate of the Protestants, whose interests were connected with her own, [1] she was engaged, notwithstanding her aversion from all rebellion, and from all opposition to the will of the sovereign, to give them secretly some assistance. Besides employing her authority with the German princes, she lent money to the queen of Navarre, and received some jewels as pledges for the loan. And she permitted Henry Champernon to levy, and transport over into France, a regiment of a hundred gentlemen volunteers; among whom Walter Raleigh, then a young man, began to distinguish himself, in that great school of military valor. [2]

* Haynes, .

* * Camden, .

The admiral, constrained by the impatience of his troops, and by the difficulty of subsisting them, fought with the duke of Anjou the battle of Moncontour in Poictou, where he was wounded and defeated. The court of France, notwithstanding their frequent experience of the obstinacy of the Hugonots, and the vigor of Coligny, vainly flattered themselves that the force of the rebels was at last finally annihilated; and they neglected further preparations against a foe, who, they thought, could never more become dangerous. They were surprised to hear, that this leader had appeared, without dismay, in another quarter of the kingdom; had encouraged the young princes, whom he governed to like constancy; had assembled an army; had taken the field; and was even strong enough to threaten Paris. The public finances, diminished by the continued disorders of the kingdom, and wasted by so many fruitless military enterprises, could no longer bear the charge of a new armament, and the king, notwithstanding his extreme animosity against the Hugonots, was obliged, in 1570, to conclude an accommodation with them, to grant them a pardon for all past offences, and to renew the edicts for [liberty of conscience](/positions/liberty_of_conscience).

Though a pacification was seemingly concluded, the mind of Charles was nowise reconciled to his rebellious subjects, and this accommodation, like all the foregoing, was nothing but a snare, by which the perfidious court had projected to destroy at once, without danger, all its formidable enemies. As the two young princes, the admiral, and the other leaders of the Hugonots, instructed by past experience, discovered an extreme distrust of the king’s intentions, and kept themselves in security at a distance, all possible artifices were employed to remove their apprehensions, and to convince them of the sincerity of the new counsels which seemed to be embraced. The terms of the peace were religiously observed to them; the [toleration](/positions/toleration) was strictly maintained; all attempts made by the zealous Catholics to infringe it were punished with severity; offices, and favors, and honors were bestowed on the principal nobility among the Protestants; and the king and council every where declared that, tired of civil disorders, and convinced of the impossibility of forcing men’s consciences, they were thenceforth determined to allow every one the free exercise of his religion.

Among the other artifices employed to lull the Protestants into a fatal security, Charles affected to enter into close connections with Elizabeth; and as it seemed not the interest of France to forward the union of the two kingdoms of Great Britain, that princess the more easily flattered herself that the French monarch would prefer her [friendship](/concepts/friendship) to that of the queen of Scots. The better to deceive her, proposals of marriage were made her with the duke of Anjou; a prince whose youth, [beauty](/concepts/beauty), and reputation for valor might naturally be supposed to recommend him to a woman who had appeared not altogether insensible to these endowments. The queen immediately founded on this offer the project of deceiving the court of France; and being intent on that artifice, she laid herself the more open to be deceived. Negotiations were entered into with regard to the marriage; terms of the contract were proposed; difficulties started and removed; and the two courts, equally insincere, though not equally culpable, seemed to approach every day nearer to each other in their demands and concessions. The great obstacle seemed to lie in adjusting the difference of religion; because Elizabeth, who recommended toleration to Charles, was determined not to grant it in her own dominions, not even to her husband; and the duke of Anjou seemed unwilling to submit, for the sake of interest, to the dishonor of an apostasy. [1]

* Camden, . [Davila](/schools/reactionary_traditionalism), lib. v. Digger’s Complete Ambassador , 110, 111

The artificial politics of Elizabeth never triumphed so much in any contrivances as in those which were conjoined with her coquetry; and as her character in this particular was generally known, the court of France thought that they might, without danger of forming any final conclusion, venture the further in their concessions and offers to her. The queen also had other motives for dissimulation. Besides the advantage of discouraging Mary’s partisans by the prospect of an alliance between France and England, her situation with Philip demanded her utmost vigilance and attention; and the violent authority established in the Low Countries made her desirous of fortifying herself even with the bare appearance of a new confederacy.

The theological controversies which had long agitated Europe, had from the beginning penetrated into the Low Countries; and as these provinces maintained an extensive commerce, they had early received, from every kingdom with which they corresponded, a tincture of religious innovation. An opinion at that time prevailed, which had been zealously propagated by priests, and implicitly received by sovereigns, that heresy was closely connected with rebellion, and that every great or violent alteration in the church involved a like [revolution](/positions/revolution) in the civil government. The forward zeal of the reformers would seldom allow them to wait the consent of the magistrate to their innovations: they became less dutiful when opposed and punished; and though their pretended spirit of reasoning and inquiry was in reality nothing but a new species of implicit faith, the prince took the alarm, as if so institutions could be secure from the temerity of their researches. The emperor Charles, who proposed to augment his authority under pretence of defending the Catholic faith, easily adopted these political principles; and notwithstanding the limited prerogative which he possessed in the Netherlands, he published the most arbitrary, severe, and tyrannical edicts against the Protestants; and he took care that the execution of them should be no less violent and sanguinary. He was neither cruel nor bigoted in his natural disposition; yet an historian, celebrated for moderation and caution, has computed, that in the several persecutions promoted by that monarch, no less than a hundred thousand persons perished by the hands of the executioner. [1] But these severe remedies; far from answering the purposes intended, had rather served to augment the numbers as well as zeal of the reformers; and the magistrates of the several towns, seeing no end of those barbarous executions, felt their humanity rebel against their principles, and declined any further persecution of the new doctrines.

* Grotii Annal. lib. i. Father Paul, another great authority, computes, in a passage above cited, that fifty thousand persons were put to death in the Low Countries alone.
