<span class="atom-split" data-atom="659" data-title="CHAPTER LIV. (parte 13)" data-chapter="CHAPTER LIV." data-kind="atom" data-srclang="en"></span>

He wanted that consolation which commonly supports those who perish by the stroke of injustice and oppression: he was not buoyed up by glory, nor by the affectionate compassion of the spectators; yet his mind, erect and undaunted, found resources within itself, and maintained its unbroken resolution amidst the terrors of death, and the triumphant exultations of his misguided enemies. His discourse on the scaffold was full of decency and courage. “He feared,” he said, “that the omen was bad for the intended reformation of [the state](/concepts/state), that it commenced with the shedding of innocent blood.” Having bid a last adieu to his brother and friends who attended him, and having sent a blessing to his nearer relations who were absent, “And now,” said he, “I have nigh done! One stroke will make my wife a widow, my dear children fatherless, deprive my poor servants of their indulgent master, and separate me from my affectionate brother and all my friends! But let God be to you and them all in all!” Going to disrobe and prepare himself for the block, “I thank God,” said he, “that I am nowise afraid of death, nor am daunted with any terrors; but do as cheerfully lay down my head at this time as ever I did when going to repose!” With one blow was a period put to his life by the executioner. [1]

Thus perished, in the forty-ninth year of his age, the earl of Strafford, one of the most eminent personages that has appeared in England. Though his death was loudly demanded as a satisfaction to justice, and an atonement for the many violations of the constitution, it may safely be affirmed, that the sentence by which he fell was an enormity greater than the worst of those which his implacable enemies prosecuted with so much cruel industry. The people, in their rage, had totally mistaken the proper object of their resentment. All the necessities, or, more properly speaking, the difficulties by which the king had been induced to use violent expedients for raising supply, were the result of measures previous to Strafford’s favor; and if they arose from ill conduct, he at least was entirely innocent. Even those violent expedients themselves, which occasioned the complaint that the constitution was subverted, had been, all of them, conducted, so far as appeared, without his counsel or assistance. And whatever his private advice might be, [2] this salutary maxim he failed not often and publicly to inculcate in the king’s presence, that, if any inevitable necessity ever obliged the sovereign to violate the laws, this license ought to be practised with extreme reserve, and, as soon as possible, a just atonement be made to the constitution for any injury which it might sustain from such dangerous precedents. [3] The first parliament after the restoration reversed the bill of attainder; and even a few weeks after Strafford’s execution, this very parliament remitted to his children the more severe consequences of his sentence; as if conscious of the violence with which the prosecution had been conducted.

* Rush, vol, v. .

* * That Strafford was secretly no enemy to arbitrary counsels, appears from some of his letters and despatches, particularly vol. ii. , where he seems to wish that a standing army were established.

* * * Rush. vol. iv. , 568, 569, 570.

In vain did Charles expect, as a return for so many instances of unbounded compliance, that the parliament would at last show him some indulgence, and would cordially fall into that unanimity to which, at the expense of his own power and of his friend’s life, he so earnestly courted them. All his concessions were poisoned by their suspicion of his want of cordiality; and the supposed attempt to engage the army against them, served with many as a confirmation of this jealousy. It was natural for the king to seek some resource, while all the world seemed to desert him, or combine against him; and this probably was the utmost of that embryo scheme which was formed with regard to the army. But the popular leaders still insisted, that a desperate plot was laid to bring up the forces immediately, and offer violence to the parliament; a design of which Piercy’s evidence acquits the king, and which the near neighborhood of the Scottish army seems to render absolutely impracticable. [1] By means, however, of these suspicions, was the same implacable spirit still kept alive; and the commons, without giving the king any satisfaction in the settlement of his revenue, proceeded to carry their inroads with great vigor into his now defenceless prerogative. [2]

* The project of bringing up the army to London, according to Piercy, was proposed to the king: but he rejected it as foolish; because the Scots, who were in arms, and lying in their neighborhood, must be at London as soon as the English army. This reason is so solid and convincing, that it leaves no room to doubt of the veracity of Piercy’s evidence; and consequently acquits the king of this terrible plot of bringing up the army, which made such a noise at the time,

and was a pretence for so many violences.

* * Clarendon, vol. i. .

The two ruling passions of this parliament were, zeal for liberty, and an aversion to the church; and to both of these, nothing could appear more exceptionable than the court of high commission, whose institution rendered it entirely arbitrary, and assigned to it the defence of the ecclesiastical establishment. The star chamber also was a court which exerted high discretionary powers and had no precise rule or limit, either with regard to the causes which came under its jurisdiction, or the decisions which it formed. A bill unanimously passed the houses to abolish these two courts; and in them to annihilate the principal and most dangerous articles of the king’s prerogative. By the same bill, the jurisdiction of the council was regulated, and its authority abridged. [1] Charles hesitated before he gave his assent. But finding that he had gone too far to retreat, and that he possessed no resource in case of a rupture, he at last affixed the royal sanction to this excellent bill. But to show the parliament that he was sufficiently apprised of the importance of his grant, he observed to them, that this statute altered in a great measure the fundamental laws, ecclesiastical and civil, which many of his predecessors had established. [2]

* Clarendon, vol. i. , 284. Whitlocke, . Rush. vol. iii. , 1384.

* * Rush. vol. v. .

By removing the star chamber, the king’s power of binding the people by his proclamations was indirectly abolished; and that important branch of prerogative, the strong symbol of arbitrary power, and unintelligible in a limited constitution, being at last removed, left the system of government more consistent and uniform. The star chamber alone was accustomed to punish infractions of the king’s edicts: but as no courts of judicature now remained except those in Westminster Hall, which take cognizance only of common and statute law, the king may thenceforth issue proclamations, but no man is bound to obey them, It must, however, be confessed, that the experiment here made by the parliament was not a little rash and adventurous. No government at that time appeared in the world, nor is perhaps to be found in the records of any history, which subsisted without the mixture of some arbitrary authority committed to some magistrate; and it might reasonably, beforehand, appear doubtful, whether human society could ever reach that state of perfection, as to support itself with no other control than the general and rigid maxims of law and equity. But the parliament justly thought, that the king was too eminent a magistrate to be trusted with discretionary power, which he might so easily turn to the destruction of liberty. And in the event, it has hitherto been found, that, though some sensible inconveniencies arise from the maxim of adhering strictly to law, yet the advantages overbalance them, and should render the English grateful to the memory of their ancestors, who, after repeated contests, at last established that noble, though dangerous principle.

At the request of the parliament, Charles, instead of the patents during pleasure, gave all the judges patents during their good behavior; [1] a circumstance of the greatest moment towards securing their independency, and barring the entrance of arbitrary power into the ordinary courts of judicature.

<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Desiderava quella consolazione che solitamente sostiene coloro che periscono a causa dell’ingiustizia e dell’oppressione: né la gloria né la compassione affettuosa degli spettatori riuscirono a confortarlo; tuttavia, il suo spirito, fermo e intrepido, trovò forza dentro di sé e mantenne la propria risoluzione in mezzo ai terrori della morte e alle esultazioni trionfanti dei suoi nemici. Il suo discorso sul patibolo fu pieno di dignità e coraggio. “Temo”, disse, “che questo presagio sia negativo per la riforma che si intende attuare nello [stato](/concepts/state), poiché essa inizia con il versamento di sangue innocente”. Dopo aver detto addio per l’ultima volta a suo fratello e ai suoi amici presenti, e dopo aver inviato una benedizione alle sue parenti più prossime assenti, aggiunse: “Ora, tutto è quasi finito! Un solo colpo renderà mia moglie vedova, i miei cari figli orfani, priverà i miei poveri servitori del loro gentile padrone e mi separerà da mio fratello e da tutti i miei amici. Ma che Dio sia con voi e con loro tutti!” Mentre si preparava per l’esecuzione, disse: “Grazie a Dio non ho paura della morte, né sono intimorito da alcun terrore; posso mettere la testa giù con lo stesso spirito sereno di sempre”. Con un solo colpo, l’ufficiale giustiziere pose fine alla sua vita. [1]

Così morì, all’età di quarantanove anni, il conte di Strafford, uno dei personaggi più eminenti che siano mai apparsi in Inghilterra. Sebbene la sua morte fosse unanimemente richiesta come atto di giustizia e come espiazione per le numerose violazioni della costituzione, si può affermare con certezza che la sentenza che lo condannò rappresentava un crimine ancora più grave dei peggiori atti che i suoi implacabili nemici avevano cercato di fargli commettere con tanta crudeltà. Il popolo, nella sua furia, aveva completamente frainteso l’oggetto reale del proprio risentimento: tutte le difficoltà e le necessità che avevano costretto il re ad adottare misure violente per garantire i rifornimenti derivavano da decisioni prese molto tempo prima dell’ascesa al potere di Strafford; e se tali misure erano state causa di comportamenti errati, lui, almeno, era del tutto innocente. Anche quelle stesse misure violente, che avevano suscitato l’accusa che la costituzione venisse sovvertita, erano state attuate, a quanto pare, senza il suo consiglio né il suo aiuto. E qualunque fosse stato il suo parere personale, egli non mancava mai di ribadirlo pubblicamente davanti al re, sostenendo che, qualora una necessità inevitabile costringesse il sovrano a violare le leggi, tale comportamento dovesse avvenire con estrema cautela e che, non appena possibile, fosse necessario offrire alla costituzione un’adeguata compensazione per eventuali danni arrecati da tali precedenti pericolosi. Il primo parlamento dopo la restaurazione abolì la sentenza di condanna a morte contro Strafford; e poche settimane dopo l’esecuzione, lo stesso parlamento ridusse le conseguenze più severe della sua pena nei confronti dei suoi figli, come se fosse consapevole della violenza con cui quella causa era stata portata avanti.

* Affrettarsi, volare, v.*

* * Il fatto che Strafford, in realtà, non fosse contrario ai consigli arbitrari emerge da alcune delle sue lettere e dispacci, in particolare nel volume II, dove sembra auspicare l’istituzione di un esercito permanente.

* * * Rush, vol. IV, pagine 568, 569, 570.

Inutilmente Carlo si aspettava che, in ricompensa di tante dimostrazioni di assoluta sottomissione, il parlamento finalmente gli mostrasse un po’ di indulgenza e raggiungesse quell’unanimità che, a scapito del proprio potere e della vita del suo amico, egli aveva tanto desiderato ottenere. Tutte le sue concessioni venivano vanificate dal sospetto da parte loro riguardo alla sua mancanza di sincerità; inoltre, il presunto tentativo di coinvolgere l’esercito contro di loro fu interpretato da molti come una conferma di tale gelosia. Era naturale che il re cercasse qualche soluzione, mentre tutto sembrava abbandonarlo o coalizzarsi contro di lui; probabilmente questo rappresentava l’essenza di quel piano embrionale riguardante l’esercito. Tuttavia i leader popolari insistevano nel sostenere che fosse in corso un complotto disperato per mobilitare immediatamente le truppe e usare la violenza contro il parlamento; un piano del quale le testimonianze di Piercy scagionano il re, e che, data la vicinanza dell’esercito scozzese, sembrava assolutamente impraticabile. Tuttavia, grazie a questi sospetti, lo stesso spirito ostile continuò ad essere alimentato; i membri del parlamento, senza fornire al re alcuna soddisfazione riguardo alla regolamentazione delle sue entrate fiscali, proseguirono con grande determinazione nelle loro attività volte a limitare le sue ormai indifese prerogative.

Secondo Piercy, fu proposto al re il piano di portare l’esercito a Londra; ma egli lo rifiutò come assurdo, poiché gli scozzesi, che erano in armi e si trovavano nelle vicinanze, sarebbero arrivati a Londra esattamente nello stesso momento dell’esercito inglese. Questo ragionamento è così solido e convincente da non lasciare spazio al dubbio sulla veridicità delle affermazioni di Piercy; e di conseguenza scagiona il re da questa terribile cospirazione, che all’epoca suscitò grande scalpore.

E fu una scusa per tante violenze.

* * Clarendon, vol. I..

Le due passioni dominanti di questo parlamento erano lo zelo per la libertà e l’avversione verso la chiesa; e per entrambe queste motivazioni, nulla poteva sembrare più eccezionale della Corte della Alta Commissione, la cui istituzione la rendeva completamente arbitraria e le affidava il compito di difendere l’ordinamento ecclesiastico. Anche la Camera Stellata era un tribunale che esercitava ampi poteri discrezionali, senza alcuna regola o limite preciso, né riguardo alle cause sottoposte alla sua giurisdizione, né riguardo alle decisioni che prendeva. Un disegno di legge approvato all’unanimità dalle camere stabiliva l’abolizione di questi due tribunali e la cancellazione degli articoli principali e più pericolosi delle prerogative reali. Con lo stesso disegno di legge veniva inoltre regolamentata la giurisdizione del Consiglio e limitata la sua autorità.[1] Carlo esitò prima di dare il suo assenso; ma, rendendosi conto di essere andato troppo lontano per poter tornare indietro e di non disporre di alcuna risorsa in caso di conflitto, alla fine appose la sua sanzione reale a questo eccellente provvedimento. Tuttavia, per dimostrare al parlamento quanto fosse consapevole dell’importanza di tale concessione, osservò che tale legge modificava in modo significativo le leggi fondamentali, sia ecclesiastiche che civili, stabilite da molti dei suoi predecessori.[2]

* Clarendon, vol. I, p. 284. Whitlocke. Rush, vol. III, p. 1384.

* * Rush, volume V. * *

Con la soppressione della Camera Stellata, il potere del re di vincolare il popolo attraverso le sue proclamazioni venne indirettamente abolito; e quella importante branca delle prerogative reali, simbolo evidente di un potere arbitrario e incompatibile con una costituzione limitata, una volta eliminata, rese il sistema governativo più coerente e uniforme. Solo la Camera Stellata aveva il compito di punire le infrazioni agli editti reali; ma poiché non rimanevano altre corti giudiziarie se non quelle di Westminster Hall, che si occupavano esclusivamente di leggi comuni e statutarie, il re poteva ora emettere proclamazioni, ma nessuno era obbligato ad obbedirle. Tuttavia, bisogna ammettere che l’esperimento condotto dal parlamento fu piuttosto avventato e rischioso. A quel tempo, non esisteva alcun governo al mondo – né probabilmente si trova nelle cronache della storia – che potesse funzionare senza l’intervento di un’autorità arbitraria affidata a qualche magistrato; e sembrava davvero improbabile che la società umana potesse mai raggiungere uno stato di perfezione tale da reggersi esclusivamente sulle rigide norme della legge e dell’equità. Tuttavia, il parlamento riteneva giustamente che il re fosse un magistrato troppo influente per essere affidato a poteri discrezionali che avrebbero potuto facilmente essere utilizzati a danno della libertà dei cittadini. E infatti, si è dimostrato che, sebbene l’adesione rigorosa alla legge possa comportare alcuni inconvenienti, i vantaggi derivanti da tale approccio superano di gran lunga questi svantaggi, e dovrebbero rendere gli inglesi grati nei confronti dei loro antenati, che, dopo ripetute lotte, riuscirono infine a stabilire quel nobile principio, sebbene pericoloso.

Su richiesta del parlamento, Carlo concesse ai giudici, non in base al loro comportamento occasionale, ma in base al loro buon operato nel corso dell’anno, dei titoli ufficiali che ne garantivano l’autonomia; una misura di fondamentale importanza per assicurare l’indipendenza dei tribunali ordinari e impedire l’introduzione di poteri arbitrari in essi.

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="660" data-title="CHAPTER LIV. (parte 14)" data-chapter="CHAPTER LIV." data-kind="atom" data-srclang="en"></span>

The marshal’s court, which took cognizance of offensive, words, and was not thought sufficiently limited by law, was also for that reason abolished. [2] The stannary courts, which exercised jurisdiction over the miners, being liable to a like objection, underwent a like fate. The abolition of the council of the north and the council of Wales followed from the same principles. The authority of the clerk of the market, who had a general inspection over the weights and measures throughout the kingdom, was transferred to the mayors, sheriffs, and ordinary magistrates.

* May, .

* * Nalson, vol. i .

In short, if we take a survey of the transactions of this memorable parliament during the first period of its operations, we shall find that, excepting Strafford’s attainder, which was a complication of cruel iniquity, their merits in other respects so much outweigh their mistakes, as to entitle them to praise, from all lovers of liberty. Not only were former abuses remedied, and grievances redressed; great provision for the future was made by law against the return of like complaints. And if the means by which they obtained such advantages savor often of artifice, sometimes of violence, it is to be considered, that revolutions of government cannot be effected by the mere force of argument and reasoning; and that factions being once excited, men can neither so firmly regulate the tempers of others, nor their own, as to insure themselves against all exorbitances.

The parliament now came to a pause. The king had promised his Scottish subjects that he would this summer pay them a visit, in order to settle their government; and though the English parliament was very importunate with him, that he should lay aside that journey, they could not prevail with him so much as to delay it. As he must necessarily, in his journey, have passed through the troops of both nations, the commons seem to have entertained great jealousy on that account, and to have now hurried on, as much as they formerly delayed, the disbanding of the armies. The arrears, therefore, of the Scots were fully paid them; and those of the English in part. The Scots returned home, and the English were separated into their several counties, and dismissed.

After this, the parliament adjourned to the twentieth of October; and a committee of both houses — a thing unprecedented — was appointed to sit during the recess, with very ample powers. [1] Pym was elected chairman of the committee of the lower house. Further attempts were made by the parliament while it sat, and even by the commons alone for assuming sovereign executive powers, and publishing their ordinances, as they called them, instead of laws. The committee too, on their part, was ready to imitate the example.

A small committee of both houses was appointed to attend the king into Scotland, in order, as was pretended, to see that the articles of pacification were executed; but really to be spies upon him, and extend still further the ideas of parliamentary authority, as well as eclipse the majesty of the king. The earl of Bedford, Lord Howard, Sir Philip Stapleton, Sir William Armyne, Fiennes, and Hambden, were the persons chosen. [2]

* Rush. vol. v. .

* * Rush. vol. v.

Endeavors were used, before Charles’s departure, to have a protector of the kingdom appointed, with a power to pass laws without having recourse to the king: so little regard was now paid to royal authority, or to the established constitution of the kingdom.

Amidst the great variety of affairs which occurred during this busy period, we have almost overlooked the marriage of the princess Mary with William, prince of Orange. The king concluded not this alliance without communicating his intentions to the parliament, who received the proposal with satisfaction. [1] This was the commencement of the connections with the family of Orange; connections which were afterwards attended with the most important consequences, both to the kingdom and to the house of Stuart.

* Whitlocke, .

<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Il tribunale del maresciallo, che si occupava di giudicare parole offensive e che non era ritenuto sufficientemente vincolato dalla legge, fu anch’esso abolito per questa stessa ragione. I tribunali specializzati nel controllo dei minatori, soggetti a obiezioni analoghe, subirono lo stesso destino. L’abolizione del Consiglio del Nord e del Consiglio del Galles seguì gli stessi principi. L’autorità dell’ufficiale incaricato del controllo dei pesi e delle misure in tutto il regno fu trasferita ai sindaci, ai procuratori reali e agli altri magistrati ordinari.

* Maggio, *

* * Nalson, volume I.

In breve, se esaminiamo le azioni compiute da questo memorabile parlamento durante il primo periodo delle sue attività, scopriremo che, ad eccezione della condanna a morte di Strafford – una conseguenza di crudeli ingiustizie – i suoi meriti in altri aspetti superano di gran lunga i suoi errori, tanto da meritare lodi da parte di tutti coloro che amano la libertà. Non solo furono eliminati gli abusi precedenti e risolti i problemi esistenti; fu anche previsto, attraverso leggi specifiche, il divieto che simili lamentele potessero ripresentarsi in futuro. E se i mezzi con cui ottennero questi risultati spesso presentavano tratti di astuzia o addirittura violenza, è bene ricordare che le rivoluzioni politiche non possono essere realizzate unicamente attraverso il potere dell’argomentazione e della ragione; inoltre, una volta scatenate le fazioni, gli uomini non sono in grado di controllare con sufficiente efficacia né l’umore altrui né il proprio, per garantirsi la protezione da ogni forma di eccesso.

Il parlamento entrò ora in una pausa. Il re aveva promesso ai suoi sudditi scozzesi che quell’estate li avrebbe visitati per regolare le questioni relative al loro governo; e sebbene il parlamento inglese insistesse molto affinché rinunciasse a quel viaggio, non riuscì a convincerlo nemmeno a ritardarlo. Poiché durante il suo viaggio sarebbe stato necessariamente costretto a passare attraverso le truppe di entrambe le nazioni, i membri del parlamento inglese sembravano provare grande gelosia al riguardo, e pertanto accelerarono con ogni sforzo la dissoluzione delle armate. Di conseguenza, i debiti degli scozzesi furono completamente saldati, mentre quelli degli inglesi vennero parzialmente ripagati. Gli scozzesi tornarono a casa, mentre gli inglesi furono dispersi nelle loro rispettive contee e congedati.

In seguito a ciò, il parlamento si aggiornò al ventesimo ottobre; e fu nominato un comitato composto da membri di entrambe le camere – una cosa senza precedenti – incaricato di proseguire i lavori durante la pausa, con poteri molto ampi. [1] Pym fu eletto presidente del comitato della camera bassa. Durante il periodo in cui il parlamento era riunito, vennero fatti ulteriori tentativi da parte di alcuni membri, persino da quelli della sola camera dei comuni, per assumere poteri esecutivi sovrani e emanare ordini, che chiamavano “decreti”, al posto delle leggi. Anche il comitato, a sua volta, era pronto ad imitare tale esempio.

Fu nominato un piccolo comitato formato da membri di entrambe le camere per accompagnare il re in Scozia, con l’scusa apparente di verificare che gli articoli della pace venissero rispettati; in realtà, il loro compito era quello di spiarlo e di estendere ulteriormente i poteri del parlamento, al fine di offuscare la maestà reale. I membri scelti furono l’ conte di Bedford, Lord Howard, Sir Philip Stapleton, Sir William Armyne, Fiennes e Hambden. [2]

*Rush, volume V.*

* * Rush, volume V.

Prima della partenza di Carlo, furono compiuti sforzi per nominare un protettore del regno con il potere di emanare leggi senza dover ricorrere al re; a quel punto, l’autorità reale e la costituzione consolidata del regno venivano considerate con estrema indifferenza.

Tra la grande varietà di eventi che si sono verificati in questo periodo intenso, abbiamo quasi trascurato il matrimonio della principessa Maria con Guglielmo, principe d’Orange. Il re concluse questa alleanza senza comunicarne le intenzioni al parlamento, il quale accolse la proposta con soddisfazione. [1] Fu l’inizio di queste relazioni con la famiglia d’Orange; relazioni che in seguito avrebbero avuto conseguenze di estrema importanza, sia per il regno che per la casa Stuart.

* Whitlocke,, *

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="661" data-title="CHAPTER LV. (parte 1)" data-chapter="CHAPTER LV." data-kind="atom" data-srclang="en"></span>

CHARLES I.

1641.

THE Scots, who began these fatal commotions, thought that they had finished a very perilous undertaking much to their profit and reputation. Besides the large pay voted them for lying in good quarters during a twelvemonth, the English parliament had conferred on them a present of three hundred thousand pounds for their brotherly assistance. [1] In the articles of pacification, they were declared to have ever been good subjects; and their military expeditions were approved of, as enterprises calculated and intended for his majesty’s honor and advantage. To carry further the triumph over their sovereign, these terms, so ignominious to him, were ordered by a vote of parliament to be read in all churches, upon a day of thanksgiving appointed for the national pacification; [2] all their claims for the restriction of prerogative were agreed to be ratified; and, what they more valued than all these advantages, they had a near prospect of spreading the Presbyterian discipline in England and Ireland, from the seeds which they had scattered of their religious principles. Never did refined Athens so exult in diffusing the sciences and liberal arts over a savage world, never did generous Rome so please herself in the view of law and order established by her victorious arms, as the Scots now rejoiced in communicating their barbarous zeal and theological fervor to the neighboring nations.

* Nalson, vol. i. . May, .

* * Rush. vol. v. . Clarendon, vol. ii .

Charles, despoiled in England of a considerable part of his authority, and dreading still further encroachments upon him, arrived in Scotland, with an intention of abdicating almost entirely the small share of power which there remained to him, and of giving full satisfaction, if possible, to his restless subjects in that kingdom.

The lords of articles were an ancient institution in the Scottish parliament. They were constituted after this manner: The temporal lords chose eight bishops: the bishops elected eight temporal lords: these sixteen named eight commissioners of counties, and eight burgesses, and without the previous consent of the thirty-two, who were denominated lords of articles, no motion could be made in parliament. As the bishops were entirely devoted to the court, it is evident, that all the lords of articles, by necessary consequence, depended on the king’s nomination; and the prince, besides one negative after the bills had passed through parliament, possessed indirectly another before their introduction; a prerogative of much greater consequence than the former. The bench of bishops being now abolished, the parliament laid hold of the opportunity, and totally set aside the lords of articles: and till this important point was obtained, the nation, properly speaking, could not be said to enjoy any regular [freedom](/concepts/freedom). [1]

It is remarkable that, notwithstanding this institution, to which there is no parallel in England, the royal authority was always deemed much lower in Scotland than in the former kingdom. Bacon represents it as one advantage to be expected from the union, that the too extensive prerogative of England would be abridged by the example of Scotland, and the too narrow prerogative of Scotland be enlarged from the imitation of England. The English were at that time a civilized people, and obedient to the laws; but among the Scots it was of little consequence how the laws were framed, or by whom voted, while the exorbitant aristocracy had it so much in their power to prevent their regular execution.

The peers and commons formed only one house in the Scottish parliament: and as it had been the practice of James, continued by Charles, to grace English gentlemen with Scottish titles, all the determinations of parliament, it was to be feared, would in time depend upon the prince, by means of these votes of foreigners, who had no interest or property in the nation. It was therefore a law deserving approbation, that no man should be created a Scotch peer, who possessed not ten thousand marks (above five hundred pounds) of annual rent in the kingdom. [2]

A law for triennial parliaments was likewise passed; and it was ordained, that the last act of every parliament should be to appoint the time and place for holding the parliament next ensuing. [3]

* Burnet, Mem.

* * Burnet, Mem.

* * * Burnet, Mem.

The king was deprived of that power formerly exercised of issuing proclamations which enjoined obedience under the penalty of treason; a prerogative which invested him with the whole legislative authority, even in matters of the highest importance. [1]

So far was laudable: but the most fatal blow given to royal authority, and what in a manner dethroned the prince, was the article, that no member of the privy council, in whose hands during the king’s absence the whole administration lay, no officer of state, none of the judges, should be appointed but by advice and approbation of parliament. Charles even agreed to deprive of their seats four judges who had adhered to his interests; and their place was supplied by others more agreeable to the ruling party. Several of the Covenanters were also sworn of the privy council. And all the ministers of state, counsellors, and judges, were by law to hold their places during life or good behavior. [2]

The king while in Scotland conformed himself entirely to the established church, and assisted with great gravity at the long prayers and longer sermons with which the Presbyterians endeavored to regale him. He bestowed pensions and preferments on Henderson, Gillespy, and other popular preachers, and practised every art to soften, if not to gain, his greatest enemies. The earl of Argyle was created a marquis, Lord Loudon an earl, Lesley was dignified with the title of earl of Leven. [3] His friends he was obliged for the present to neglect and overlook: some of them were disgusted; and his enemies were not reconciled, but ascribed all his caresses and favors to artifice and necessity.

* Burnet, Mem.

* * Burnet, Mem.

* * * Clarendon, vol. ii .

Argyle and Hamilton, being seized with an apprehension, real or pretended, that the earl of Crawfurd and others meant to assassinate them, left the parliament suddenly, and retired into the country; but upon invitation and assurances, returned in a few days. This event, which had neither cause nor effect that was visible, nor purpose, nor consequence, was commonly denominated the incident. But though the incident had no effect In Scotland; what was not expected, it was attended with consequences in England. The English parliament, which was now assembled, being willing to awaken the people’s tenderness by exciting their fears, immediately took the alarm; as if the malignants — so they called the king’s party — had had laid a plot at once to murder them and all the godly in both kingdoms. They applied therefore to Essex, whom the king had left general in the south of England; and he ordered a guard to attend them. [1]

But while the king was employed in pacifying the commotions in Scotland, and was preparing to return to England, in order to apply himself to the same salutary work in that kingdom, he received intelligence of a dangerous rebellion broken but in Ireland, with circumstances of the utmost horror, bloodshed, and devastation. On every side this unfortunate prince was pursued with murmurs, discontent, faction, and civil wars, and the fire from all quarters, even by the most independent accidents, at once blazed up about him.

The great plan of James in the administration of Ireland, continued by Charles, was, by justice and peace to reconcile that turbulent people to the authority of laws; and, introducing art and industry among them, to cure them of that sloth and barbarism to which they had ever been subject. In order to serve both these purposes, and at the same time secure the dominion of Ireland to the English crown, great colonies of British had been carried over, and, being intermixed with the Irish, had every where introduced a new face of things into that country. During a peace of near forty years, the inveterate quarrels between the nations seemed, in a great measure, to be obliterated; and though much of the landed property forfeited by rebellion had been conferred on the new planters, a more than equal return had been made, by their instructing the natives in tillage, building, manufactures, and all the civilized arts of life. [2] This had been the course of things during the successive administrations of Chichester, Grandison, Falkland, and, above all, of Strafford. Under the government of this latter nobleman, the pacific plans, now come to great maturity, and forwarded by his vigor and industry, seemed to have operated with full success, and to have bestowed at last on that savage country the face of a European settlement.

* Whitlocke, . Dugdale, . Burnet’s Memoirs of the House of Hamilton, , 185. Clarendon, vol. ii. .

* * Sir John Temple’s Irish Rebellion, .

<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CARLO I.

1641.

Gli scozzesi, che avevano scatenato queste fatali turbolenze, credevano di aver compiuto un’impresa molto pericolosa ma estremamente vantaggiosa per loro in termini di profitto e reputazione. Oltre alla generosa retribuzione concordata per il periodo di dodici mesi trascorso in luoghi sicuri, il parlamento inglese aveva anche concesso loro trecentomila sterline come ringraziamento per il loro “fratellolesco aiuto”. Negli accordi di pace veniva dichiarato che gli scozzesi fossero sempre stati sudditi fedeli; inoltre, le loro spedizioni militari venivano considerate imprese volte ad onorare e vantaggiare la maestà reale. Per celebrare ulteriormente questa vittoria sui loro sovrani, tali termini, così umilianti per questi ultimi, furono ordinati dal parlamento di essere letti in tutte le chiese nel giorno della ringrazianza dedicato alla pacificazione nazionale; vennero inoltre accettate tutte le loro richieste relative alla limitazione dei poteri sovrani. E ciò che valeva più di tutti questi vantaggi era la prospettiva concreta di diffondere nella Gran Bretagna e in Irlanda la disciplina presbiteriana, grazie ai semi delle loro idee religiose. Mai l’affinata Atene si era rallegrata tanto per aver diffuso le scienze e le arti liberali in un mondo barbaro; mai la generosa Roma si era compiaciuta tanto nel vedere stabilite legge e ordine grazie alle sue armi vittoriose. Come gli scozzesi, ora gioivano nel trasmettere il loro zelo barbarico e il loro fervore teologico ai popoli vicini.

* Nalson, vol. I. Maggio.

* * Rush, volume V. Clarendon, volume II.

Carlo, privato in Inghilterra di una parte considerevole del proprio potere e temendo ulteriori limitazioni ai propri diritti, giunse in Scozia con l’intenzione di abdicare quasi completamente al poco potere che gli rimaneva e di soddisfare, se possibile, le richieste dei suoi sudditi in quel regno.

I “lordi degli articoli” erano un’antica istituzione del parlamento scozzese. Venivano eletti nel seguente modo: i lord temporali sceglievano otto vescovi; questi, a loro volta, eleggevano altri otto lord temporali; insieme, questi sedici individui nominavano otto commissari per le contee e otto borghesi. Senza il previo consenso dei trentadue membri denominati “lordi degli articoli”, nessuna proposta poteva essere presentata in parlamento. Poiché i vescovi erano interamente fedeli alla corte reale, era evidente che tutti i “lordi degli articoli” dipendessero necessariamente dalla nomina del re; inoltre, il principe possedeva un’altra prerogativa ancora più importante: dopo l’approvazione delle proposte in parlamento, aveva il potere di opporsi a esse. Ora che la carica dei vescovi è stata abolita, il parlamento ha sfruttato questa opportunità per eliminare completamente i “lordi degli articoli”; fino al raggiungimento di questo risultato, si può dire che la nazione non godesse di alcuna vera e propria [libertà](/concepts/freedom). [1]

È degno di nota che, nonostante l’esistenza di questa istituzione, la quale non ha alcun equivalente in Inghilterra, l’autorità reale fosse sempre ritenuta molto più limitata in Scozia rispetto al regno precedente. Bacon considerava questo aspetto uno dei vantaggi derivanti dall’unione: le eccessive prerogative dell’Inghilterra sarebbero state ridotte dall’esempio della Scozia, mentre le troppo ristrette prerogative della Scozia sarebbero state ampliate imitando l’Inghilterra. All’epoca gli inglesi erano un popolo civile e obbediente alle leggi; ma in Scozia non aveva alcuna importanza il modo in cui queste venivano redatte o da chi venivano votate, poiché l’eccessiva aristocrazia aveva il potere di impedirne l’applicazione regolare.

I nobili e i comuni costituivano un’unica camera nel parlamento scozzese; poiché era stata prassi di Giacomo, continuata da Carlo, conferire titoli scozzesi ai gentiluomini inglesi, si temeva che tutte le decisioni del parlamento dipendessero, col tempo, dal principe, attraverso questi voti di stranieri che non possedevano alcun interesse né proprietà nel paese. Fu quindi emanato un decreto che approvava l’idea secondo cui nessuno potesse essere nominato nobile scozzese se non possedesse almeno diecimila marchi (equivalenti a oltre cinquecento sterline) di reddito annuo nel regno. [2]

Fu inoltre approvata una legge che prevedeva la convocazione di parlamenti ogni tre anni; venne inoltre stabilito che l’ultima attività di ogni parlamento fosse quella di designare il luogo e la data della successiva sessione. [3]

* Burnet, Memorie.*

* * Burnet, Memorie.

* * * Burnet, Memorie.

Al re fu revocato quel potere che in precedenza gli permetteva di emettere proclamazioni che imponevano obbedienza sotto pena di tradimento; una prerogativa che gli conferiva l’intera autorità legislativa, anche su questioni di estrema importanza. [1]

Fino a quel punto tutto era lodevole; ma il colpo più fatale inflitto all’autorità reale, e ciò che di fatto degradò il principe dal suo ruolo di sovrano, fu l’articolo che stabiliva che nessun membro del consiglio privato – nel cui pugno, in assenza del re, ricadeva l’intera amministrazione – né alcun funzionario di stato, né giudice potesse essere nominato se non su consiglio e approvazione del parlamento. Carlo acconsentì persino a privare dei loro incarichi quattro giudici che avevano sostenuto i suoi interessi; al loro posto furono nominati altri più graditi al partito al potere. Anche diversi membri dei Covenanters furono espulsi dal consiglio privato. Inoltre, tutti i ministri di stato, i consiglieri e i giudici erano obbligati, per legge, a mantenere le loro cariche per tutta la vita o finché non si fossero comportati in modo indegno. [2]

Il re, durante la sua permanenza in Scozia, si attenne completamente alle pratiche della chiesa ufficiale e partecipò con grande serietà alle lunghe preghiere e ai lunghi sermoni con cui i presbiteriani cercavano di compiacerlo. Concedette pensioni e favori a Henderson, Gillespy e ad altri predicatori popolari, e adottò ogni mezzo possibile per addolcire, se non per conquistare, i suoi più grandi nemici. L’ conte di Argyle fu elevato al rango di marchese, Lord Loudon a quello di conte, mentre Lesley ricevette il titolo di conte di Leven. Per il momento, fu costretto a trascurare e ignorare i propri amici: alcuni di loro erano disgustati; i suoi nemici, invece, non si riconciliarono con lui, attribuendo tutte le sue attenzioni e favori a calcoli strategici o a necessità pratiche.

* Burnet, Memorie.*

* * Burnet, Memorie.

* * * Clarendon, vol. ii.

Argyle e Hamilton, presi da un timore reale o fingito che il conte di Crawfurd e altri avessero intenzione di assassinarli, lasciarono improvvisamente il parlamento e si ritirarono in campagna; ma su invito e dopo aver ricevuto garanzie, tornarono dopo pochi giorni. Questo evento, che non presentava né cause né conseguenze evidenti, fu comunemente definito “un incidente”. Tuttavia, sebbene quell’incidente non avesse alcuna ripercussione in Scozia, in Inghilterra ebbe conseguenze impreviste. Il parlamento inglese, allora riunito, volle suscitare la paura del popolo per destare la sua solidarietà; quindi dichiarò immediatamente lo stato di allarme, come se i nemici del re avessero pianificato di assassinare loro e tutti i fedeli in entrambi i regni. Chiesero quindi l’aiuto di Essex, che il re aveva nominato generale nel sud dell’Inghilterra; egli ordinò pertanto di fornire una scorta per proteggerli. [1]

Ma mentre il re era impegnato a placare le rivolte in Scozia e si preparava a tornare in Inghilterra per proseguire lo stesso lavoro benefico in quel regno, ricevette notizie di una pericolosa ribellione scoppiata in Irlanda, caratterizzata da circostanze estremamente orribili: spargimento di sangue e devastazione. Da ogni parte, questo sfortunato principe era assediato da mormori, dissenso, fazioni e guerre civili; il fuoco della discordia, alimentato anche da eventi casuali, si accese improvvisamente intorno a lui.

Il grande piano di Giacomo per la amministrazione dell’Irlanda, continuato da Carlo, consisteva nel riconciliare quel popolo turbolento con l’autorità delle leggi attraverso giustizia e pace; inoltre, introducendo tra loro arte e industria, si mirava a eliminare la pigrizia e il barbarismo che caratterizzavano quella nazione. Per realizzare entrambi questi obiettivi e al contempo assicurarsi il dominio dell’Irlanda alla corona inglese, furono insediati numerosi coloni britannici i quali, mescolandosi con gli irlandesi, introdussero in quel paese nuovi modelli di organizzazione sociale. Durante un periodo di pace durato quasi quarant’anni, le continue lotte tra le due nazioni sembrarono in gran parte essere scomparse; e sebbene gran parte delle proprietà terriere confiscate a causa dei ribelli fosse stata assegnata ai nuovi coloni, questi ultimi ottennero un risultato ancora più significativo insegnando ai nativi l’agricoltura, la costruzione, le arti manifatturiere e tutte le altre pratiche della vita civile. Questo fu il corso degli eventi durante le successive amministrazioni di Chichester, Grandison, Falkland e, soprattutto, di Strafford. Sotto il governo di quest’ultimo nobile, i piani pacifici, ormai giunti a piena maturità grazie alla sua energia e al suo impegno, sembrarono aver avuto completo successo, conferendo finalmente a quella terra selvaggia l’aspetto di una colonia europea.

* Whitlocke. Dugdale. I Memorie della Casa di Hamilton di Burnet, pag. 185. Clarendon, vol. II.

* * La ribellione irlandese di Sir John Temple.

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="662" data-title="CHAPTER LV. (parte 2)" data-chapter="CHAPTER LV." data-kind="atom" data-srclang="en"></span>

After Strafford fell a victim to popular rage, the humors excited in Ireland by that great event could not suddenly be composed, but continued to produce the greatest innovations in the government.

The British Protestants transplanted into Ireland, having every moment before their eyes all the horrors of Popery, had naturally been carried into the opposite extreme, and had universally adopted the highest principles and practices of the Puritans. Monarchy, as well as the hierarchy, was become odious to them; and every [method](/axes/method) of limiting the authority of the crown, and detaching themselves from the king of England, was greedily adopted and pursued. They considered not, that as they scarcely formed the sixth part of the people, and were secretly obnoxious to the ancient inhabitants, their only method of supporting themselves was by maintaining royal authority, and preserving a great dependence on their mother country. The English commons, likewise, in their furious persecution of Strafford, had overlooked the most obvious consequences; and, while they imputed to him as a crime every discretionary act of authority, they despoiled all succeeding governors of that power by which alone the Irish could be retained in subjection. And so strong was the current for popular government in all the three kingdoms, that the most established maxims of policy were every where abandoned, in order to gratify this ruling passion.

Charles, unable to resist, had been obliged to yield to the Irish, as to the Scottish and English parliaments; and found, too, that their encroachments still rose in proportion to his concessions. Those subsidies which themselves had voted, they reduced, by a subsequent vote, to a fourth part; the court of high commission was determined to be a grievance; martial law abolished; the jurisdiction of the council annihilated; proclamations and acts of state declared of no authority; every order or institution which depended on monarchy was invaded; and the prince was despoiled of all his prerogative, without the least pretext of any violence or illegality in his administration.

The standing army of Ireland was usually about three thousand men; but, in order to assist the king in suppressing the Scottish Covenanters, Strafford had raised eight thousand more, and had incorporated with them a thousand men drawn from the old army; a necessary expedient for bestowing older and discipline on the new-levied soldiers. The private men in this army were all Catholics; but the officers, both commission and non-commission, were Protestants, and could entirely be depended on by Charles. The English commons entertained the greatest apprehensions on account of this army, and never ceased soliciting the king till he agreed to break it. Nor they consent to any proposal for augmenting the standing army to five thousand men; a number which the king deemed necessary for retaining Ireland in obedience.

Charles, thinking it dangerous that eight thousand men accustomed to idleness, and trained to the use of arms, should be dispersed among a nation so turbulent and unsettled, agreed with the Spanish ambassador to have them transported into Flanders, and enlisted in his master’s service. The English commons, pretending apprehensions, lest regular bodies of troops, disciplined in the Low Countries, should prove still more dangerous, showed some aversion to this expedient; and the king reduced his allowance to four thousand men. But when the Spaniards had hired ships for transporting these troops, and the men were ready to embark, the commons, willing to show their power, and not displeased with an opportunity of curbing and affronting the king, prohibited every one from furnishing vessels for that service. And thus the project formed by Charles, of freeing the country from these men was unfortunately disappointed. [1]

The old Irish remarked all these false steps of the English, and resolved to take advantage of them. Though their animosity against that nation, for want of an occasion to exert itself, seemed to be extinguished, it was only composed into a temporary and deceitful tranquillity. [2] Their interests, both with regard to property and religion, secretly stimulated them to a [revolt](/positions/revolution). No individual of any sept, according to the ancient customs, had the property of any particular estate; but as the whole sept had a title to a whole territory, they ignorantly preferred this barbarous community before the more secure and narrower possessions assigned them by the English. An indulgence, amounting almost to a [toleration](/positions/toleration), had been given to the Catholic religion: but so long as the churches and the ecclesiastical revenues were kept from the priests, and they were obliged to endure the neighborhood of profane heretics, being themselves discontented, they continually endeavored to retard any cordial reconciliation between the English and the Irish nations.

* Clarendon, vol. i. . Rush. vol. v. p, 381. Dugdale, May, book ii. .

* * Temple,

There was a gentleman called Roger More, who, though of a narrow fortune, was descended from an ancient Irish family and was much celebrated among his countrymen for valor and capacity. This man first formed the project of expelling the English, and asserting the independency of his native country. [1]

* Nalson, vol. iii. .

He secretly went from chieftain to chieftain, and roused up every latent principle of discontent. He maintained a close correspondence with Lord Maguire and Sir Phelim O’Neale, the most powerful of the old Irish. By conversation, by letters, by his emissaries, he represented to his countrymen the motives of a revolt. He observed to them, that, by the rebellion of the Scots, and factions of the English, the king’s authority in Britain was reduced to so low a condition, that he never could exert himself with any vigor in maintaining the English dominion over Ireland: that the Catholics in the Irish house of commons, assisted by the Protestants, had so diminished the royal prerogative and the power of the lieutenant, as would much facilitate the conducting to its desired effect any conspiracy or combination which could be formed: that the Scots, having so successfully thrown off dependence on the crown of England, and assumed the government into their own hands, had set an example to the Irish, who had so much greater oppressions to complain of: that the English planters, who had expelled them their possessions, suppressed their religion, and bereaved them of their liberties were but a handful in comparison of the natives: that they lived in the most supine security, interspersed with their numerous enemies, trusting to the protection of a small army, which was itself scattered in inconsiderable divisions through out the whole kingdom: that a great body of men, disciplined by the government, were now thrown loose, and were ready for any daring or desperate enterprise: that though the Catholics had hitherto enjoyed, in some tolerable measure, the exercise of their religion, from the moderation of their indulgent prince, they must henceforth expect that the government will be conducted by other maxims and other principles: that the Puritanical parliament, having at length subdued their sovereign, would no doubt, as soon as they had consolidated their authority, extend their ambitious enterprises to Ireland, and make the Catholics in that kingdom feel the same furious persecution, to which their brethren in England were at present exposed: and that a revolt in the Irish, tending only to vindicate their native liberty against the violence of foreign invaders, could never at any time be deemed rebellion, much less during the present confusions, when their prince was in a manner a prisoner, and obedience must be paid, not to him, but to those who had traitorously usurped his lawful authority. [1]

By these considerations, More engaged all the heads of the native Irish into the conspiracy. The English of the pale, as they were called, or the old English planters, being all Catholics, it was hoped would afterwards join the party which restored their religion to its ancient splendor and authority. The intention was, that Sir Phelim O’Neale and the other conspirators should begin an insurrection on one day throughout the provinces, and should attack all the English settlements; and that, on the same day, Lord Maguire and Roger More should surprise the Castle of Dublin. The commencement of the revolt was fixed on the approach of winter, that there might be more difficulty in transporting forces from England. Succors to themselves and supplies of arms they expected from France, in consequence of a promise made them by Cardinal Richelieu. And many Irish officers, who served in the Spanish troops, had engaged to join them, as soon as they saw an insurrection entered upon by their Catholic brethren. News, which every day arrived from England, of the fury expressed by the commons against all Papists, struck fresh terror into the Irish nation, and both stimulated the conspirators to execute their fatal purpose, and gave them assured hopes of the concurrence of all their country men. [2]

<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Dopo che Strafford divenne vittima della furia popolare, gli umori suscitati in Irlanda da quell’evento non poterono essere immediatamente placati; continuarono invece a generare le più grandi innovazioni nel [governo](/axes/method).

I protestanti britannici, trasferitisi in Irlanda e costantemente esposti agli orrori del papismo, erano naturalmente portati all’estremo opposto e adottarono universalmente i principi e le pratiche più rigorose dei puritani. La monarchia, così come la gerarchia ecclesiastica, divennero per loro oggetto di profondo disprezzo; ogni mezzo possibile per limitare l’autorità della corona e allontanarsi dal re d’Inghilterra fu accettato con entusiasmo. Tuttavia, essi non consideravano che, essendo soltanto una sesta parte della popolazione irlandese e odiati segretamente dagli abitanti autoctoni, l’unico modo per sopravvivere consisteva nel mantenere l’autorità reale e nel conservare un forte legame con la loro madrepatria. Anche i comuni inglesi, nella loro furiosa persecuzione di Strafford, trascurarono le conseguenze più evidenti delle loro azioni: mentre lo accusavano di ogni atto di autorità discrezionale, privarono tutti i governatori successivi della potere necessario per mantenere l’Irlanda sotto il dominio inglese. Così forte era la tendenza verso un governo popolare in tutti e tre i regni, che le più consolidate massime politiche furono abbandonate ovunque al solo scopo di soddisfare questa passione dominante.

Charles, incapace di resistere, fu costretto a cedere agli irlandesi, così come ai parlamenti scozzese ed inglese; inoltre si rese conto che le loro pretese aumentavano proporzionalmente alle sue concessioni. Quei sussidi che essi stessi avevano votato per concedere, venivano successivamente ridotti a un quarto del loro importo originale; la Corte della Alta Commissione fu dichiarata una fonte di ingiustizie; la legge marziale venne abolita; la giurisdizione del consiglio fu annullata; le proclamazioni e gli atti di stato furono riconosciuti come privi di qualsiasi autorità legittima; ogni ordinanza o istituzione legata alla monarchia veniva violata; e il principe si trovò privato di tutte le sue prerogative, senza che vi fosse alcun pretesto legato a violenza o illegalità nelle sue azioni.

L’esercito permanente d’Irlanda contava solitamente circa tremila uomini; tuttavia, al fine di aiutare il re a sopprimere i Covenanters scozzesi, Strafford ne aveva arruolati altri ottomila, incorporando tra loro mille soldati provenienti dall’esercito precedente: una misura necessaria per conferire maggiore esperienza e disciplina ai nuovi reclutati. Gli uomini semplici che componevano quest’esercito erano tutti cattolici; gli ufficiali, sia di grado elevato che inferiore, invece erano protestanti, e potevano quindi essere completamente affidabili da parte di Carlo. I membri del Parlamento inglese nutrivano grandi preoccupazioni riguardo a quest’esercito, e non cessarono mai di sollecitare il re affinché lo sciogliesse. Non acconsentirono nemmeno a alcuna proposta volta ad aumentare le dimensioni dell’esercito permanente a cinquemila uomini: una cifra che il re riteneva necessaria per mantenere l’Irlanda sotto il suo controllo.

Carlo, ritenendo pericoloso che ottemila uomini abituati all’ozio e addestrati all’uso delle armi venissero dispersi in una nazione così turbolenta e instabile, concordò con l’ambasciatore spagnolo nel farli trasportare in Fiandra affinché si arruolassero al servizio del loro sovrano. I comuni inglesi, fingendo di temere che truppe regolari e disciplinate nei Paesi Bassi potessero rivelarsi ancora più pericolose, mostrarono qualche avversione verso questa soluzione; il re ridusse quindi il numero degli uomini da trasportare a quattromila. Tuttavia, quando gli spagnoli noleggiarono navi per il trasporto di queste truppe e gli uomini furono pronti a imbarcarsi, i comuni, desiderosi di dimostrare la loro forza e non dispiaciuti dell’opportunità di limitare l’autorità del re, proibirono a chiunque di fornire navi per tale scopo. E così il piano di Carlo, volto a liberare il paese da questi uomini, fallì sfortunatamente. [1]

Gli antichi irlandesi osservavano attentamente tutti questi errori e sbagli degli inglesi e decisero di approfittarne. Sebbene il loro odio verso quella nazione, a causa della mancanza di occasioni per manifestarsi, sembrasse essersi estinto, in realtà si era soltanto trasformato in una tranquillità temporanea e ingannevole. I loro interessi, sia in termini di proprietà che di religione, li spingevano segretamente verso una [rivolta](/positions/revolution). Secondo le antiche usanze, nessun individuo all’interno di un clan possedeva una proprietà specifica; tuttavia, poiché l’intero clan aveva diritto su un intero territorio, preferivano ignorantemente questa forma di comunità barbarica alle proprietà più sicure e limitate che gli inglesi импоневали loro. Alla religione cattolica veniva concessa una sorta di [tolleranza](/positions/toleration); tuttavia, poiché le chiese e i redditi ecclesiastici venivano sottratti ai preti, e questi erano costretti a convivere con eretici profani, essi stessi, essendo insoddisfatti, si impegnavano costantemente per ostacolare qualsiasi riconciliazione sincera tra gli inglesi e gli irlandesi.

* Clarendon, vol. I. Rush, vol. V, p. 381. Dugdale, maggio, libro II.

* * Tempio,

C’era un gentiluomo di nome Roger More che, sebbene possedesse una fortuna modesta, discendeva da un’antica famiglia irlandese ed era molto stimato dai suoi connazionali per il suo coraggio e le sue capacità. Fu lui ad ideare per primo il progetto di scacciare gli inglesi e affermare l’indipendenza della sua patria natale. [1]

* Nalson, vol. III.*

Si recò segretamente da un capo all’altro, risvegliando ogni principio latente di insoddisfazione. Mantenne una stretta corrispondenza con Lord Maguire e Sir Phelim O’Neale, i più potenti tra gli irlandesi dell’epoca. Attraverso conversazioni, lettere e i suoi emissari, fece comprendere ai suoi connazionali le motivazioni di una rivolta. Spiegò loro che, a causa della ribellione degli scozzesi e delle fazioni inglesi, l’autorità del re in Britannia era stata ridotta al punto che egli non poteva più esercitare con efficacia il dominio inglese sull’Irlanda; che i cattolici presenti nella Camera dei Comuni irlandese, con il sostegno dei protestanti, avevano così indebolito le prerogative reali e il potere del luogotenente da rendere molto più facile attuare qualsiasi complotto o alleanza avesse potuto essere formato; che gli scozzesi, essendo riusciti con successo a liberarsi dalla dipendenza dalla corona inglese e ad assumersi il governo in proprio pugno, avevano dato l’esempio agli irlandesi, i quali soffrivano di oppressioni ancora più gravi; che gli coloni inglesi, che li avevano espulsi dalle loro proprietà, soppresso la loro religione e privati delle loro libertà, erano in realtà una minoranza rispetto ai nativi; che vivevano in una condizione di totale sicurezza, circondati da numerosi nemici, affidandosi alla protezione di un esercito ridotto e disperso in varie parti del regno; che un gran numero di persone, fino ad allora disciplinate dal governo, era ora libero di intraprendere qualsiasi azione audace o disperata; che, sebbene i cattolici avessero finora potuto praticare la loro religione in modo tollerabile grazie alla moderazione del loro sovrano, da quel momento in poi si poteva aspettarsi che il governo seguisse principi diversi; che il parlamento puritano, una volta consolidata la propria autorità, avrebbe sicuramente esteso le sue ambizioni anche all’Irlanda, facendo sì che i cattolici di quel regno subissero lo stesso tipo di persecuzioni a cui erano esposti i loro fratelli in Inghilterra; e che una rivolta irlandese, volta soltanto a difendere la propria libertà contro l’oppressione degli invasori stranieri, non poteva mai essere considerata ribellione, soprattutto nelle attuali condizioni di caos, quando il loro sovrano era praticamente prigioniero e l’obbedienza doveva essere resa non a lui, ma a coloro che avevano traditoriamente usurpato la sua legittima autorità. [1]

Sulla base di queste considerazioni, More riuscì a coinvolgere tutti i capi del popolo irlandese nella congiura. Gli inglesi della “pale”, come venivano chiamati, ovvero gli antichi coloni anglofoni, essendo tutti cattolici, si sperava che in seguito si unissero al partito che avrebbe restituito alla loro religione il suo antico splendore e autorità. L’intenzione era che Sir Phelim O’Neale e gli altri congiurati scatenassero una rivolta in tutte le province nello stesso giorno, attaccando tutte le colonie inglesi; nel contempo, Lord Maguire e Roger More avrebbero assaltato il Castello di Dublino. L’inizio della rivolta era stato fissato all’avvicinarsi dell’inverno, affinché fosse più difficile trasportare truppe dall’Inghilterra. Per quanto riguarda i rifornimenti e le armi, si contava sull’aiuto della Francia, in seguito a una promessa fatta loro dal Cardinale Richelieu. Inoltre, molti ufficiali irlandesi che prestavano servizio nelle truppe spagnole avevano promesso di unirsi a loro non appena avessero visto i loro connazionali cattolici iniziare la rivolta. Le notizie che arrivavano ogni giorno dall’Inghilterra, riguardanti l’odio profondo dei cittadini comuni verso tutti i papisti, incutevano nuovo terrore nel popolo irlandese; queste notizie, oltre a incoraggiare i congiurati ad attuare il loro piano, gli davano la certezza del sostegno di tutti i loro connazionali. [2]

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="663" data-title="CHAPTER LV. (parte 3)" data-chapter="CHAPTER LV." data-kind="atom" data-srclang="en" data-tags="assi/human_nature,concepts/religion,concepts/compassion,concepts/suffering"></span>

Such propensity to a [revolt](/positions/revolution) was discovered in all the Irish, that it was deemed unnecessary, as it was dangerous to intrust the secret to many hands; and the appointed day drew nigh, nor had any discovery been yet made to the government. The king, indeed, had received information from his ambassadors, that something was in agitation among the Irish in foreign parts; but though he gave warning to the administration in Ireland, the intelligence was entirely neglected. [3]

* Temple, , 73, 78. Dugdale, .

* * Dugdale, .

* * * Bush vol. v. . Nalson, vol ii. .

Secret rumors likewise were heard of some approaching conspiracy; but no attention was paid to them. The earl of Leicester, whom the king had appointed lieutenant, remained in London, The two justices, Sir William Parsons and Sir John Borlace, were men of small abilities; and, by an inconvenience common to all factious times, owed their advancement to nothing but their zeal for the party by whom every thing was now governed. Tranquil from their ignorance and inexperience, these men indulged themselves in the most profound repose, on the very brink of destruction.

But they were awakened from their security on the very day before that which was appointed for the commencement of hostilities. The Castle of Dublin, by which the capital was commanded, contained arms for ten thousand men, with thirty-five pieces of cannon, and a proportionable quantity of ammunition; yet was this important place guarded, and that too without any care, by no greater force than fifty men. Maguire and More were already in town with a numerous band of their partisans; others were expected that night and next morning they were to enter upon what they esteemed the easiest of all enterprises, the surprisal of the castle. O’Conolly, an Irishman, but a Protestant, betrayed the conspiracy to Parsons. [1] The justices and council fled immediately for safety into the castle, and reënforced the guards. The alarm was conveyed to the city, and all the Protestants prepared for defence. More escaped; Maguire was taken; and Mahone, one of the conspirators, being likewise seized, first discovered to the justices the project of a general insurrection, and redoubled the apprehensions which already were universally diffused throughout Dublin. [2]

But though O’Conolly’s discovery saved the castle from a surprise, the confession extorted from Mahone came too late to prevent the intended insurrection. O’Neale and his Confederates had already taken arms in Ulster. The Irish, every where intermingled with the English, needed but a hint from their leaders and priests to begin hostilities against a people whom they hated on account of their religion, and envied for their riches and prosperity. [3]

* Rush, vol. v. . Nalson, vol. ii. . May, book ii

* * Temple p 17, 18, 19, 20. Rush. vol. v .

* * * Ten ple, , 40, 79.

The houses, cattle, goods, of the unwary English were first seized. Those who heard of the commotions in their neighborhood, instead of deserting their habitations, and assembling for mutual protection, remained at home in hopes of defending their property, and fell thus separately into the hands of their enemies. [1] After rapacity had fully exerted itself, cruelty, and the most barbarous that ever in any nation was known or heard of, began its operations. A universal massacre commenced of the English, now defenceless, and passively resigned to their inhuman foes. No age, no sex, no condition was spared. The wife weeping for her butchered husband, and embracing her helpless children, was pierced with them, and perished by the same stroke. [2] The old, the young, the vigorous, the infirm, underwent a like fate, and were confounded in one common ruin. In vain did flight save from the first assault: destruction was every where let loose, and met the hunted victims at every turn. In vain was recourse had to relations, to companions, to friends: all connections were dissolved, and death was dealt by that hand from which protection was implored and expected. Without provocation, without opposition, the astonished English, living in profound peace and full security were massacred by their nearest neighbors, with whom they had long upheld a continued intercourse of kindness and good offices. [3]

But death was the lightest punishment inflicted by those rebels. All the tortures which wanton cruelty could devise all the lingering pains of body, the anguish of mind, the agonies of despair, could not satiate revenge excited without injury, and cruelty derived from no cause. To enter into particulars would shock the least delicate humanity. Such enormities, though attested by undoubted evidence, appear almost incredible. Depraved nature, even perverted religion encouraged by the utmost license, reach not to such a pitch of ferocity, unless the pity inherent in human breasts be destroyed by that contagion of example which transports men beyond all the usual motives of conduct and behavior.

The weaker sex themselves, naturally tender to their own sufferings, and compassionate to those of others, here emulated their more robust companions in the practice of every cruelty. [4] Even children, taught by the example and encouraged by the exhortation of their parents, essayed their feeble blows on the dead carcasses or defenceless children of the English.

* Temple, .

* * Temple, .

* * * Temple, , 40

* * * * Temple, , 101. Rush. vol. v. .

v Temple,

The very avarice of the Irish was not a sufficient restraint to their cruelty. Such was their frenzy, that the cattle which they had seized, and by rapine made their own, yet, because they bore the name of English, were wantonly slaughtered, or, when covered with wounds, turned loose into the woods or deserts. [1]

The stately buildings or commodious habitations of the planters, as if upbraiding the sloth and ignorance of the natives, were consumed with fire, or laid level with the ground. And where the miserable owners, shut up in their houses, and preparing for defence, perished in the flames, together with their wives and children, a double triumph was afforded to their insulting foes. [2]

If any where a number assembled together, and, assuming courage from despair, were resolved to sweeten death by revenge on their assassins, they were disarmed by capitulations and promises of safety, confirmed by the most solemn oaths. But no sooner had they surrendered, than the rebels, with perfidy equal to their cruelty, made them share the fate of their unhappy countrymen. [3]

Others, more ingenious still in their barbarity, tempted their prisoners, by the fond love of life, to imbrue their hands in the blood of friends, brothers, parents; and having thus rendered them accomplices in guilt, gave them that death which they sought to shun by deserving it. [4]

Amidst all these enormities, the sacred name of religion resounded on every side; not to stop the hands of these murderers, but to enforce their blows, and to steel their hearts against every movement of human or social [sympathy](/positions/moral_sentiment). The English, as heretics, abhorred of God and detestable to all holy men, were marked out by the priests for slaughter; and of all actions, to rid the world of these declared enemies to Catholic faith and piety, was represented as the most meritorious. Nature, which in that rude people was sufficiently inclined to atrocious deeds, was further stimulated by precept: and national prejudices empoisoned by those aversions, more deadly and incurable, which arose from an enraged superstition. While death finished the sufferings of each victim, the bigoted assassins, with joy and exultation, still echoed in his expiring ears, that these agonies were but the commencement of torments infinite and eternal.[v*]

* Temple, .

* * Temple, , 106. Rash. vol. v.

* * * Whitlocke, . Rush. vol. v. .

* * * * Temple, p 100.

v Temple, , 106.

v* Temple, p 94, 107, 108. Rush. vol. v. .
